s: Target picture, guiding principles, target audiences, glossary, node lifecycle, roles, scaling tiers and scope of "Das Cloud Projekt" (DCP).
h: Open questions at the time of the vision
x: Target picture # Das Cloud Projekt ( DCP for short) is an open-source, decentralized cloud platform . It takes in arbitrary hardware – from a Raspberry Pi to laptops to rack servers – over a network cable and turns it into a multi-tenant cloud with the core services of a hyperscaler . It covers everything from a two-node homelab to a data center with thousands of nodes. The short version for outsiders: Plug in the cable – node appears – approve – assign a role – done. Everything via portal, API or MCP. What "hyperscaler-like" means in concrete terms # Category Platform service Roughly equivalent to Compute Virtual machines AWS EC2, Azure VMs, GCE Compute Container Instances Azure Container Instances, Cloud Run, Fargate Compute Managed Kubernetes EKS, AKS, GKE Storage Block volumes EBS, Managed Disks, Persistent Disk Storage Object storage (S3-compatible) S3, Blob Storage, GCS Network VPCs, subnets, security groups, load balancers, floating IPs VPC, VNet Identity Tenants, projects, users, roles, API keys IAM, Entra ID, Cloud IAM Platform Registry, KMS, monitoring, audit log ECR, KMS, CloudWatch, CloudTrail Later expansion stages add databases, secrets, DNS, queues, serverless, file storage and GPU/NPU accelerators (see Hyperscaler analysis and AI platform ). Guiding principles # Decentralized, no central controller. Every node runs the agent; portal, API and MCP run on the hardware they manage. If a node fails, another one takes over. API-first, three equivalent access paths. Every function at every level is available via API, web portal and MCP – including initial setup and adoption. The API is the single source of truth (see API-first ). Zero-touch after the cable. Once plugged in, no screen, keyboard or SSH is needed. The only deliberate action is the approval (adoption) – or an auto-adopt rule. Auto-adopt is disabled by default and only permitted permanently with hardware attestation. Scales in both directions. Two nodes are a full-fledged operating mode, not a demo. Growth to thousands of nodes happens through cells and regions, without reinstalling. Heterogeneous from day one. ARM64 and x86_64 mixed; nodes with and without a BMC, with little and lots of RAM. Declarative and self-healing. The desired state is described; reconcilers bring it about. Immutable nodes. Image-based operating system with A/B updates; no manual maintenance on nodes (see OS image ). Secure & compliant by design. mTLS everywhere, tenant isolation at every layer, logging of every change, exportable evidence for ISO 27001, BSI C5 and BSI IT-Grundschutz (see Compliance by design ). Open source throughout. Only open-source dependencies; in-house components in Rust (see Rust stack and License governance ). Integrate what is proven, build what is missing. No in-house hypervisor – the project builds the control plane, the automation and the unified interface. Target audiences and deployment scenarios # Tier Nodes Typical hardware Typical operator Distinctive feature Homelab 2–10 Pis, old laptops, mini PCs, 1–2 servers Individual, developer Two-node operation with witness; coexists with the router's DHCP; single site Edge / SMB 10–100 Mini PCs, servers Small company, association, school, branch office Multiple tenants, first compliance requirements Data center 100–10,000+ Rack servers with BMC Hosting provider, public authority, enterprise IT Cells and regions, multiple sites, operator certification (ISO 27001 / C5) The MVP focuses on the homelab . However, the architecture must not contain any decision that blocks the path to the data center. Terminology (glossary) # Infrastructure # Term Meaning Platform All regions of one operator taken together. Node A physical device running the agent; the smallest unit. Agent Rust service on every node: lifecycle, roles, local API/portal/MCP, request forwarding. Role Function a node performs (e.g. boot , control , compute-vm ). A node can have multiple roles. Roles are assigned, not installed. Control group Small, automatically elected set of nodes (3 or 5) with the control role that holds a cell's state via Raft consensus. Witness node Lightweight node (e.g. a Pi) that only votes, so that two-node clusters have a quorum. Cell Unit of failure and scaling with its own control group (guideline: up to about 500–1,000 nodes). Cells fail independently of one another. Region One or more cells at a site or federation sharing a network and a common region API. Site Physical location (homelab, data center room). Sites are connected via the WireGuard underlay. Federation Combination of several regions under one global identity and API (later expansion stage). Underlay Encrypted WireGuard mesh between nodes – the platform's transport network. Overlay / VPC Virtual, tenant-owned network on top of the underlay (see Network ). Boot service Role boot : proxyDHCP, iPXE/UEFI HTTP boot, Pi netboot, image delivery. Present multiple times, never a single point of failure. Organization and usage # Term Meaning Operator Runs the platform; manages hardware, regions and tenants. Tenant Organizationally and technically isolated customer with its own users, networks, keys and billing. Project Subdivision within a tenant; boundary for resources, quotas and permissions. Resource Anything managed via the API (node, VM, volume, VPC, bucket …). Every resource has a desired and an actual state. Service Offering to tenants (VM service, object storage …), implemented through roles on nodes. Quota Upper limit on resources per tenant or project. Scope Where an operation takes place: platform → region → cell → node (operator) or tenant → project → resource . At every level: API = portal = MCP. The Identity page describes the tenant and permission model in detail. Node lifecycle # Every node goes through a fixed lifecycle that is controlled entirely via API, portal or MCP: State Meaning Transition triggered by Discovered Device has sent a DHCP/boot request Plugging in the cable Inventoried Discovery image has booted and reported the hardware automatic Pending No auto-adopt match; waiting for approval automatic Adopted Approval granted or an auto-adopt rule matched Portal / API / MCP or rule Rejected Approval denied Portal / API / MCP Provisioned Identity and certificate issued, OS image rolled out automatic Active Roles assigned and healthy automatic Maintenance Drain: workloads are moved elsewhere Operator Degraded Health check failed; self-healing back to "Active" automatic Quarantine Integrity in doubt automatic, from any adopted state Decommissioned Data securely erased, certificate revoked Operator Key rules: Unknown hardware never automatically gets access to tenant data. Discovery runs in an isolated network or mode; only adoption assigns an identity (see Boot & adoption and Security model ). Quarantine can be reached directly from any adopted state (Provisioned, Active, Maintenance, Degraded) – not only via "Degraded". Triggers include attestation failures, anomaly findings, a mismatched hardware fingerprint or the same node identity appearing twice; in the latter case both nodes are quarantined. The way back from quarantine to "Active" requires fresh attestation and human approval . Decommissioning includes verifiable erasure (BSI CON.6, ISO 27001 A.7.14) – a compliance-relevant step. Non-goals # No in-house hypervisor, no in-house database, no distributed file system from scratch – proven components such as Cloud Hypervisor are integrated. Clarification from 2026-11-14: block and object storage based on the platform Raft and an in-house chunk layer are in-house developments (block replication using a primary-copy scheme is not a distributed file system). Ceph is not a mandatory component , only an optional external driver for data centers that already run Ceph (see Storage ). No API compatibility with AWS, Azure or GCP – the exception is the S3-compatible object storage; tooling integration is via OpenTofu/Terraform providers. No network boot over Wi-Fi – onboarding requires Ethernet (Wi-Fi nodes possibly later via a boot stick). No proprietary dependencies , not even mandatory "open core" components. No Kubernetes distribution – Kubernetes is a service of the platform, not its foundation. No hardware without 64-bit support – Pi 1, Pi 2 and Pi Zero W are excluded; a Pi Zero 2 W is only suitable as a witness via boot stick. s: Architecture decision on the agent's Rust libraries – runtime, APIs, consensus, gossip, TLS, persistence, testing, supply chain, toolchain and licenses.
h: Open points at the time of the decision
x: Status: accepted (review 2026-11-12). Version information reflects the state as of November 2026; the project's locked dependency list is authoritative in each case. Context # Rust is settled as the implementation language. This architecture decision (ADR) defines which libraries (crates) form the foundation of the agent. The choice is long-lived: the async runtime, consensus, gossip, persistence and wire formats can only be replaced later with considerable effort. The constraints follow from the Vision : Requirement Consequence for the stack One agent on every node (from a Pi with a small memory budget to a server) Small memory footprint, a single statically linked binary, no JVM or Python runtime No central controller ; gossip for membership, Raft per cell Mature Raft library with membership changes, learners and witness support; SWIM-style gossip up to about 1,000 nodes per cell API = portal = MCP at every level One source of truth (Rust types) → OpenAPI → generated portal client and MCP tools ARM64 and x86_64 mixed All dependencies must build for both architectures; cross-compilation mTLS everywhere , BSI TR-02102, C5, Cyber Resilience Act Configurable TLS, in-house PKI, SBOM, vulnerability process Open source throughout OSI licenses only; make copyleft risks visible Distributed logic must be correct Deterministic simulation (network partitions, clocks, node failures) in CI Decision at a glance # Area Decision Fallback / alternative Async runtime tokio – (de facto standard) HTTP/REST axum with tower, tower-http, hyper – Internal gRPC tonic + prost – Consensus openraft raft-rs Gossip / membership foca (SWIM with Lifeguard ideas, I/O-free) chitchat (Scuttlebutt) TLS / mTLS rustls with aws-lc-rs as the only crypto provider – ( ring and OpenSSL excluded) Certificates rcgen (generation), x509-parser (validation) x509-cert OpenAPI utoipa (OpenAPI 3.1) aide JSON Schema schemars – MCP SDK rmcp (official SDK) – Local persistence redb (Raft log, state machine, key-value) SQLite for relational auxiliary data Serialization serde , serde_json, toml; prost on the wire; postcard for compact internal data – Netlink / WireGuard rtnetlink ; WireGuard via defguard_wireguard_rs (kernel WireGuard) wireguard-uapi Observability tracing + OpenTelemetry (OTLP) – Error handling thiserror in libraries, anyhow only in binaries/tests snafu Configuration Own lean layer of serde + toml + environment variables figment, config CLI clap (derive) with shell completions – Testing proptest , insta , cargo-nextest , turmoil + Raft simulator, loom madsim Supply chain cargo-deny , cargo-audit , cargo-auditable , cargo-cyclonedx , optionally cargo-vet – Cross-build cargo-zigbuild or musl targets cross Rationale by area # Runtime, REST and gRPC # tokio is the ecosystem standard; axum, tonic, rmcp, openraft and turmoil build on it. On Pi nodes, the number of worker threads is limited. io_uring-based runtimes (thread-per-core) are interesting for a future storage data path, not for the control plane. axum is tower-based and shares its middleware with tonic. It integrates best with utoipa and with the MCP SDK, whose Streamable HTTP server is itself a tower service. actix-web brings its own runtime layer; dropshot (Oxide) is instructive as a model for "API-first with OpenAPI generation", but has a smaller ecosystem. tonic is used for node ↔ node communication: Raft transport, forwarding requests to the control group, role agents. Protobuf schemas are language-neutral and versionable. gRPC is not a public contract – externally, the interface remains REST/JSON (see API-first ). Consensus: openraft # Criterion openraft raft-rs Architecture Async, event-driven, traits for storage and network, deterministic simulator Core state machine only, synchronous, bring your own log/network Features Joint consensus, learners, leader transfer, pre-vote, lease reads, snapshot streaming mature, but without I/O Maintenance very active hardly any releases anymore openraft is tokio-native, ships many building blocks ready to use (membership, learners as a precursor to the witness, snapshots, configurable quorum rules) and includes a deterministic simulator. Risk: the chosen major version was brand-new at the time of the decision, and 0.x versions break APIs. Mitigation: Raft is encapsulated behind an in-house consensus crate, the version is pinned and every upgrade is checked beforehand with Jepsen-style simulation tests. How the witness is implemented in two-node operation is described on the Control plane page. Gossip: foca # foca implements SWIM with parts of Lifeguard and incarnation numbers, is I/O-free and therefore ideal for deterministic simulation. Transport runs over the authenticated WireGuard underlay. This matches the principle "gossip only for membership, Raft for state". Bootstrapping before the underlay exists (discovery, adoption) deliberately does not use gossip, but the boot service and the adoption API. chitchat remains the fallback in case node metadata is to be distributed via gossip as replicated key-value state. TLS, mTLS and PKI # rustls is memory-safe and supports TLS 1.3 and hybrid post-quantum key exchange. aws-lc-rs is the only permitted crypto provider ; ring (no PQ key exchange, duplicate maintenance) and OpenSSL (C dependency) are banned by the supply-chain checks. rcgen generates the internal PKI: cell CA, node certificates at adoption, short lifetimes, automatic rotation. Private keys are zeroed after use; TPM integration will follow later. Alignment with BSI TR-02102 is complete: TLS 1.3 only, hybrid key agreement with ML-KEM preferred, secp curves permitted (Brainpool is not available in rustls/aws-lc-rs, which TR-02102 explicitly allows). Algorithms are never hard-coded, but selected via the active crypto profile (see Cryptography ). OpenAPI and MCP # utoipa generates OpenAPI 3.1 from attributes on handlers and types. To keep specification and code from drifting apart, the generated specification is checked in and compared via snapshot test; breaking changes are detected automatically. The generated OpenAPI file is the source for the portal client and the MCP tool catalog. rmcp is the official MCP SDK with the stdio and Streamable HTTP transports. The MCP server runs inside the agent under the same HTTP server, with the same authentication and authorization as the REST API. MCP tools are not handwritten but generated from the OpenAPI description – otherwise parity cannot be maintained. Because of its high release frequency, the version is pinned and updated quarterly. Persistence and serialization # redb is used for the Raft log, the Raft state machine (desired state of a cell's resources) and local node state: pure Rust, ACID, crash-safe, simple. SQLite is additionally permitted for local relational auxiliary data (e.g. audit buffer, inventory history). sled is excluded because its development has stalled. Raft log entries survive software upgrades, so an evolvable format (Protobuf) is preferred. Configuration files use TOML; the maintenance status of YAML libraries for Rust is currently unclear. bincode has been discontinued and is not used. Network, observability, errors, configuration, CLI # Network: rtnetlink for links, addresses, routes and bridges; defguard_wireguard_rs for the underlay (kernel WireGuard is included in the OS image ). Everything sits behind a trait abstraction so that tests run without root privileges. The overlay technology is not part of this decision (see Network ). An LGPL-licensed WireGuard library was excluded because of the relinking problem. Observability: tracing as the sole instrumentation API, exported via OpenTelemetry/OTLP. The audit log is separate from this: its own append-only, signed format. Errors: typed errors in all libraries; mapping to API errors in RFC 9457 format in exactly one place. Configuration: the agent deliberately has little local configuration – most of it arrives as desired state via the API and Raft. Only bootstrap values are needed locally. Order of precedence: defaults → configuration file → environment variables → command line; unknown keys are rejected. CLI: two binaries – the agent cp-agent (subcommands for operation, bootstrap, diagnostics) and the user CLI cpctl , which uses only the public REST API , via a client generated from OpenAPI. Testing and deterministic simulation # Distributed logic – gossip events, Raft integration, reconcilers, the adoption flow – is structured so that clock, randomness and network are injected . This way an entire cell runs under turmoil with a fixed seed in a single process. Every failing seed found is checked in as a regression test. In addition: property-based tests (reconcilers, quotas, IP allocation), snapshot tests (OpenAPI specification, MCP catalog, error messages) and exhaustive concurrency tests. Also mandatory are fuzzing for every parser at a trust boundary (netboot and discovery requests, certificates, API/MCP input, gRPC, metadata) with a nightly run, and a ban on unsafe code as the crate default; exceptions are justified and registered. Supply chain and Cyber Resilience Act # Tool Purpose When cargo-deny License allowlist, banned crates, permitted C bindings, sources, advisories every pull request cargo-audit RustSec advisories, also against shipped binaries every pull request and daily cargo-auditable Embed the dependency list in the binary every release build cargo-cyclonedx SBOM (CycloneDX) per binary every release cargo-vet Audits of dependencies from public releases onward cargo-semver-checks API compatibility of published libraries release In addition: locked dependencies, reproducible builds, signed artifacts, update metadata following the TUF pattern and targeted SLSA provenance (see Release signing and Vulnerability management ). Workspace structure # The workspace separates binaries (agent, user CLI, simulation environment) from library crates with clear responsibilities: resource model and types, REST API, MCP server, generated client, internal RPC, consensus, membership, storage layer, PKI, network, reconciler framework, roles, audit log, telemetry, configuration and test helpers. Guidelines: One agent binary for all roles – one image, one update path. Roles are runtime modules and can be disabled for minimal builds (e.g. a pure witness on a Pi Zero 2 W). Strict layering: the types crate depends on nothing internal to the project; roles know only interfaces, not the consensus or gossip library directly. External components only across a process boundary: Cloud Hypervisor, k3s, Garage and an optional Ceph driver are controlled as processes via API/CLI, never linked in as libraries. Each such process runs with its own user, minimal capabilities, systemd sandboxing, seccomp/Landlock and its own service identity. This prevents license mixing and creates clean update boundaries. Edition, MSRV and toolchain policy # Edition 2024 for all crates. Build toolchain pinned ; bumps happen deliberately via change request, at most every six weeks and no earlier than two weeks after a stable release. MSRV 1.95 at launch, driven by the WireGuard library. After that: MSRV at most "stable minus four releases" (about six months), checked in CI; MSRV-aware dependency resolution is enabled. The MSRV is primarily a signal to packagers; the project ships its own binaries anyway. Cross-compilation ARM64/AMD64 # Targets are Linux on aarch64 and x86_64 (glibc); for the agent in the immutable OS, optionally fully static with musl. Tool Assessment cargo-zigbuild Zig as linker/C compiler, selectable glibc version, no container needed – primary choice cross Container-based, robust for exotic C dependencies – fallback only Native builds on ARM64 and x86 runners in CI Simulation tests are architecture-independent; netlink and KVM integration tests run on real hardware (Pi 4/5, x86 nodes). C dependencies are minimized and controlled via an allowlist. The release profile uses maximum optimization with link-t

t: API-first – API, Portal and MCP as Equals
s: Why every function is first an API operation, how resources and operations are structured, and how the portal and MCP are derived from them and checked for parity.
h: Deriving the portal and MCP from the schema
Special cases: bootstrap and failure behavior
Example: "adopt node" via three access paths
x: Principle # Every platform function is first and foremost an API operation. The portal and MCP are two further representations of the same operation – never their own logic, never their own state. This applies without exception at every level (see the glossary in the Vision ): Area Levels Examples Operator Platform → region → cell → node Initial setup, adoption, assigning roles, drain, decommissioning, updates, creating cells Tenant Tenant → project → resource/service Users, roles, quotas, VM, volume, VPC, bucket, Kubernetes cluster Special cases Bootstrap, adoption First node without an identity service; approval of pending hardware The API is the single source of truth: The desired state of every resource exists only in the API and is stored in the control group of the responsible cell or region (see Control plane ). Apart from UI and session data, the portal and MCP hold no state of their own. The API schema is the sole definition of resources, fields, validation, permissions and documentation. Portal forms, MCP tools, the CLI, SDKs and the future OpenTofu provider are derived from it. There is no side channel : no portal-only switches, no configuration file on nodes that bypasses the API, no SSH by default. Emergency and diagnostic access are also API operations with special auditing: time-limited, justified and recorded diagnostic sessions and – only for the highest operator tier – SSH exclusively with short-lived certificates. Rationale # Otherwise parity cannot be maintained. Three hand-maintained access paths drift apart; ones generated from a single schema do not. Decentralization. Without a central controller, every node must serve the same interface – this is only possible if it is generated generically from the schema and embedded in the agent. Compliance. A single enforcement point for authentication, authorization, validation and the audit log (ISO 27001 A.8.15/A.8.16, BSI C5 OPS-10 ff., IT-Grundschutz OPS.1.1.5) instead of three. Automation. Infrastructure as code, GitOps and AI agents are first-class citizens. Testability. Every function can be tested without a browser; portal and MCP tests only verify the mapping. Resource model # The model is based on the Kubernetes API Conventions and the Google AIPs (resource-oriented design) – without using Kubernetes as its foundation. Structure of a resource # Every resource consists of three parts: metadata : name (chosen by the user, unique within the parent), immutable uid (UUIDv7, never reused), URN, parent, labels (selectable) and annotations, generation (incremented on every change to the desired state), resourceVersion for optimistic concurrency, timestamps, finalizers and owners. spec : the desired state – written by the user. status : the actual state – written only by the system, via a dedicated subresource that is open only to reconcilers. observedGeneration and conditions show whether the desired state has been reached. An abbreviated example: yaml apiVersion: compute.example.com/v1alpha1 kind: VirtualMachine metadata: name: web-01 urn: cp:eu-hl1:tenant/acme/project/shop/compute/vm/web-01 labels: { env: prod } generation: 7 spec: machineType: small-2c-4g arch: any # arm64 | x86_64 | any network: { vpc: default, subnet: web } status: phase: Running observedGeneration: 7 conditions: - type: Ready status: "True" Fields are classified in the schema: immutable, output only, required, sensitive (never returned or logged), personal data (for the data deletion concept), untrusted (freely populated by tenants or devices – normalized and never treated as an instruction or HTML) as well as the data class (metadata, content, IAM, audit, billing). Operator objects (node, cell, role, adoption rule) follow the same structure as tenant objects. A node , too, is a resource with a spec (roles, labels, maintenance flag) and a status (lifecycle phase, hardware inventory, health). Levels and resource names # Every resource has exactly one parent. This yields a hierarchical name and a globally unique URN : text cp:global:platform cp:eu-hl1:region cp:eu-hl1:cell/c1 cp:eu-hl1:node/n-17 cp:eu-hl1:discovery/d-8c1f2a cp:global:tenant/acme/project/shop cp:eu-hl1:tenant/acme/project/shop/compute/vm/web-01 The URN contains only what never changes over the resource's lifetime. Cell, rack or site are properties, not part of the URN; only the cell itself and objects inseparably bound to a cell carry cell/<c> . The second segment (region or global ) determines routing : every node derives from it which region or cell is responsible. Projects are named globally, their resources live regionally; data residency is controlled by project policy (permitted regions). The REST path can be mapped directly from the URN. Names follow the rules for DNS labels (lowercase letters, digits, hyphen, 1–63 characters). Permission scopes are the same path prefixes : a role binding on a project applies to everything beneath it (see Identity ). Versions # API groups are versioned independently. Until the MVP, all groups carry v1alpha1 ; the path via v1beta1 to v1 follows afterwards. Changes to the desired state are retained as revisions for audit and rollback (default 90 days). Operations # Standard methods # Method HTTP Semantics Get GET /v1/{name} single resource List GET /v1/{parent}/{kind} pagination, filtering, sorting Create POST /v1/{parent}/{kind}?id={name} name chosen by the client, idempotently retryable Update PATCH /v1/{name} JSON Merge Patch with If-Match Replace PUT /v1/{name} complete desired state (GitOps/OpenTofu) Delete DELETE /v1/{name} asynchronous with finalizers Actions # Anything that is not simply setting a field is an action with its own verb ( POST /v1/{name}:{verb} ), such as platform:initialize , discovery:adopt , node:drain , node:decommission , cell:split , region:rotateCa , tenant:suspend or vm:start . Where possible, actions are backed declaratively : node:drain internally sets the maintenance flag in the desired state – the action is a convenient, auditable declaration of intent, and the reconciler takes care of the rest. Long-running operations, watch and events # Every mutation that does not complete immediately responds with 202 Accepted and an Operation resource with progress and the current step. It can be queried, awaited and canceled, and is itself auditable – in the portal as a task list, in MCP as a task. Watch delivers a stream of changes (externally as server-sent events, internally as gRPC streaming) with resumption from a known version. Idempotency, concurrency and dry run # All mutating calls accept an Idempotency-Key ; the portal and MCP always set it – important for AI agents that retry calls. Optimistic concurrency via If-Match → 412 Precondition Failed on conflict. Dry run for every mutation ( ?validateOnly=true ): validates, checks permissions and quotas, computes the effects ("drain moves 4 VMs and 2 volumes") and changes nothing. Error format # All errors are returned as application/problem+json per RFC 9457 – with a stable, machine-readable code, localized title and detail (German/English), trace ID, field-level violations and a hint as to whether retrying makes sense. The portal shows field errors at the form field; MCP returns the problem object in structured form so that an AI agent can correct itself. Internal details such as stack traces never end up in error messages. Protocols: REST/OpenAPI externally, gRPC internally # External (users, portal, MCP, CLI, OpenTofu) Internal (agent ↔ agent, reconcilers) Protocol HTTPS/JSON, server-sent events for watch gRPC over mTLS in the WireGuard underlay Description OpenAPI 3.1 + JSON Schema 2020-12 Protobuf Authentication OIDC bearer tokens, API keys, setup token Node certificates plus the forwarded original token with DPoP proof One source: resource types are defined once as Rust types . OpenAPI, portal forms, MCP tools, the CLI and SDKs are generated from them. Protobuf is used only for internal node-to-node communication; API objects are carried in it as a versioned payload, not maintained as a second schema. Protobuf as the source with HTTP transcoding was rejected because the tooling for it in Rust is weak. The REST facade is not a second code path: validation and authorization happen in exactly one place (see Rust stack ). Versioning and deprecation # alpha can break without notice and is disabled by default; beta has at least six months or two releases of lead time; v1 permits only backward-compatible changes within the major version. GA fields have a deprecation period of at least 12 months , announced via Deprecation and Sunset headers, OpenAPI, the changelog, portal banners and notices in MCP. Breaking changes without a version bump fail CI. During rolling updates, a new API version is only activated once all members of the control group support it. Deriving the portal and MCP from the schema # OpenAPI and JSON Schema are generated from the schema; from these, in turn, the portal, MCP server, CLI, SDKs, OpenTofu provider, documentation and the parity check are derived. Schema annotations # The API description carries all the information the portal and MCP need – via project-specific schema extensions: level, display texts (de/en), input type, effect (read, create, update, destructive, irreversible), required permission, long-running yes/no, tool assignment, marking of untrusted fields, data class, and step-up and confirmation requirements. From these follow the navigation, form elements, confirmation dialogs and visible buttons in the portal, as well as tool descriptions, tool hints and confirmation requirements in MCP. Exceptions to derivation are only permitted with a justification; security-relevant annotations are enforced by lint. Portal # Generic core: list, detail, form and action dialogs are rendered at runtime from OpenAPI and JSON Schema. A new resource therefore appears in the portal automatically – with validation, help texts, permission checks and a dry-run preview. Curated where it makes sense: for key flows (initial setup, adoption, VPC topology, node map) there are hand-built views. They call only the public API – they may look nicer, but cannot do anything the API cannot. The portal is a static single-page app, embedded in the agent and served by every node, without a backend with special privileges (for the technology, see Portal ). MCP server # The MCP server is built into the agent and reachable on every node via Streamable HTTP (stateless per the current MCP specification); locally also via stdio through the CLI. Tool design – not every endpoint is a tool. Hundreds of fine-grained tools overwhelm language models. Instead, tools are grouped based on the annotations: Tool (example) Bundles cp_get , cp_list , cp_search all reads of all kinds cp_describe_schema schema of a resource kind cp_apply creating, updating, replacing any kind (with dry run) cp_delete deletion (with confirmation) node_lifecycle adopt, reject, drain, decommission, restart cluster_topology cell, region, control group tenant_admin tenant, project, users, roles, quotas operation_wait track long-running operations Every tool has an input and output schema and returns structured data plus a short text summary. The tool list is dynamic : it contains only tools the token has permissions for; a tenant token does not see node tools. MCP resources make objects, events, inventory and the audit log available read-only; MCP prompts correspond to the portal wizards (e.g. first installation, onboarding a node, creating a project, analyzing an incident). Follow-up questions and confirmations use elicitation. Destructive and irreversible actions, privileged IAM changes and adoption require confirmation on a platform page outside the AI client (out-of-band). Special cases: bootstrap and failure behavior # The first node # For the first node there is neither an identity service nor a control group – yet setup must still work via all three access paths. The node boots from the US

s: Agent, gossip membership (SWIM), Raft consensus per cell, two-node operation with witness, cells and regions, reconcilers, bootstrap and failure behavior.
h: State: one Raft group per cell
x: The control plane is the heart of DCP: it holds the desired state of all resources, decides on placement and membership, and enforces both on the nodes – without a central controller . Terms such as node, cell, control group and witness are explained in the Vision ; the chosen libraries in the Rust stack . Core decisions # # Decision 1 One agent process per node , roles as runtime modules. External components (Cloud Hypervisor, Garage, k3s …) run as separate systemd units controlled by the agent. 2 Two levels of truth: Raft (per cell) for desired state, assignments, leases and relevant status transitions; gossip (SWIM, per cell) for membership, reachability and fast-changing metadata. Gossip never triggers a destructive action on its own. 3 The control group is elected automatically: 1 → 2 data nodes + witness → 3 → 5 voters, never 7. New members always start as learners ; at most one membership change at a time. 4 The witness is a full but lightweight voter that never becomes leader. The default is the blind witness , which receives only hashes instead of payload data. 5 Single-node fallback operation is read-only. Writes resume only with a quorum – or via a local emergency override with recovery key and audit, never automatically. 6 Cell guideline ≤ 1,000 nodes (warning threshold 500; with Pi control nodes ≤ 100). Region data lives in its own small Raft group, which "collapses" into the cell group when there is only one cell. 7 Routing by URN: region from the URN, cell from a versioned shard map. 8 Reconcilers are level-triggered, idempotent and fenced: cell controllers run as shards with leases in Raft; stale writes are discarded. 9 Static stability: a control plane outage does not stop running workloads. The agent # Process model # One binary, one main process , started and supervised by systemd (watchdog, automatic restart). On a panic the agent restarts rather than continuing in a half-broken state. Raft and gossip run in a separate, high-priority runtime so that API load (portal, watch streams, MCP) does not delay heartbeats and elections. Roles are modules in the same process and are activated via desired state. Exception: the boot and discovery service runs as a separate sandboxed process without access to the node key; in general, parsers at trust boundaries run without such access. External components do not run as child processes but as independent systemd units with their own cgroup and resource limits. An agent restart (update, crash) therefore does not terminate any workloads. Privileged operations are to be bundled in a small helper service with a fixed command set, so that the main process runs with reduced privileges. Components # Every agent contains a supervisor, identity and PKI, the WireGuard underlay, gossip membership, an API ingress with router, an RPC server, the node reconciler, audit, time monitoring and update control. Raft consensus additionally runs only on control group members, learners and witnesses; a full watch cache is held only by control nodes and learners – worker nodes cache only their own objects and therefore never see other tenants' data. Cell controllers run on nodes that hold a lease for them. Resource budgets # Target budgets on a Pi 4: worker node ≤ 96 MB RAM, control node ≤ 384 MB (with SSD/NVMe mandatory , no SD card), witness ≤ 48 MB (SD card permitted). This means a Pi 4 with 2 GB may serve as a control node; one with 1 GB only as a worker or witness node. Membership via gossip # Gossip follows the SWIM protocol with Lifeguard extensions. The gossip scope is the cell ; in addition there is a small region pool made up of the control nodes of all cells. There is no region-wide pool of all nodes. Joining # Phase Mechanism Before adoption No gossip. Discovery via the boot service and discovery API; unknown hardware sees no gossip packets. Adoption The adoption package contains a one-time provisioning credential, the WireGuard configuration for at least three seed nodes and the cell ID. The node generates its own key and obtains its certificate via CSR. Join Underlay to the seeds, gossip key via mTLS, announcement to several seeds – after that, all members are known. Restart New incarnation with the same node ID; seeds from the local cache. Details of the adoption flow: Boot & adoption . Failure detection # A node is pinged directly, then indirectly via several other members, then marked as suspect and finally as failed . Lifeguard reduces false alarms caused by overloaded nodes – important for Pis under load. Detection takes about 5–15 seconds. Crucially: "failed" via gossip is only a signal, not a decision. Signal Consequence suspect display only; the router avoids the node for any reads failed < 5 min Node is marked unreachable – only after the controller's own health check failed ≥ 5 min and voter Control group is reconfigured failed ≥ 10 min Rescheduling only for workloads without local state or with replicated volumes – fencing first Metadata # Gossip carries only small, fast-changing, loss-tolerant information: underlay endpoints, actual roles, agent version, rough free capacity, health flags, leader hint and clock offset – at most 512 bytes per node, signed by the originating node. A periodic digest exchange with random peers compensates for lost messages. Everything that must be correct lives in Raft. Scaling and partitions # Experience shows that gossip scales to several thousand nodes per pool and does not limit cell size. In a network partition, only the side with the Raft quorum can reconfigure, fence and reschedule; the minority becomes read-only, and workloads keep running. A mass-failure brake kicks in when more than a third of a cell's nodes drop out within 60 seconds: a network or power event is then assumed – no automatic reconfiguration, no evacuation, alert to the operator. State: one Raft group per cell # Every cell has its own Raft group; log and state are stored locally in a crash-safe way. If a voter loses its data, it rejoins as a new member with a new Raft incarnation – so no "amnesiac voter" can vote with an old identity. Automatic election of the control group # The control group controller always runs on the Raft leader. Hard criteria: at least 2 GB RAM (witness 512 MB); SSD/NVMe with measured low fsync latency; lifecycle state Active ; matching agent version; wired network and low clock skew; minimum trust level according to the operating profile; minimum uptime. Eligibility data comes exclusively from the controller's measurements and from operator labels – a node cannot declare itself "eligible". Soft criteria , weighted: Spread across failure zones (site, room, rack, power circuit, switch): no single zone may hold a majority of the voters. Stability (availability, flapping, battery operation). Hardware quality (fsync latency, RAM, CPU class). Network latency to the other voters. Load – control and heavy workloads are kept apart. Changes are made only for a clear improvement (hysteresis), to avoid constant reconfiguration. Eligible nodes Voters Learners 1 1 – 2 without witness 1 1 (hot standby) 2 + witness 2 data voters + witness – 3–20 3 0–1 > 20 or ≥ 3 failure zones 5 1–2 Five voters survive two simultaneous failures; seven would increase latency and replication load without being necessary for the failure model. Two data voters without a witness are never formed, because any single failure would block the cell. Reconfiguration on failure # Gossip has reported a voter as failed for five minutes. The leader confirms via a direct health check, checks the mass-failure brake and the stability of the quorum, and selects a candidate – preferably from the same failure zone. The candidate is added as a learner and catches up via snapshot and log. Joint consensus commits the new membership in a single step. If the old voter returns, it becomes a regular node and can be elected again later. What lives in Raft – and what does not? # Data Location Desired state and metadata of all resources in the cell Raft Phase and condition transitions, placement, assigned IPs Raft (aggregated) Controller leases, fencing epochs, assignments, quota usage Raft WireGuard keys, certificate serial numbers, revocation list Raft Audit entries for mutations, long-running operations Raft Reachability, node metadata Gossip Metrics, logs, traces Observability role, not in the control plane Events (human-readable history) local + aggregation, loss permitted Guiding rule: anything that justifies a decision (placement, fencing, permissions, quota) is stored in Raft. Anything that is only observed or changes more often than roughly once a minute is not. The state grows from about 4 MB in a homelab to just under 1 GB at 1,000 nodes; snapshots are compressed, hash-verified and created in the background. Two-node operation with witness # Starting point # The Raft library used only knows voters and learners, not a "log-less" witness. A voter with no log at all would only be possible by modifying the consensus algorithm. The witness is therefore a full voter with restrictions : it may never become a candidate or leader, does not apply entries (null state machine) and receives only metadata snapshots. Variants # Variant Description Assessment A – log witness receives the complete log but does not apply it local only and only on trusted hardware B – blind witness like A, but every payload is replaced by its SHA-256 hash before sending default for all witnesses , local and external C – witness may lead briefly to bring a lagging data node up to date to be evaluated after the MVP D – log-less arbiter custom consensus extension rejected (correctness risk) E – no witness 1 voter + 1 learner transitional mode Why this is safe: Raft safety depends on the vote, log IDs and persisted acknowledgment – not on applying the entries. The witness persists log IDs (or hashes), votes correctly, never becomes leader and never serves as a replication or read source. Commit rule (decided on 2026-11-12): as long as both data nodes are healthy, a write is acknowledged to the client only once both data nodes have it. Only after a data node failure has been detected does an explicitly declared, alerted and audited degraded mode with the witness vote become active; the return to normal is automatic. In the elevated operating profile and with witnesses operated by third parties, "always both" applies. Deliberately accepted limitation: if the data node with the most recent state fails permanently, the witness cannot bring the other one up to date – the cell remains write-locked until the node returns or an emergency override is performed. Witness as hardware or external # Suitable witnesses are a Pi Zero 2 W, Pi 3 or another micro node via boot stick – ideally in a separate failure zone –, an external witness over WireGuard (e.g. a VPS or a second homelab, with election timeouts adjusted to the latency) or a container on third-party hardware such as a NAS. One witness can serve several cells. A shared external witness is permitted only as a blind witness and only with a trusted operator , because Raft does not protect against malicious participants. Fallback operation with a single node # Situation (data nodes A, B, witness W) Behavior B fails fully writable, warning "no redundancy" W fails fully writable, warning "witness missing" B and W fail read-only ; workloads on A keep running; node can be operated locally Partition A ∣ B+W B side writes, A becomes read-only and catches up after healing The emergency override can only be invoked locally on the surviving node, with the recovery key generated during initial setup or under the four-eyes principle. A dry run shows the potential loss window; the operator confirms that the other members are switched off. The node then starts as a single voter with a new cell epoch ; old members are locked out via the epoch and must rejoin. There is no automatic override , not even after a timeout: a split brain with duplicate I

s: How nodes join the platform – the first node via USB stick, further nodes via network boot, a boot service without a single point of failure, discovery quarantine, secured adoption, plus rejection, decommissioning and replacement.
x: Overview # A node enters the platform in exactly two ways: the first node starts from a USB stick or an SD card and sets up the platform; every further node boots over the network (or, as a fallback, from the stick as well), is discovered as unknown hardware, lands in quarantine and only becomes a full member through an explicit adoption . The flow in brief: Start via USB/SD, PXE, UEFI HTTP Boot, Raspberry Pi netboot or through a server's BMC. The discovery system runs in memory, collects a hardware inventory and reports to the boot service – state "pending" , in quarantine. A human or a rule adopts the node. The node installs the OS locally (default) or runs diskless from the network, receives its certificate, joins the cluster and takes on roles. Key decisions # Topic Decision Image one universal image per architecture for initial setup, discovery/installer and operation (see OS image ) Boot service own Rust implementation in a sandboxed process without access to the node key ; proxyDHCP instead of replacing DHCP; active-active on at least two nodes Integrity all boot artifacts signed; with Secure Boot, a dedicated iPXE build signed with the installation's own key Quarantine two-tier: optionally a dedicated VLAN, always cryptographic Adoption manual or rule-based, secured by confirmation code, TPM attestation, enrollment token or adoption window; never MAC matching alone Keys the node's private key never leaves the node ; certificates are valid for 7 days The first node # Media # Platform Medium Notes amd64 (notebook, mini PC, server) hybrid image for USB sticks, ISO for BMC virtual media bootable via UEFI and BIOS arm64 with UEFI image or ISO UEFI only Raspberry Pi 4/5 image for SD card, USB or NVMe writable with common imager tools The same image later serves as fallback medium for further nodes: if it finds a boot service or platform API on the network, it offers "Join this platform"; it only creates a new platform when that is explicitly chosen at the console. Headless devices decide automatically. Initial setup flow # The operator plugs in the stick and powers on the device. It obtains an address from the existing router and searches for a platform. If none is found, it generates a one-time setup token and a TLS fingerprint and shows both on the console (and additionally as a file on the stick). Using the token, the operator opens the setup wizard in the portal, API or MCP. The wizard explores the network and proposes a configuration; the platform then creates the CA, platform, region and first cell, starts Raft with a single member and activates the control, identity and boot roles. The OS is installed on the chosen disk, and the node reboots from disk. The operator receives a one-time invitation link and the root CA fingerprint. At the final portal address, they register the first admin passkey . The wizard is the guided form of a single API operation, so that API and MCP remain on equal footing (see API-first ). It walks through hardware suitability, network exploration (existing DHCP, competing PXE services, VLANs, DNS, time sources), names, first admin and portal address, installation target, boot service, adoption policy (default: manual with confirmation code) and a dry run; at the end, recovery shares and the invitation link are shown once. For the portal address, the platform issues a server certificate from its own CA whose key never leaves the node; it is renewed automatically. Public certificates are possible via an upstream reverse proxy. Transition to a cluster # Until the second node arrives, the first node is deliberately a single point of failure – the portal points this out. With the second suitable node, the role rule distributes the boot service to it and fills its artifact cache. From three nodes on, boot, API, portal and MCP survive the failure of one node. The stick is no longer needed and remains usable as a rescue medium. Network boot of further nodes # proxyDHCP # In a homelab, addresses are usually assigned by an existing router that knows nothing about PXE options. The boot service therefore operates as proxyDHCP : it only answers requests carrying a boot identifier, without assigning addresses; the client combines the address from the real DHCP server with the boot information from the proxy. Depending on the reported architecture, it delivers: PXE clients (BIOS and UEFI) receive iPXE via TFTP, UEFI HTTP clients a URL to iPXE, iPXE itself the URL of its script, and the Pi bootloader its specific identifier. If another PXE service already answers in the segment, the boot service reports a conflict and by default only serves known clients – an existing PXE environment remains usable. A full DHCP mode of its own is only permitted on a dedicated interface, after verifying that no other DHCP server answers there. Network boot over IPv6 is not part of the MVP. iPXE and UEFI HTTP Boot # iPXE is the uniform second stage for x86 and arm64 UEFI and is shipped as a standalone binary artifact, not linked (see License governance ). Dedicated build per installation: it is built reproducibly and automatically during initial setup and on every change of the boot CA, contains the installation's boot CA as trust anchor and verifies every subsequently loaded image against a signature. With Secure Boot, it is signed with the installation's own db key – own platform, KEK and db keys instead of a third-party shim. Upstream-signed iPXE shim: only as a fallback for devices whose firmware does not allow setup mode; not permitted in the elevated protection profile and assigned a lower trust level. The iPXE script generated by the boot service is the decision point; it contains no secrets and is signed. With UEFI HTTP Boot , the firmware loads either iPXE (default) or directly a signed unified kernel image of the discovery stage. Raspberry Pi 4/5 # Raspberry Pi 4 and 5 boot from a bootloader in EEPROM that supports netboot via TFTP and – with signed images – via HTTP; the Pi 5 can additionally do HTTPS with its own CA. Brand-new devices, however, do not have the network in their boot order. The platform therefore provides a small preparation image that writes the EEPROM configuration once; alternatively, the Pi boots the universal image from a medium once and the agent changes the EEPROM after adoption. Variant Integrity Use TFTP no verification by the firmware, lowest trust level getting started, compatibility Signed HTTP (target) firmware verifies the signature, Pi 5 additionally HTTPS homelab and data center Pi Secure Boot firmware only starts signed images; key fused into OTP – irreversible only on explicit request USB/SD image signature fallback Because the Pi already sends its serial number in the first boot request, the boot service can create the discovery entry very early, and pre-registrations take effect immediately. Other devices # Arm64 servers with UEFI behave like x86 UEFI. Notebooks without PXE: a tiny netboot stick that contains only iPXE and loads everything else from the network. Without a network path to the boot service, the universal image starts from the stick and reports in over a routed network. Servers with a BMC: via Redfish, the platform reads the inventory, automatically creates a pre-registration, sets a one-time network boot and powers on – or mounts the universal ISO as virtual media. Credentials exist only as a secret reference, and access happens exclusively from the out-of-band network. Time budget: from "power on" to "pending" takes about 0.5 to 1.5 minutes on x86 and on the Pi with HTTP boot, and 1 to 3 minutes on the Pi with TFTP – the target is at most 5 minutes. The boot service # Components # All components run in a dedicated sandboxed process ( cp-bootd ) with its own user, minimal privileges and its own service identity – without access to the node key , gossip secrets or the KMS. Only this process holds the key used to sign boot scripts. The components are proxyDHCP (with rate limiting), a read-only TFTP server for first stages, an HTTP(S) server for content-addressed, signed artifacts, the script generator, the discovery inbox and the boot projection – a local, replicated read view "known hardware → action" without any tenant data. All parsers are fuzzing targets. Replication without a single point of failure # Active-active: all boot nodes answer broadcasts; the client takes the first offer. If a node fails mid-boot, the firmware retries; the iPXE script also lists all boot nodes as fallback targets. Placement: at least two boot nodes in different failure zones with access to the boot segment. State: decisions only read the boot projection; new discovery entries are written idempotently via the Raft leader. Without quorum: known nodes keep booting with the last known profile – important, for example, for diskless nodes after a power outage. New reports are buffered; adoptions are not possible without quorum. Artifacts and provenance # All artifacts come from signed release manifests and are obtained either from the release repository, from other boot nodes over the underlay, or via offline import (air gap). Every boot node verifies signature, hash and version monotonicity before serving an artifact. Which version is served is determined by the region's desired state; every artifact comes with an SBOM. Details under Release bundle and Release signing . Decision per boot request # Device state Response unknown discovery image, create entry "discovered" pending discovery image again rejected no offer or local boot; event, optional alert installed node "boot locally" diskless node signed OS image from the network reinstallation requested installer decommissioned like unknown, with a reference to the former node For servers, "network first" is recommended (central control of reinstallation and rescue, fallback to local); for the Pi, "local first, network as fallback", because its bootloader does not understand a "boot locally" command from the network. What gets booted # Mode Contents Persistence Discovery / installer kernel and initramfs, agent in restricted mode, inventory tools – no SSH, no login RAM only; writes to disks only after adoption, in installation mode Diskless immutable OS from the network, local state in RAM or on an encrypted scratch disk persistent identity only with TPM or Pi device key Local installation (default) A/B partitions on disk, encrypted state partition persistent; mandatory for control and storage roles Hardware profile # The discovery entry contains an inventory: identity (SMBIOS UUID, serial number, manufacturer, model), CPU, RAM and virtualization capability, disks with serial numbers and SMART summary, network interfaces with LLDP neighbor and boot path, firmware versions, security features (Secure Boot, TPM, Pi Secure Boot) and an assessment of role suitability and the expected trust level. Device-supplied fields are data, not instructions: free-text values such as model or firmware strings are marked as untrusted, normalized and only output in structured form via MCP. Suitability and trust level are never derived from self-reported information alone. The discovery ID is derived from stable hardware attributes, so reboots do not create duplicates. Discovery phases # Discovered → Inventoried → Pending → Adopting → Adopted. If a rule matches, the device goes directly from "inventoried" to "adopting". From "pending", a device can be rejected (and later unblocked); entries not seen for more than 30 days are considered orphaned and are cleaned up. Discovery quarantine # Tier Mechanism Protection Q1 Network (where possible) dedicated boot/discovery VLAN; underlay and management as tagged VLANs that only the adopted node configures reduces the attack surface, but is not sufficient on its own Q2 Cryptographic (always) control, gossip and tenant networks run exclusively in the WireGuard underlay with mTLS a discovered node has neither a WireGuard key nor a certificate nor a gossip key – no acce

s: Network zones, the encrypted WireGuard underlay, the in-house tenant overlay cp-vnet, workload attachment and north-south traffic with floating IPs, gateways and platform DNS.
x: Overview # The platform splits its network into two layers: an underlay that cryptographically connects all nodes, and a tenant overlay in which the tenants' virtual networks (VPCs) run. Everything that flows between nodes – control traffic (Raft, gRPC), gossip, storage replication, live migration and the traffic of tenant workloads – runs in the encrypted underlay. On the physical network, only WireGuard UDP, the boot and discovery services, a channel for additional keys and the public entry points (API, portal, MCP, floating IPs) remain visible. The concept is designed to scale from a homelab with a single router to a data center with a leaf-spine fabric. The protection it provides does not depend on the physical build-out: it is always cryptographic and is additionally reinforced physically where the infrastructure allows it. Key decisions # Topic Decision Zones seven network zones, mappable to three physical build-out levels flat , vlan , routed Underlay one kernel WireGuard interface per node, IPv6 only inside (ULA); peers exclusively from the desired state; additional post-quantum PSK Tenant overlay in-house development cp-vnet on the Linux kernel data path (VRF + VXLAN + nftables); not OVN, not Cilium; overlay packets only inside the WireGuard underlay North-south network-gateway role for NAT, floating IPs and L4 load balancers; ownership via Raft lease with fencing Network layers and zones # Zone model # Zone Contents Protection Z0 Physical / transport LAN or data center fabric, carries WireGuard UDP baseline rule set (only permitted ports), WireGuard cookie against handshake floods Z1 Boot / discovery proxyDHCP, TFTP, boot HTTP, discovery inbox cryptographic quarantine always, VLAN separation optional or mandatory depending on profile; signed artifacts Z2 Underlay (inside WireGuard) control, gossip, storage replication, live migration, overlay transport WireGuard (+ PQ PSK) and per-service mTLS or AEAD; adopted nodes only Z3 Tenant overlay (VXLAN inside Z2) VPCs, subnets, VM and container traffic VRF per VPC, conntrack zones, security groups, anti-spoofing Z4 North-south / uplink floating IPs, NAT gateway, LB VIPs, internet egress nftables boundary, basic DDoS protection, security group at the destination Z5 Management API, portal, MCP, local node API TLS 1.3, authentication, permitted source networks, rate limits Z6 Out-of-band BMC/Redfish, serial consoles never in tenant or internet networks; credentials only as secret references Principle: a zone is only a zone once its boundary is enforced and observable. Every node reports the actual zone assignment of its interfaces; deviations – such as tenant VXLAN on a physical interface or a BMC in the same segment as the uplink – show up as an alert condition and in the topology export. Physical build-out levels # Level Typical environment Mapping flat homelab: one router with DHCP, simple switch, devices with a single NIC Z0, Z1, Z4, Z5 share the LAN; Z2/Z3 separated purely cryptographically vlan VLAN-capable switch untagged access ports = discovery; tagged VLANs for underlay, uplink and management; tagged sub-interfaces only after adoption routed data center, leaf-spine each host with its own loopback address as WireGuard endpoint, BGP to the top-of-rack switch, boot segment per rack with DHCP relay The level is a property of the site; switching from flat to vlan can be done as a rolling change during operation. Embedding the discovery quarantine # Unknown hardware first lands in zone Z1 (see Boot and adoption ). The boot services are answered by a dedicated sandboxed process ( cp-bootd ) with its own service identity, without access to node or WireGuard keys and without access to Z2/Z3. A discovered node has neither WireGuard keys nor a peer entry on any platform node – so it sees neither the underlay nor the tenant networks. On the physical interfaces of an adopted node, only the following is allowed inbound: WireGuard UDP, the PSK channel (only from known peers), boot services (only on boot nodes), HTTPS for API/portal/MCP from the permitted source networks, floating IPs (only on gateways) and rate-limited ICMP error messages. Everything else – in particular VXLAN, gossip and gRPC – is dropped. WireGuard underlay # Why WireGuard # Thanks to ChaCha20, kernel WireGuard is fast on Raspberry Pis without AES instructions (roughly gigabit speed), has no negotiation state and comes with roaming and NAT traversal. IPsec is a possible later profile; custom TLS/QUIC tunneling in user space was rejected. The lack of algorithm agility is addressed architecturally: the underlay is encapsulated behind an interface, so an IPsec profile can be introduced without changes to the overlay or control. The cryptographic assessment is on the Cryptography page. Interfaces and addressing # One WireGuard interface per node ( cp-ul0 ) with one UDP port. A second interface exists only if there is a separate physical storage fabric. Inner addresses IPv6 only (ULA per RFC 4193): one /48 per platform, one /64 per cell, one /128 per node. The addresses are derived deterministically from trust domain, region, cell and node identifier – no address registry is needed, and planning detects conflicts. Advantage: no collision with IPv4 home networks, and the physical network does not need IPv6. Allowed IPs per peer are exactly its /128. WireGuard thereby authenticates the source address – the basis for gossip and VXLAN being able to trust the sender. Traffic classes are distinguished by ports and DSCP (control before gossip before overlay before storage before migration), not by separate tunnels. In the MVP, at least control and gossip traffic is prioritized so that storage rebalancing on small nodes does not trigger Raft re-elections. Topology within a cell: "intent mesh" # Kernel WireGuard has no notion of "peer on demand". That is not needed either, because the agent knows from the desired state whom it has to talk to: control group and seeds, gossip partners, hosts with workloads in the same VPCs, storage partners, gateways and migration targets. Because the gossip protocol (SWIM) probes random members, the underlay within a cell is effectively a full mesh (up to just under 1,000 peers per node). Peers only become active when there is traffic, however; configuration changes are applied incrementally via netlink, never as a full replacement. Between cells, sites and regions # Relationship Topology cells of the same region at the same site direct peers as needed sites within a region relay nodes per site (at least two), direct connections where both sides are reachable regions relay to relay only, no cross-region full mesh external witness peer of the control group or of a relay Relays route in the kernel: they decrypt, forward and re-encrypt. They therefore see the underlay contents in plaintext. For this reason, the relay function is tied to a high minimum trust level of the node (see Security model ); a downgrade revokes it automatically. Relays that only pass through encrypted packets are planned for a later phase. Nodes behind NAT establish outbound connections to the relays (keepalive only on those peers). Endpoints come from a signed self-description, gossip provides liveness – but never identity : the key always comes from the Raft state. Key distribution and rotation # Step Mechanism Generation the node generates its key pair locally during adoption; the private key never leaves the node and resides on the encrypted data partition Publication the node signs its announcement (public key, next key, endpoints, inner address) with its node key; every agent verifies it against the cell registry Distribution every agent watches the keys of its cell and updates its interface incrementally Revocation decommissioning or quarantine removes the entry; all peers delete it within a few seconds (target under 5 s) Rotation every 30 days, staggered – never several nodes of a cell at the same time In the MVP, the switchover is coordinated : the node announces the next key together with a switchover time; all peers create an entry for the new key in advance and move the address assignment in a single step at that time. The interruption thus shrinks to the clock skew. A full "make before break" with a second interface follows in phase 2. Operators can trigger a rotation via the API action node:rotateUnderlayKey . Post-quantum additional key # WireGuard allows an optional pre-shared key that protects session keys against future quantum attacks. The platform derives these PSKs from one long-lived, time-limited hybrid TLS 1.3 session (classical + ML-KEM) per peer pair – per two-minute epoch, matching the WireGuard rekey, so running sessions are never interrupted. The channel runs outside the tunnel, is open only to known peers and does not depend on the control plane. So that a longer control outage does not drag the underlay down with it, expired node certificates are accepted during a 72-hour grace period with an alert – revoked or quarantined nodes never are. Keys and netlink access reside in a privileged helper process; the agent itself only knows the public view. Performance and MTU # Targets (VM to VM across two hosts): Pi 4 at least 600 Mbit/s, Pi 5 at least 900 Mbit/s, amd64 server at least 5 Gbit/s per peer pair. Layer Overhead at physical 1,500 at jumbo 9,000 WireGuard (worst case IPv6 outer) 80 bytes 1,420 8,920 VXLAN over inner IPv6 70 bytes 1,350 8,850 Kubernetes with flannel VXLAN in the VPC 50 bytes 1,300 8,800 The underlay MTU is fixed regardless of the outer address family, so switching between an IPv4 and IPv6 endpoint changes nothing. The VPC MTU auto is the minimum across all participating sites, with a lower bound of 1,280; it is distributed via DHCP or router advertisement. The NAT gateway applies MSS clamping, and ICMP messages for path MTU discovery are never filtered. Tenant overlay: choice of technology # The requirements are VPCs with overlapping address spaces, security groups, peering, NAT, floating IPs, load balancers and DHCP/DNS/metadata – with a small memory footprint on Raspberry Pi, a single source of truth in the platform's own Raft, and static stability during control outages. Options # Criterion OVN/OVS Cilium (eBPF) Own solution cp-vnet VPC feature set very complete pod network of a Kubernetes cluster; no overlapping tenant address spaces must be built; the kernel provides all building blocks First-class VMs yes only via Kubernetes yes (TAP directly) Second consensus database yes (own northbound/southbound databases) without Kubernetes: etcd no Memory per host several services, not plannable on a Pi agent typically 100–300 MB just a module in the existing agent, data path in the kernel Troubleshooting OpenFlow tables, three databases Kubernetes knowledge required standard Linux tools ( ip , nft , bridge , conntrack ) EVPN connectivity in the data center possible possible natural fit: the model matches the Linux EVPN model Maturity very high very high new (own risk) Decision for cp-vnet # One source of truth: OVN brings its own Raft-clustered database; the desired state would have to be mirrored – two consensus systems with independent failure modes and a duplicated backup question. Resource budget: a Pi worker node is supposed to host VMs; an additional network stack with its own database cannot be planned for there. Cilium does not fit VPC semantics – it remains an option inside tenant Kubernetes clusters. Linux provides the building blocks: VRF, VXLAN with static tables, nftables with sets, conntrack zones, NAT, flowtables, tc. Testability: the controller is pure logic (desired state → netlink/nftables operations) and can be tested in simulation and in network namespaces. Risks are contained by a strictly limited MVP scope, structural isolation (VRF + conntrack zone + anti-spoofing) instead of rules alone, property tests "no packet between VPCs without peering" and a backend interface that keeps OVN open as a later opti

s: The DNS role cp-dnsd – authoritative zones of the cluster, DNSSEC, floating service addresses (VIPs) with Raft leases, and integration with the operator's DNS.
x: Goal # A DCP cluster manages its DNS records itself . Portal and API, nodes, boot service and release holders change with the cluster state – nodes join, roles move, holders fail. Maintaining these names by hand in the operator's DNS would be error-prone. Instead, the rule is: The operator's central DNS only points to the cluster; everything below that is answered by the cluster itself. For this purpose there is the node role dns with the service cp-dnsd . It is distinct from the VPC-internal name resolution for tenant workloads, which is answered locally on every host (see Network ). Tenant zones in public DNS are a later expansion stage. Decisions # Question Decision Scope platform records automatically from the cluster state, plus custom records via API, command line, MCP and portal Integration with central DNS NS delegation and conditional forwarding; two fixed service addresses (VIPs) per region that automatically move to healthy dns nodes Implementation own, purely authoritative server in Rust; separate unit without the node key, port 53 only, hard limits, fuzzing DNSSEC configurable per zone (ECDSA P-256, rotation, DS record in the portal); default "on" in the standard and erhoeht profiles, "off" in the homelab profile The decision for an in-house implementation follows the project's principle of implementing core functions itself and keeping them lean (see Vision ). From a widely used Rust DNS library, only the wire format encoding is used; zone logic, signing, response behavior and limits are the project's own code. Zones and records # A zone is a platform resource DnsZone . Like any other resource it is managed via the API – create, update, delete, plus a dedicated action for key rotation (see API-first ). When a region is initialized, the setup wizard proposes a zone derived from the portal address and indicates what needs to be entered in the central DNS. The platform automatically creates in every zone: Name Contents zone apex SOA and NS records ns1 / ns2 ns1.<zone> , ns2.<zone> the two service addresses (both the same if there is only one VIP) portal name addresses of the ready nodes, if the portal address lies within the zone <node>.nodes.<zone> the node's LAN addresses <node>.underlay.<zone> the node's underlay address boot.<zone> nodes with an active boot role releases.<zone> current holders of the platform releases (see Release bundle ) Custom records are added from the zone's specification. If a custom record tries to override a name managed by the platform, it is skipped; the zone reports this as a warning in its status. Building the zone is a pure derivation: the agent computes the desired zone from the replicated cluster state and hands it to cp-dnsd . When the state changes – a node becomes ready, a role moves – the zone changes automatically along with it. This follows the level-triggered reconciler pattern of the control plane (see Control plane ). The cp-dnsd service # cp-dnsd answers DNS queries over UDP and TCP on port 53. Its behavior is deliberately narrow: Authoritative only , no recursion. Queries for foreign names are refused. No zone transfers ; queries of type ANY return only a single RRset (RFC 8482); no wildcards. EDNS(0) is supported; UDP responses are limited to a conservative size. If a response is too large, it is marked as truncated, and the client retries the query over TCP. Limits: maximum query size, a limited number of concurrent TCP connections with an idle timeout; malformed or oversized queries are dropped. Process boundary # DNS parsers process data from the network and are a classic attack target. That is why cp-dnsd runs as a separate service with its own user : it has no access to the node key and no access to the replicated database, holds only the privilege to bind port 53, and is additionally restricted by a mandatory access control profile. Each parser has its own fuzzing target. A bug in the DNS server therefore does not lead to a takeover of the node (see Security model ). Control interface # The agent talks to cp-dnsd over a local Unix socket with a simple, line-based message format. The peer is verified via the operating system's process identity – only the agent may deliver zones. This channel carries: the desired zones (platform and custom records in canonical form), encrypted key envelopes for DNSSEC (see below). cp-dnsd itself decides nothing about the cluster; it only answers what the agent hands it as desired state. DNSSEC # If DNSSEC is enabled for a zone, cp-dnsd signs it online (RFC 4033–4035, RFC 6605): Algorithm: exclusively ECDSA P-256 with SHA-256 (algorithm 13) – compact and widely supported. Non-existence is proven via an NSEC chain. Since the platform zones are small and contain no names worth protecting, zone enumeration via NSEC is not a concern. Re-signing happens on every change to the zone and, independently, at regular intervals (at least every few days), so that signatures never expire. What is signed is exactly what is served: the records are held in canonical wire form (names uncompressed, lowercase), and the same bytes go into the response. Rotation of the zone keys via a dedicated API action; the portal displays the DS record for the parent zone. Handling the zone keys # The private zone keys are generated in cp-dnsd and reside only there, locally with restrictive permissions – never in the agent. Because several dns nodes must sign the same zone, keys are distributed between them, but exclusively as an envelope : encrypted to a transport key of the receiving cp-dnsd (ephemeral ECDH, key derivation, authenticated encryption; zone and key are bound into the authentication). This transport key is created anew at every start and is held only in memory. The agent and the replicated database therefore only ever see ciphertext. Details on the procedures are on the Cryptography page. Floating service addresses (VIPs) # So that the operator's central DNS has stable targets, each region gets up to two fixed service addresses in the LAN. They are not permanently assigned to one node but move automatically to healthy dns nodes – similar to VRRP, but as an in-house development based on the replicated control plane. Raft lease with fencing # Each VIP belongs to a lease object in the replicated database with holder, fencing epoch and renewal counter. Every write is a compare-and-swap on the revision and is therefore only possible with Raft quorum. The holder renews regularly. It carries the VIP only until the end of its last successful renewal minus a safety margin – measured with its local monotonic clock. If renewal fails, for example because of a network partition or missing quorum, it releases the VIP beforehand . Another node takes over only after it has observed the unchanged revision for at least one full lease duration. This guarantees that the old holder's ownership ends before the takeover – without synchronized clocks; limited clock drift is covered by the safety margin. Every takeover increments the epoch. Without quorum there is neither renewal nor takeover. The address can therefore never be claimed twice. The platform uses the same lease pattern for other floating addresses too, such as floating IPs on gateways (see Network ). Assigning and announcing addresses # Assigning the address to a network interface is a privileged operation. The agent is not allowed to do this itself; instead, it instructs the node's privileged helper service via a fixed, small command format: configure permitted VIPs, assign a VIP, release one of its own VIPs, list held VIPs. The helper service independently checks that the address is on the configured list, lies within the network of an existing LAN interface (not loopback, not underlay) and is not already one of the node's own addresses. It cannot remove foreign addresses. After the takeover, the LAN must learn about the new assignment. Instead of working with raw sockets, the agent sends a packet with the VIP as source address to a not yet resolved address in the LAN. This triggers ARP or neighbor solicitation with the VIP as sender and updates the neighbor tables of the other devices. Rate limiting # An authoritative DNS server can be abused for reflection attacks. cp-dnsd therefore limits the response rate per source network (IPv4 per /24, IPv6 per /56) with a token bucket. Above the limit, responses are dropped; however, every second dropped UDP response goes out as an empty, truncated response. Legitimate clients thus fall back to TCP and continue to be served, while spoofed senders gain no amplification effect. The total number of tracked source networks is capped; the oldest entries are evicted. Integration with the operator's DNS # The operator has two options, which can also be combined: NS delegation: the region's zone is delegated in the parent zone to ns1 / ns2 , which point to the two VIPs. With DNSSEC, the DS record from the portal is also added. Conditional forwarding: internal resolvers forward queries for the zone to the two VIPs – practical in networks without public delegation. Status and operation # Like any other node role, the dns role is started and monitored by the role reconciler. The region reports the DNS state in its status, in particular which node holds which VIP. If a dns node fails, its VIP moves to another healthy node after the lease expires; the zone itself is identical on all dns nodes. A region's portal address can lie within such a zone; what to keep in mind when changing it is described in Changing the portal hostname .

s: Hierarchy of platform, tenant and project, identity types, sign-in with passkeys and OIDC federation, a hybrid authorization model combining a relationship graph and Cedar, tenant isolation, quotas, lifecycle and recertification.
x: Overview # The platform is multi-tenant from the ground up.
