This concept defines who acts in the platform (identities), how these identities prove who they are (authentication), what they are allowed to do (authorization), and how tenants are isolated from each other and from the operator across all technical layers. Key decisions # Topic Decision Hierarchy platform → tenant → project → resource ; the tenant is the organization; optional folders, not part of the URN Identity service own lean OIDC/OAuth 2.1 server in Rust, passkeys first , plus federation with customer IdPs Tokens short-lived, sender-constrained, validated locally ; they carry identity, not permissions Authorization own relationship store (Zanzibar-style) plus Cedar as an embedded policy language Operator and tenants operator roles see metadata, never content – except via a logged access request Lifecycle deletion with crypto erasure and a signed deletion certificate; export at any time Hierarchy # The comparison with AWS, Azure and GCP yields three lessons: if the identity boundary and the isolation boundary diverge, the model becomes hard to understand – hence the tenant is both . Hierarchical guardrails are indispensable for large customers – hence guardrails at every level . Names in paths that break during reorganization are costly – hence folders are not part of the URN . Levels # Level Purpose Example URN Platform operator, global policies, tenant management cp:global:platform Region / cell / node infrastructure, operator only cp:eu-hl1:cell/c1 Tenant the customer's organization with its own IdP, its own keys and its own billing cp:global:tenant/acme Folder (optional) grouping of projects, inheritance of permissions and guardrails separate resource, not a prefix of the project URN Project resource, quota and permission boundary, location binding cp:global:tenant/acme/project/shop Resource VM, volume, bucket … cp:eu-hl1:tenant/acme/project/shop/compute/vm/web-01 Project names are unique per tenant; moving a project between folders only changes a relationship, never the URN. Every project carries a list of allowed regions – the basis for data residency. An additional "organization" level was rejected because it would be superfluous for the vast majority of users (homelab, SMEs) and would raise the question of which level is the isolation boundary. For resellers and hosting providers, a grouping of tenants with delegated partial operator permissions is planned for later – without access to tenant content and without URN changes. The URN conventions are described under API-first . Identities # Principal and actor # Every request carries two pieces of information: the principal is on whose behalf and with whose permissions the action is taken; the actor is who technically acts (portal, CLI, AI client, reconciler). The audit log stores both separately. Type Home Sign-in Typical lifetime Human (operator) platform passkey (mandatory), optionally federated session 8–12 h, access token 10 min Human (tenant) tenant passkey/MFA locally or federated (OIDC/SAML) as above Group tenant / platform local or synchronized from the IdP or via SCIM – Service account project workload identity, federation, API key token 5–60 min, key at most 1 year Workload (VM, container, pod) resource platform attestation via placement 5–15 min, renewed automatically Node region mTLS with a cell CA certificate certificate 7 days, rotated AI agent (actor) MCP client or service account OAuth 2.1 at most 1 h Break-glass platform offline hardware key + recovery shares one-time, at most 4 h Humans and groups # Users exist per tenant ; the same person in two tenants has two identities. This avoids cross-references between tenants and follows the principle of data minimization. Groups are local or mirrored from the external IdP and may be nested. The mandatory attributes are minimal; the e-mail address is marked as personal data, and the last sign-in is used for inactivity checks. Service accounts and workload identities # Workload identities follow the SPIFFE model: paths within a trust domain mirror the URN. Infrastructure and workload paths are firmly bound to separate certificate authorities ; workloads only receive the trust bundle of the workload CA, and their identities are always rejected at infrastructure interfaces. A service account is assigned to a VM, container instance or Kubernetes cluster. This requires a dedicated permission ("actAs") – so nobody can escalate their permissions by starting a VM with a more powerful service account. Tokens are issued by the agent of the host node that verifiably placed the workload – the placement in the control plane is the attestation. VMs preferably receive them via virtio-vsock, container instances as a rotated file, Kubernetes clusters via token projection and OIDC federation. Each host signs with its own short-lived issuer key (24 h), bound to the node identifier. Verifiers require that this key belongs to exactly the node on which the workload is supposed to run. A compromised node therefore cannot mint tokens for other workloads. Inbound federation: external issuers (CI systems, third-party Kubernetes clusters) are registered on the project; their OIDC tokens are exchanged via token exchange (RFC 8693) for a short-lived platform token, subject to conditions on their claims. This way, automation needs no static secrets. Nodes # During adoption , nodes receive a cell CA certificate with their immutable identifier. They are not principals for tenant operations, but act with narrowly scoped permissions for the reconcilers – for example, only writing the status of the resources placed on them. A compromised node therefore affects at most the tenants running on it. Trust levels and attestation are described in the Security model . AI agents via MCP # AI agents are a separate actor type in two variants: Delegated: a human authorizes an MCP client (OAuth 2.1 with PKCE). The token carries the human as principal and the agent as actor, with restricted scopes (read, write, destructive). Autonomous: a service account with actor type "agent", for example a nightly capacity planner. Destructive actions then only run after approval by a human; irreversible actions, privileged IAM changes, the adoption of nodes and the assignment of critical roles are forbidden for autonomous agents. What effectively applies is the intersection of principal permissions, token scopes and agent guardrails. Guardrails are deny rules at platform or tenant level, such as "AI agents may never grant IAM permissions or delete keys". Chained delegation is allowed, but is fully audited and limited in depth. Break-glass # An emergency account with access outside the IdP (hardware key in a safe plus recovery key, optionally split among several people) works even if the identity service fails completely. It grants time-limited operator admin permissions, but no access to tenant content; every use triggers an alert, a post-incident review and rotation. Authentication # Own identity service plus federation # Embedding Zitadel, Keycloak or Kanidm would have meant a second central data store, partly missing Pi suitability, license risks and duplicate maintenance of the tenant model; pure federation would not allow operation without an external IdP. The chosen approach combines an own, deliberately narrow authorization server with federation : OIDC/OAuth 2.1 with authorization code + PKCE, refresh, client credentials, token exchange, device authorization (for the CLI on devices without a browser), discovery, JWKS and protected resource metadata for MCP. Local sign-in with passkeys only by default; passwords are optional and disabled. Federation broker per tenant to any customer IdP via OIDC or SAML, with group mapping and SCIM 2.0 provisioning. No full-blown customer identity management with registration flows or social logins – anyone who needs that federates a specialized IdP. Zitadel, Keycloak or Kanidm are first-class external IdPs for this purpose. The in-house implementation is safeguarded by the OpenID conformance suite in CI, fuzzing of the parsers and an external audit before general availability. MFA, passkeys, step-up # Passkeys first (WebAuthn); for operators and privileged roles, device-bound, attested keys can be enforced. MFA is mandatory for all privileged roles. With federation, the platform checks whether the external IdP asserts MFA; if that evidence is missing, it requires its own passkey as a second factor. Step-up: irreversible actions and changes to privileged roles require a fresh sign-in (at most 10 minutes old), regardless of channel. Via MCP, the human confirms such actions on a platform page that renders the impact report itself and requires passkey presence. The confirmation is bound to all parameters and valid only once. Tenants may tighten this requirement, but not disable it. Progressive lockouts after failed attempts and notification about new devices. Tokens # Access tokens as JWT per RFC 9068, signed with ES256 (in the compatible crypto profile also Ed25519), lifetime of 10 minutes for humans, audience is a specific endpoint. Sender constraining with DPoP for CLI, SDKs and MCP clients, mTLS for workloads; the portal uses an HttpOnly cookie session. No roles, groups or permissions in the token – they are determined on every request from the current permission state. Revocation takes effect immediately, and the token stays small. Refresh tokens rotate and are bound to the session; reuse revokes the session. API keys exist only for service accounts, never for humans. They carry a recognizable prefix for secret scanners, are stored only as a hash, have a mandatory expiration (default 90 days, at most one year) and can be restricted to scopes, source networks and projects. The recommendation is to exchange them for a short-lived token; tenants can forbid API keys entirely by policy. Decentralized behavior during outages # Every node holds the public keys of all issuers and the revocation list, replicated locally. An ingress node validates the token and forwards the request to the responsible cell; that cell validates the original token including the DPoP proof itself and never trusts a user context created by the ingress node. Outage Behavior A region's identity service unreachable existing tokens remain valid until they expire; new sign-ins fail with a notice in the portal; the host continues to issue workload tokens A tenant's external IdP fails no new federated sign-ins; existing sessions run until their maximum duration; optionally local emergency admins of the tenant Cell without quorum reads marked as "stale", permission changes not possible (fail-closed) Signing key compromised rotation, the old key disappears from the JWKS; short exposure thanks to 10-minute tokens Multiple identity nodes each sign with their own key under a common issuer; all public keys reside in the replicated state. This way, no key transport is needed, and ongoing sign-ins, codes and sessions work across node boundaries. Session revocation reaches all nodes of a region within a few seconds. At the very first start (without an IdP), a one-time token sets up the first operator admin including a passkey; this bootstrap access is automatically disabled after the first successful passkey sign-in. Authorization # Requirements # Role-based permissions along the hierarchy, relationships across the hierarchy (sharing an image with another project, VPC peering, folder membership), conditions (channel, actor type, MFA freshness, labels, time of day), guardrails where denials take precedence , decentralized evaluation in under a millisecond without an external service, explainability ("Why am I allowed to do this?") and analysis ("Who has access to X?") – and consistency: after a permission is revoked, no older view may grant access anymore. Options # OpenFGA, Cedar, OPA/Rego, SpiceDB and an own Zanzibar-style core were compared. OpenFGA h

s: The immutable node operating system – a Debian base built with mkosi, erofs and dm-verity, Unified Kernel Images, Secure and Measured Boot per platform, TPM-bound encryption, A/B updates with a health gate, plus hardening and SBOM.
x: Overview # Every node of the platform is an appliance with a single job : it runs the agent and the role components the agent controls – securely, updatably and without manual work. To do this, the platform ships its own image-based operating system, working name cpOS . Five guidelines follow from this: Immutable and verifiable: everything executable comes from a signed, integrity-protected image. Atomically updatable with fallback: an update is a slot switch, never a package-by-package rebuild. State clearly separated: there is exactly one encrypted state partition; everything else is reproducible. API instead of shell: configuration, diagnostics and maintenance go through the platform API, not SSH. Right-sized: small enough for a Raspberry Pi 4 with 2 GB (and witness nodes on even smaller devices), large enough for data center servers. Key decisions # Topic Decision Base own image, built with mkosi from Debian 13 packages ; building blocks from systemd (UKI, systemd-boot, repart, dm-verity, sysupdate, sysext, cryptenroll) Raspberry Pi native Pi bootloader without UEFI , A/B via the built-in "tryboot" mechanism; kernel and firmware from the Raspberry Pi archive File systems only /usr in the image (erofs with dm-verity, A/B slots); / volatile, /etc regenerated on every boot; persistence only in one encrypted state partition; no package manager Contents one base image per architecture (amd64, arm64-UEFI, arm64-Pi); role-specific runtimes as signed system extensions , versioned in lockstep Operating modes discovery, installer, initial setup, operation (local or diskless) and rescue are all built from the same build sources Updates write the inactive slot, reboot, health gate ; automatic fallback on failure (boot counter or "tryboot" plus watchdog) Rollout rolling, via the control plane; at most one control-plane member per cell at a time, leader last; automatic updates on by default Hardening no login, no passwords, no SSH by default; kernel lockdown, mandatory module signing, default-deny firewall, sandboxing per service Secure / Measured Boot own keys per installation, TPM 2.0-bound disk encryption via signed PCR policies Supply chain SBOM, source bundle and provenance per artifact; reproducible build Choice of base # The criteria were native Pi support, image-based mechanics, an established security team with a long support period, reproducibility, maintenance effort, size and licenses. Rejected were Fedora/CentOS Stream (short cycle, Pi 5 not officially supported), Buildroot (no security team), a Talos-style custom OS (would have to rebuild systemd features), Flatcar and Fedora CoreOS (Pi only via UEFI), NixOS (learning curve, size) and Ubuntu Core (tied to a vendor store). Yocto remains a fallback option for very small profiles. A UEFI path for the Pi was rejected because the community firmware is barely maintained anymore. Only Debian with mkosi combines native Pi support, the systemd image building blocks and an established security team without the project having to maintain a distribution – what is maintained is a recipe , not packages. Package versions are pinned via timestamped snapshots, and the licensing situation is clear (Debian main plus firmware with a redistribution license). Moving to the next Debian release is planned as a regular minor release of the platform. For amd64 and arm64-UEFI the Debian kernel is used (signed modules, lockdown, security updates by the kernel team); for the Pi, the Raspberry Pi kernel in an LTS line. The C library is glibc, against which the Rust components are built. Image structure # Layers # Layer Contents Property Boot UEFI: systemd-boot and Unified Kernel Images (UKI) for slots A and B; Pi: boot slots A/B with kernel, device trees and initramfs signed /usr base (systemd, agent, privileged helper service, kernel modules, network and crypto tools) plus extensions per role immutable, erofs + dm-verity, slot A/B volatile / , /etc , /run tmpfs, regenerated on every boot State Raft data, node identity, audit buffer, journal, extension cache, container data persistent, LUKS2-encrypted Data volumes of the storage roles own encryption per volume (see Storage ) Immutable /usr with dm-verity # /usr is a compressed, reproducibly built erofs file system, followed by a verity partition (hash tree) and a signature partition over the root hash, laid out according to the Discoverable Partitions Specification . The root hash is part of the kernel command line of the signed UKI or the Pi boot image. In the elevated protection profile, the kernel additionally verifies the verity signature against the installation's keys, so that even a tampered boot path cannot mount a foreign /usr . Any hash error triggers a reboot; a corrupt slot is thereby detected by the boot counter and discarded. Because / is a tmpfs and /etc is generated from signed defaults on every boot, there is no place where configuration can silently accumulate – the OS is drift-free. Partition layout # UEFI (amd64, arm64) – GPT, created at installation: Partition Size (guideline) Contents EFI system partition 1 GiB systemd-boot, UKIs for slots A and B, rescue UKI usr A + verity + signature 2.5 GiB + hash tree base /usr version N usr B + verity + signature same as A version N+1 or N−1, initially empty State (LUKS2 → ext4) 16–64 GiB persistent node state Data (optional) remainder reserve for storage roles on single-disk nodes Raspberry Pi 4/5: additionally a small control partition with the A/B selection and a rescue configuration, plus two boot slots each holding a signable boot image (capped at 180 MB, target ≤ 120 MB), followed by the same usr slots, state and data partitions as with UEFI. Very small devices for witness nodes use the same layout without a data partition. Persistence and configuration # The state partition holds the node identity and certificate (where no TPM is present), the Raft database (only on fsync-capable storage, for control-plane nodes), local node state and audit buffer, a content-addressed artifact cache, active extensions, container data, the persistent journal and the last known valid time. Configuration is built in four levels, without a package manager : Level Source Image defaults signed /usr : units, sysctl profile, base firewall rules, AppArmor profiles, default network Boot hints kernel command line – hints only, not a basis of trust Node desired state control plane: roles, network, operating mode, update channel – the agent renders the runtime configuration from it Secrets adoption package and KMS; TPM-sealed or encrypted on the state partition, never in the image Humans do not change /etc persistently; the agent detects any deviation from the desired state during periodic reconciliation and heals it. Software arrives exclusively via image updates or signed extensions. Services # The agent ( cp-agent ) runs as its own user with minimal privileges and strict sandboxing. Privileged operations (network configuration, partitions, extensions, updates, wiping) are handled by a separate helper service ( cp-privd ) with a fixed, audited command set , reachable only by the agent. The boot service ( cp-bootd ) runs only on boot nodes, as its own sandboxed process without access to node keys or the KMS. A console display shows the setup token, confirmation code and status – without a login. Role services run with their own users, cgroup limits and sandboxing. Base image and extensions # The base image contains the kernel and signed modules, only the firmware actually needed, systemd, the platform services, nftables and WireGuard, crypto and storage tools (cryptsetup, TPM support, wiping tools), chrony with NTS and, on the Pi, the EEPROM tools. Size target: /usr uncompressed at most about 600 MB. Role-specific runtimes come as system extensions (sysext) : Extension Contents Roles compute Cloud Hypervisor, virtiofsd, containerd, a Rust OCI runtime, Kata Containers VM and container nodes k8s k3s Kubernetes garage Garage object storage (separate process) object storage sdn network components overlay, gateways observability metrics and log storage observability debug diagnostic tools, SSH server for tier-0 access diagnostic sessions only Why extensions instead of a monolith: small nodes do not carry hundreds of megabytes of runtimes they never use – less code means less attack surface. Role changes work without reinstallation. Extensions are themselves disk images with dm-verity and a signature, and are tightly bound to the version of the base. Rules: a platform release consists of the base, all extensions and the discovery artifacts with one version number and one manifest; extensions are activated at boot, at runtime only when a role is added, and removed only after the node has been drained. Third-party components remain separate processes (see Rust stack , License governance ). Operating modes # Operating mode Artifact Writes to disk? Discovery small, signed discovery UKI or Pi boot image with the agent in restricted mode no Installer like discovery, plus partitioning and wiping tools yes, after adoption Initial setup universal USB stick image with discovery UKI and a complete /usr slot only after initialization Local operation UKI or boot slot A/B yes (state partition) Diskless operation UKI and /usr image via HTTP no (optional scratch disk) Rescue rescue UKI or rescue entry no All artifacts are built from the same package versions . How the operating modes are used in the boot flow is described in Boot and adoption . Local installation: after adoption, the installer checks the manifest signature and minimum version, creates the GPT layout, sets up the encrypted state partition with TPM, network-bound or Pi device-key binding, writes slot A, marks slot B as empty and boots into operation. There the node generates its long-term key, receives its certificate and confirms the boot only after the health gate. The initial-setup node copies its running slot block by block to the target disk – no download at all. Existing data is protected: unless specified otherwise, only an empty disk is written; an existing cpOS installation only after confirmation, and foreign data only if the disk is explicitly selected, with its own confirmation and a warning in the dry run. Diskless: the initramfs loads the /usr image into RAM via HTTP, verifies it with dm-verity against the root hash from the signed command line and mounts it. An update is simply the next network boot; a rollback means serving the previous version. Diskless requires sufficient RAM; persistent identity exists only with a TPM or Pi device key. Updates # Versions, channels, manifest # The entire platform release (agent, base, extensions, discovery) is versioned as MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH . PATCH contains only security and bug fixes , MINOR features and base changes, MAJOR deliberately incompatible changes with a migration path. There are the channels stable (default), candidate (pre-release testing) and edge (development only), as well as release lines with patch maintenance. A signed release manifest describes the version, channel, a security epoch (downgrading below the epoch is forbidden), the minimum version for a direct update path, all artifacts with hash and verity root hash, references to SBOM, source bundle and provenance, and an expiry date to prevent freezing on an old manifest. Details in Release bundle and Release signing . Flow on the node # The control plane approves a target version for the node. The agent fetches the manifest and artifacts (content-addressed, also from other nodes) and checks signature, channel, security epoch, minimum version and expiry. Via systemd-sysupdate, the privileged helper service writes the inactive slot , the new UKI with boot counter (or Pi slot B) and the required extensions – during normal operation and with throttled I/O. Only now is the node drained (workloads migrate, leader change if needed) and rebooted. The new slot boots; the health gate decides. Green: t

s: How platform updates reach the nodes in a rolling, quorum-safe way – release plans, ordering and gates, the health gate on the node, pausing and rollback.
x: Overview # A platform update replaces the entire platform release on every node – agent, OS base, extensions – via an A/B slot switch (see OS image ). Getting there has three parts: Import: the signed release is imported into the region and distributed to at least two holders (see Release bundle ). Rollout controller: it decides which node is updated when – rolling, quorum-safe, pausing on errors. Node side: the agent and the privileged helper service download, verify and write the inactive slot, reboot and confirm the new state only after a green health gate. The responsibilities are clearly separated: the OS provides the node-local mechanics, the controller the orchestration. The controller only writes the target version, the maintenance state and a rollout marker on the node object; the agent only writes the OS status of its own node. The controller # The rollout controller runs in the agent on the current Raft leader of the control plane (see Control plane ). It is level-triggered : each pass derives everything from the observed state; the status only records the start and time limit of the current step. A leader change therefore does not interrupt the rollout – the new leader continues it from the same state. The decision logic is a pure, deterministic function without clock, network or storage. This allows it to be tested exhaustively in a simulation: model nodes with reboots, downtimes and leader changes; the metrics are write availability, simultaneously failed voters and the reboot order. The leader measures health itself – based on the replication responses and the lag in the replication log, never based on the node's self-report. Release plan # Before a target version is set, a plan can be retrieved (dry run via the API action region:planUpdate ). The same plan is checked again when the target version is actually set. It contains: the order of the nodes, whether a write pause is needed (small cluster) and how long it is expected to last – estimated from the measured reboot duration, the blockers that prevent a rollout. Blocker Meaning Release not available still importing, failed, or too few holders Version skew more than two versions would be in use simultaneously within a cell Minimum version the lowest running version is below the release's minVersion – no direct update path A lower security epoch is not a blocker in the plan, but requires privileged approval. Like every platform function, the controls are available via API, command line, MCP and portal (see API-first ). Ordering and gates # One node at a time # There is always exactly one node in progress . A node counts as in progress as long as its target version differs from the running one or the rollout marker is set. Only then is the next one released. At most one node is in the maintenance state at a time. Order within the region # The rollout proceeds cell by cell , regions one after another. Within a cell: worker nodes and learners, the witness, follower voters one at a time, the leader last – before that, it hands leadership over to a healthy, caught-up voter. Quorum protection # A voter (and the witness) is only updated when all other data voters are healthy and caught up – so the quorum is stable even without it. For small clusters: a single voter: the update means a brief write lock; it is only allowed with a warning and explicit confirmation. two data voters with a witness: one data voter after the other, only if the witness is reachable. A planned reboot is not an outage # Before the reboot, the controller puts the node into the maintenance state (drain): workloads are migrated, live where possible, otherwise restarted according to the tenant policy; storage roles wait for a healthy replication state (see Storage ). Nodes in maintenance do not count toward the control plane's mass-failure brake – a planned reboot should not trigger an emergency response. Leases and fencing remain in effect unchanged. Version skew and feature gates # At most two versions run simultaneously within a cell (N and N−1). New formats for the replicated database or storage may only be written once all nodes can read them – otherwise a node running the previous version could no longer apply the log. This is what feature gates are for: Each gate names the minimum version from which the format can be read. It is only switched on once the rollout is complete and the lowest running version has reached this minimum version. Once switched on, a gate stays on. After that, going back to the previous version is no longer possible; a rollback is only possible within the version. Flow on the node # The node follows a fixed contract that it derives from its target version and its state: Node sees Node does reports target version = running version nothing, finish any open phase Running new target version W download release from the holders, verify, write inactive slot – during operation, throttled Staging → Staged or Failed with reason Staged , maintenance and rollout approval for W reboot into the new slot Rebooting beforehand after boot W is running, health gate green confirm the new slot ( bless ) Running (W), previous version recorded after boot the old version is running – RolledBack with reason from the journal RolledBack or Failed for W no new attempt unchanged Download, verification and slot writing run without interrupting operation; the node is only affected from the drain onward. Verification and writing # The agent places the release in a staging area and instructs the privileged helper service via a fixed, small message format. The agent only specifies the version and the verification timestamp ; paths, file names, partitions and commands are determined by the helper service itself. The helper service does not trust the agent : it re-verifies the signature chain against the root in the image, checks the manifest against the release rules (see Release signing ) and copies only the artifacts for its architecture into its own source – checking length, SHA-256 and SHA-512 while copying. Later changes in the staging area then no longer have any effect. The actual writing is done by systemd-sysupdate with this local source in its own isolated unit; it protects the running version and gives the new boot image a boot counter . Security epoch on the node # In addition to the manifest check, the helper service records the verified security epoch per version and, as a lower bound, the highest epoch of a confirmed boot. Writing below this lower bound and booting a slot below it are refused. A rollback to the previous slot is therefore only possible within the same epoch. Health gate # After the reboot, the health gate decides whether the new slot is confirmed. It uses systemd's Automatic Boot Assessment : only when the gate is green is the boot counter removed. Checks run with a time limit (default ten minutes; exceeding it counts as red): The verity-protected /usr is mounted, all system extensions are active, the state area is unlocked. The agent is running, servicing its watchdog and holds a valid certificate. The underlay to at least one seed is up, the gossip join has completed (see Network ). All role units are active, role reconciliation runs without errors. For control-plane nodes: the replication log has caught up with the leader, the node has its previous role again. For boot nodes: boot data loaded, ports bound. For this, the agent regularly writes a small, atomically replaced report with a timestamp, running version, overall result and individual checks. The gate itself runs without network access, requires a fresh report and additionally checks the role units itself. Abort and rollback # On the node: if the gate is red or the boot hangs, the watchdog triggers a reboot. The boot counter of the new slot is then used up, and the node automatically boots the old slot. On Raspberry Pi hardware, the firmware's one-time tryboot mechanism performs the same task. The node reports RolledBack with the reason from the journal of the failed attempt. In the controller: if a node reports RolledBack or Failed , or a step times out, the controller pauses the rollout: it sets the condition RolloutPaused , creates an audit entry and an alert, and releases no further nodes. The affected node does not try again. A failure on the first node thus stops the entire rollout before it spreads. By the operator: a rollback via the node:rollback action is possible as long as the target version has the same security epoch and the previous slot still exists; otherwise only with privileged approval. Going back further is only possible by reinstalling the node. A node can also be pinned to its version and released again. Expansion stages # The current core comprises a target version per region and node, rolling one node at a time, quorum protection, leader last, rollback via the health gate, pausing on errors and operator rollback. Also planned are update policies with stages – for example a single canary node with an observation period, then worker nodes in a limited proportion, boot nodes one at a time, control-plane nodes one at a time with the leader last –, maintenance windows , automatic updates on by default with the option to apply urgent security patches outside the window as well, and distribution of releases between arbitrary nodes (peer-to-peer). How security releases and rollout work together is described in Vulnerability management .

s: Block, object and file storage from two nodes to thousands – the in-house block storage cp-blk with metadata in the cell Raft, tenant encryption on the compute node and a maturity gate before replication.
x: The storage concept describes how the platform provides block, object and file storage – on two Raspberry Pis just as on a thousand servers. Decided on 2026-11-14. Key decisions # Block storage built in-house in Rust ( cp-blk ) with one data path for all sizes: driver local in the first release, replicated (2–3 copies) after passing the maturity gate, erasure coding later for cold and object classes. Metadata in the existing cell Raft , payload data never. No second consensus mechanism. Tenant encryption on the compute node: storage nodes store and replicate only ciphertext. Object storage initially Garage behind a dedicated S3 front end cp-s3gw ; versioning, Object Lock and bucket events come with an in-house object store on the cp-blk chunk layer, with cp-s3gw remaining the stable interface. File storage via one NFS server per share on a replicated volume, replaceable behind a narrow control interface. Ceph only as an optional external driver for data centers with existing Ceph – not in the default path. Replication by default: with fewer than three storage hosts, two copies with a witness; from three hosts, three copies. Requirements and size classes # Class Nodes Block expectation Object expectation G0 single node 1 local, snapshots, external backup simple G1 two nodes + witness 2 two copies, continued operation if one node fails twofold G2 homelab/SMB 3–10 three copies across hosts threefold G3 edge/site 10–100 three copies across racks, QoS threefold across zones G4 cell 100–1,000 like G3 plus rebalancing at large scale cluster per cell G5 region thousands pools per cell, cross-cell only asynchronous replication between cells Hard requirements are a separate key per volume with crypto erase, encryption at rest by default, no single point of failure from three nodes, fair IOPS distribution between tenants, the tight storage budget of small devices and the process-boundary rule for third-party components (see Rust stack ). Options and decision # The original plan "Ceph from three nodes, lightweight mode below that" was rejected. At the small end, Ceph does not fit the target hardware (memory per daemon, no sensible two-node mode), brings a second consensus mechanism alongside the platform Raft, its own identities instead of X.509, and a break between "small" and "large" with two data paths and a migration when growing. Its maturity is the strongest counterargument – but the price is too high for this product. Four variants were compared: Ceph across a process boundary, everything in-house, a hybrid "block in-house, object initially Garage", and a classic hybrid with an in-house lightweight mode and Ceph above it. Third-party alternatives such as DRBD/LINSTOR, Longhorn or SeaweedFS either cannot handle two nodes or need a second consensus. The hybrid was chosen: it uses what the platform already has – Raft, failure domains, fencing, key management, PKI, scheduler –, replaces two external systems with a single in-house path and avoids the scope of S3 semantics for the start. Garage does not violate the "one consensus" principle, since it works with CRDT metadata and quorums; its layout is set by the agent from the control plane. The non-goal "no in-house distributed file system" is thereby made precise: no in-house distributed file system , no in-house database , no Ceph as a mandatory component – block and object storage based on the platform Raft and the chunk layer are in-house developments. Architecture of cp-blk # Component Location Task Agent storage module every node disk inventory and adoption, pool membership, control of cp-blkd , status reporting Placement controller cell controller compute the placement map, epoch changes on failure, rebalancing, capacity cp-blkd separate, isolated process on-disk storage, replication, recovery, scrubbing; client part on compute nodes cp-privd every node privileged steps with a fixed command set (set up encryption, create devices) cp-blkd deliberately runs outside the agent so that a fault in the data path does not affect the agent. Data model and data path # A pool is a set of disks of the same media class in a cell with a replication rule. Placement groups are the unit of distribution. A volume is a sequence of fixed-size chunks; each chunk is assigned to a placement group by hash, and each placement group to an ordered set of replicas. The Raft holds pools, deviations from the computed placement, epochs, volume metadata, snapshot trees and disk states – only a few megabytes even with a thousand nodes. Payload data and chunk indexes are never stored in the Raft. Writing: the client writes to the primary copy of the placement group, which writes locally and in parallel to the replicas; the acknowledgment comes only once the minimum number of copies has been durably stored. Requests with a stale epoch are rejected. Epoch changes happen only through a write by the controller to the Raft. As a result there is no split brain , not even with two nodes: without quorum (with a witness), no new epoch. Every chunk carries a self-describing header (pool, volume, index, epoch, version, checksum) – the basis for emergency reconstruction. On the compute node , cp-blkd provides a block device via ublk; on top of it sits dm-crypt with the volume key. Hypervisor and containers see only the decrypted device. NBD serves as a fallback. Transport via mTLS with a dedicated service certificate in the underlay; the payload is already tenant ciphertext at that point (see Network ). Drivers # Driver From Contents local first release thin volumes and snapshots on one node, encryption per volume replicated after maturity gate cp-blk with copy count and minimum copies ec later erasure coding as an additional class, default for object, backup and archive from about six storage hosts ceph-rbd later, optional the operator's external Ceph cluster, client side only All drivers share the API, snapshots, backups and encryption. A driver change is a volume migration; since the tenant layer sits above the driver, the ciphertext remains unchanged. As long as replicated has not passed the maturity gate, tenant volumes use local . To compensate, every volume gets a snapshot and backup policy targeting another node by default – it can only be opted out of explicitly, and opting out is audited. This deviation is documented and time-limited. API resources # The storage API follows the platform's resource model (see API-first ): Operator side: Disk (disk with type, size, health, media class), StoragePool (driver, replication rule, failure domain), StorageClass (pool selection, QoS, encryption – cannot be disabled –, permitted data classes). Tenant side: Volume , VolumeAttachment , VolumeSnapshot , Bucket , AccessKey , FileShare , as well as backup policies, vaults and recovery points. Long-running operations such as resizing, cloning, migration, snapshot restore, disk adoption, draining, decommissioning and secure wiping. Disk and pool operations are operator permissions; formatting and wiping require explicit confirmation. API, CLI, MCP and portal offer the same functionality. Placement across failure domains # Topology labels (site, room, rack, power circuit, switch, host, disk) form a tree. Placement uses weighted rendezvous hashing per level: deterministic from placement group, pool epoch and topology, so that every node can recompute it. When adding or removing, only what is necessary moves. If there are too few domains, placement falls back one level lower and reports this visibly; two copies on the same disk never happen. Unsuitable media such as SD cards and USB sticks are allowed, but clearly flagged, given a low weight and limited to at most one copy per failure domain. Location boundaries: pools end at the cell; policies can restrict storage to specific sites. Trust levels: since storage nodes only hold ciphertext, the lowest level suffices by default; what matters is the level of the compute node that receives the key (see Security model ). The scheduler binds workloads with local volumes to their node and, for replicated , prefers nodes with local copies. Before a VM is restarted on another node, the controller increments the attachment epoch so that the old client can no longer write. Disk lifecycle # A disk passes through the states discovered → proposed → adopting → active → draining / failed → decommissioned → securely wiped . Adoption only for empty or explicitly approved disks, with a warning for unsuitable media. Replacement: a new disk is adopted as a new resource; the rebuild is spread across many sources. Health: SMART queries, daily light and regular deep scrubbing with comparison of copies, wear monitoring – when thresholds are reached, draining is proposed. Secure wiping: tenant data by crypto erase; decommissioned disks by wiping the encryption header and hardware sanitize, with signed wipe evidence. Security # Topic Implementation Platform layer LUKS2 on every storage disk, key TPM-sealed or network-bound Tenant layer separate key per volume, encryption on the compute node, wrapped under the tenant key Key release only to nodes with a valid attachment epoch and sufficient trust level; storage nodes never receive tenant keys Tenant isolation random volume identifiers; every call to cp-blkd carries the caller's epoch and certificate, authorized from the control plane Integrity checksums against media errors; authenticated encryption for elevated protection requirements is planned as a later option Object the S3 front end derives a key per object from the bucket key; Garage stores no keys Details of the methods and the key hierarchy are in Cryptography . Durability and maturity gate # Mathematically, even twofold replication is very durable for independent failures. In practice, however, correlated failures and software bugs dominate – for an in-house build, the correctness of the code is the real risk. Therefore a maturity gate applies before tenant data goes on replicated : deterministic simulation with partitions, restarts, epoch changes and clock skew, checked for linearizability; real fault injection over weeks without data loss; crash-consistency tests with power loss; emergency reconstruction of volumes solely from the self-describing chunks, without Raft; upgrade and downgrade tests; external design and code review by storage experts. Recovery: crash-consistent snapshots, tenant backups with change tracking as encrypted, deduplicated backups in S3, platform backups of the metadata (without payload data) and asynchronous snapshot shipping between cells for disaster scenarios. Immutable backups follow with the in-house object store. Findings from measurements # Initial measurements support the decision qualitatively: synchronous replication costs hardly more than a local write with sync – latency is determined by the medium , which is why the choice of media matters more than the replication factor. Erasure coding is cheap to encode on ARM but expensive to reconstruct, and therefore comes only later and only on powerful nodes. Hardware-accelerated checksums are significantly faster than cryptographic hashes and suffice against media errors. AES encryption is comfortably fast enough on devices with crypto extensions; devices without these extensions are the bottleneck and will be re-measured on real hardware before being approved for compute with volumes.

s: Whom the platform trusts, for what, how that trust is proven and what happens when trust is lost – from trust anchors through node trust levels and remote attestation to break-glass and compromise.
h: Secret distribution and protection of the control state
x: The security model defines whom the platform trusts, for what , how this is proven and what happens when trust is lost . Algorithms, key lengths, lifetimes and the PKI hierarchy are covered in the cryptography concept ; boot paths and the adoption flow in Boot and adoption . The attacker models come from the threat model . Key decisions # Two separate axes: the adoption evidence describes how certain it is that exactly this device was meant (confirmation code, enrollment token, pre-registration, attestation). The trust level describes how well the integrity of the running node is proven with hardware backing. Placement and roles depend only on the trust level. Five trust levels T0–T4 , computed rather than claimed: the level drops immediately and rises only after fresh evidence. Levels are placement and role conditions: control group, key management (KMS), identity service and certificate signing require minimum levels depending on the operating profile. Remote attestation via TPM quote against signed reference values from the release manifest. Quarantine is a hard, technically enforced state – not a label. One identity per process boundary: third-party processes receive their own locally generated service identities, never the node key. Workload identity strictly separated from the infrastructure, with node-bound issuers. Secrets only on a need-to-have basis and by level , exclusively encrypted to the node key and only in memory. Operator access via the API ; interactive access only time-limited, justified and recorded. Compromise as a runbook operation with immediate revocation and targeted rotation. Trust anchors # Trust in the platform comes from exactly two sources: from signatures that chain back to a defined trust anchor, and from the authoritative state of the control plane (Raft, see Control plane ). Anchor Held by Trusted for Platform root CA custodians of recovery shares (k of n) issuing the region CAs Region and cell CA kms role on control-plane nodes node and service certificates Workload CA and workload token issuer control-plane nodes or node-bound identities of tenant workloads Identity service signing key identity role tokens for users and service accounts Release signing key project (offline root) OS images, agent, boot artifacts, reference values for attestation Secure Boot keys per installation, or project or operator boot chain on the device TPM manufacturer CAs manufacturer authenticity of a TPM Firmware baseline per device model operator (confirmed at adoption) firmware measurements of a device type Passkeys, break-glass material, recovery keys humans administration and emergencies Human confirmation (comparison code) operator at the device adoption without a hardware anchor Guiding principle: nothing on the network is trustworthy per se – neither source address, VLAN, DHCP response, gossip message nor kernel parameter. Such information is a hint, not a basis of trust. Trust boundaries and principles # The platform distinguishes an outside world (LAN, discovery segment, internet), a tenant domain (VMs, containers, Kubernetes clusters with their own workload CA) and an infrastructure domain (worker nodes and – at the core – the control-plane nodes). Checks happen always at ingress (sender-constrained tokens), between agents (mTLS plus permission table), in the state machine (node authorizer), in the KMS (placement evidence) and at the workload↔host boundary. Nodes are not principals for tenant operations. They act as system actors with permissions derived from their assignments in the control plane. Raft is not Byzantine fault tolerant. The integrity of the control-plane nodes is therefore the most important single assumption; it is secured with the highest available trust level, and cells are blast-radius boundaries . Short lifetimes instead of revocation infrastructure – but revoking a node takes effect immediately via a replicated revocation list. Trust falls quickly and rises slowly. Return from quarantine is never automatic. Fail closed for identity and secrets, static stability for running workloads: a loss of trust stops workloads only if the policy requires it. Honest labeling: what a node merely self-reports is recorded as self-reported and does not justify a high level. Trust levels for nodes # Level Name Core criterion Typical devices T0 none not adopted or in quarantine discovery, quarantined nodes T1 basic adopted, node key as a file, boot chain not hardware-verified Raspberry Pi without Secure Boot, x86 without TPM, nested VMs T2 anchored firmware-enforced signature verification of the boot chain with own key, plus a device-bound key for disk unlocking Pi with OTP Secure Boot, x86 with own Secure Boot without TPM T3 tpm TPM 2.0 protects keys and disks, but no valid attestation servers, mini PCs, notebooks with TPM T4 attested like T3 plus Secure Boot, Measured Boot and a fresh, successful attestation servers with TPM, devices with firmware TPM Additional labels (TPM type, Secure Boot mode, attestation state, type of disk unlocking, boot mode) allow finer-grained policies. Special cases: a Pi with a TPM add-on board reaches at most T3, because its firmware does not measure into the TPM. Diskless nodes without a hardware anchor are only permitted on explicit request, remain T1 and take on only stateless roles. VMs as nodes and external witnesses on third-party hosts are fixed at T1, because the platform cannot verify foreign hardware. Determination and dynamics # A trust controller in the cell computes the level from inventory, attestation results and events, and writes changes with a justification to the control plane. Operators can cap a level, never raise it – the only exception is a time-limited, justified trust exception approved under the four-eyes principle, which is visible in the compliance export. A downgrade takes effect immediately on new decisions (placement, secret issuance) and, after a grace period, on existing assignments. What each level may do # The minimum levels depend on the operating profile ( homelab , standard-c5 , erhoeht – elevated), not on the crypto profile: Function homelab standard-c5 erhoeht Raft voter, kms , identity , cell CA signing T1/T2 with a visible warning if no higher alternative exists at least T3; T4 once attestation is available T4 (until then T3 with a warning) all other nodes T1 T1 per role rules at least T3 Further rules: tenant workloads of data class sensitive run only on T3 or higher, class attested-only only on T4. Storage nodes may also be T1, because they only hold ciphertext (see Storage ). When choosing the control group, the level is a hard sorting criterion – but spreading across failure zones takes precedence : three T1 voters in three zones are better than three T4 voters in one zone. Tenant guardrails may only tighten these rules. A pure Pi homelab remains fully functional, with the degradation visibly flagged. If a node's level drops, the control group controller replaces it as a voter, the KMS discards plaintext keys immediately, workloads with protection requirements are migrated within a grace period, and secrets with a minimum level are no longer renewed. Standard workloads remain unaffected. Node identity and lifecycle # A node's identity consists of an immutable UID (new with every re-adoption), a human-readable name, a SPIFFE ID in the certificate, the node key generated on the node (in the TPM, otherwise as a file on an encrypted disk), endorsement and attestation keys on TPM devices, an underlay key and a hardware fingerprint. Node certificates are short-lived and are renewed from half of their lifetime onward. The lifecycle runs from discovery (ephemeral key, no basis of trust) through adoption and initial certification to ongoing renewal . If a node has been offline for a longer time, re-certification follows, whose evidence depends on the level: with a TPM, cryptographic evidence suffices; nodes without a TPM need human approval by default. A mismatched hardware fingerprint never leads to silent reissuance but to quarantine – the operator decides on replacement or confirmation. At the end comes revocation with a tombstone that prevents automatic re-admission. Remote attestation # Remote attestation makes level T4 possible. Attestation takes place at adoption, at every boot before joining the cluster, at every certificate renewal, periodically, after every update and on demand. The flow in brief: Once per adoption: the verifier validates the TPM's endorsement certificate against a curated, signed bundle of manufacturer CAs. Credential activation proves that the attestation key resides in the same TPM; the node key is proven to be TPM-resident. Every attestation: the verifier sends a one-time nonce, and the node returns a signed TPM quote together with the event log. Checked are the signature, nonce, monotonicity of the TPM counters and that the log matches the PCR values. Comparison against a policy made up of signed reference values from the release manifest (bootloader, kernel image, command line with dm-verity root hash, expected Secure Boot keys) and an operator-confirmed firmware baseline per device model. Verification is event by event rather than only on final PCR values – this keeps firmware updates and multiple permitted image versions manageable and deviations explainable. The reference values are read-only and come exclusively from signed manifests (see OS image and Release signing ). Attestation only decides on level and state; secrets are issued separately and only afterwards. The verifier is in-house Rust code on the control-plane nodes. Nodes without a TPM report image version, boot path and Secure Boot status signed with their node key. This detects misconfiguration and outdated images, but not an attacker with root privileges – which is why such nodes stay at T1/T2. Failure classes # Class Examples Response Indication of tampering invalid quote signature, changed key, log does not match the PCRs, nonce replay, Secure Boot suddenly off immediate quarantine, high-severity alert Unknown, plausible measurements new firmware version, image outside the permitted window downgrade to T3, alert, return after operator approval Missing evidence verifier unreachable, node offline downgrade after validity expires, never quarantine Quarantine # Quarantine can be reached directly from any adopted state and takes effect at all levels: instead of a regular certificate, the node receives a short-lived quarantine certificate that only permits diagnostics, attestation and forensic export. It loses any role in the control group, is excluded from gossip (the gossip key is rotated immediately), can be reached in the underlay only by control-plane nodes, receives no keys whatsoever, and workloads with protection requirements are stopped. Exit only via fresh evidence and human approval – or decommissioning. Service identities and mTLS # One identity per process boundary, not per role: all roles within the agent use the node certificate; which role a node may perform is authorized from the control plane on every call, not from the certificate. In-house service processes outside the agent (such as the boot service cp-bootd or the block storage service cp-blkd ) and third-party components (time service, telemetry, object storage, etc.) receive their own locally generated keys with short-lived service certificates whose SPIFFE path lies beneath the host's path. This makes it possible to answer, from the certificate and the control state alone, whether a service is running on the node the role is assigned to. Third-party processes never receive the node key, the gossip secret or KMS access; their keys are kept in unit-specific, ephemeral credential directories. For every mTLS connection between agents, a dedicated verifier checks in addition to the TLS parameters: the chain up to the cell or region CA of its own region (the workload CA and public CAs are never accepted on infras

s: Principles of the cryptography concept – alignment with BSI TR-02102, two crypto profiles, a PKI with short lifetimes, two-layer encryption of data at rest and a roadmap to post-quantum cryptography.
h: Data at rest and key hierarchy
x: The cryptography concept describes the product-side part of a cryptography concept as defined by BSI IT-Grundschutz (module CON.1): algorithms, defaults, key lifecycle and evidence functions for all platform components. The organizational parts – choice of profile, key ceremony, custody of recovery shares – are supplied by the operator. Cryptography inside tenant workloads is the tenant's responsibility; the platform provides keys, certificates and randomness for it. Who is entrusted with which key is governed by the security model . Principles # No home-grown crypto primitives – only vetted libraries (rustls with aws-lc-rs in userland, kernel cryptography, TPM). BSI TR-02102 is authoritative. Deviations are justified per finding, documented and assessed by the operator. Security level of at least 120 bits ; AES-256 for long-term confidentiality. Quantum safety for confidentiality first (protection against "harvest now, decrypt later"), then for signatures. Short lifetimes instead of revocation infrastructure , wherever possible. Purpose binding: one key, one purpose – enforced through context labels during derivation and wrapping. Crypto agility: algorithms are never hard-wired into a data format; every ciphertext carries its algorithm, key ID and version. Fail closed: an agent refuses connections if its crypto profile cannot be satisfied – except for explicitly approved exceptions. Symmetric wherever possible: the key hierarchy, backups and archives use only AES-256 and SHA-2-based schemes and are therefore already quantum-resistant today. Normative basis # The basis is the technical guideline BSI TR-02102 in its current version. Particularly relevant for the concept: TLS 1.3 is the target protocol; TLS 1.2 is only permitted as a transitional measure. Purely classical key agreement is recommended only until the end of 2031; after that only hybrid with post-quantum schemes (ML-KEM). Purely classical signatures are planned until the end of 2035; candidate post-quantum signatures are ML-DSA, SLH-DSA and hash-based schemes. For IPsec, the guideline covers only IKEv2. WireGuard, used as the underlay, is not covered there; the platform adds a post-quantum layer to it. Deviations are documented and assessed by the operator. Crypto profiles # The platform has two centrally configurable profiles. The active profile is a platform resource, applies at every level, and is enforced by every agent and reported as actual state. Regions may tighten it, never loosen it. bsi-strict (default) compatible (e.g. homelab) Transport TLS 1.3 without 0-RTT additionally TLS 1.2 at the public ingress for legacy clients Key agreement hybrid, preferably SecP256r1MLKEM768 hybrid, preferably X25519MLKEM768 Signatures ECDSA P-384 (CA) and P-256 (end-entity certificates) additionally Ed25519 Symmetric AES-256-GCM, AES-256-XTS additionally ChaCha20-Poly1305 for devices without AES acceleration Underlay WireGuard with mandatory PQ layer PQ layer on by default, can be disabled with a warning Hybrid post-quantum key agreement is the default in both profiles from the first release. Both profiles prohibit outdated schemes such as TLS up to 1.1, short RSA keys, SHA-1/MD5 for security purposes, CBC modes in TLS, and 0-RTT. The compatible profile is a deliberate decision that is visible in the compliance report. Profile changes run as a staged rollout: first accept the new schemes, then switch off the old ones. Individual nodes can be granted a time-limited, justified and approved exception , for example a device without AES acceleration. Such nodes are automatically excluded from the placement of workloads with protection requirements and appear in the compliance export. PKI # The internal PKI is hierarchical: platform root CA → region CA → cell CA → node and service certificates . Alongside it are a dedicated workload CA for tenant workloads and a separate CA (public via ACME or provided by the operator) for public endpoints. Separate trust domains: infrastructure mTLS trusts only cell and region CAs, never the workload CA. A tenant workload can therefore never identify itself as a node. Short lifetimes: node certificates are valid for days, service certificates for hours, workload certificates for minutes. Renewal starts at half the lifetime. Revocation: instead of OCSP or public revocation lists, short lifetimes suffice. Only for nodes is there additionally a replicated, signed and versioned revocation list that takes effect immediately and cannot be rolled back. Root key: during initialization, the root key is split into k-of-n recovery shares (Shamir). In the bsi-strict profile the online copy is deleted once the region CA has been issued; the root can then only be reconstructed through a ceremony under the four-eyes principle. CA keys are stored wrapped in the key management service; signing happens only on control nodes. Keys are preferably held in the TPM 2.0 . Devices without a TPM unlock their disk via a network-bound threshold release by the cell. Data at rest and key hierarchy # Data at rest is encrypted in two layers : Platform layer: every node disk is encrypted with LUKS2 (AES-256-XTS) – protection against theft and device returns. Tenant layer: every volume, every bucket and every backup has its own data encryption key (DEK). Block storage is encrypted on the compute host, so storage nodes only ever see ciphertext (see Storage ). The key hierarchy is platform root key → region KEK → tenant KEK → DEK . Wrapping uses AES-256-GCM; the additional authenticated data binds each wrapped key to object, purpose, tenant and KEK version, so it cannot be unwrapped for anything else. Plaintext keys exist only in the memory of the key management service or, briefly, on the authorized host. A host receives a DEK only for resources verifiably placed on it; operator roles never receive tenant DEKs. Crypto-shredding by destroying a key renders data, including backups, unreadable and is documented with a signed deletion certificate. Tenant-owned keys from external KMS/HSM (BYOK/HYOK) will follow in a later phase. Crypto agility and PQC roadmap # Agility is built in: the profile is configuration, all in-house formats are versioned, algorithm changes run as an expand/contract rollout, and agents report the schemes actually negotiated – old schemes are switched off only once the migration is complete. Where no standard for composite signatures exists, dual signatures are used, both of which must be valid. Every use of cryptography is recorded in a machine-readable cryptographic inventory (CycloneDX CBOM) and checked against the profile in CI. When Step First release Hybrid key agreement at all endpoints, PQ layer in the underlay, cryptographic inventory, profiles, AES-256 for data at rest Following phase ML-DSA dual signatures for updates, audit and deletion certificates; tenant-owned keys After inclusion in TR-02102 ML-DSA in the internal PKI, initially in parallel with the classical chain By end of 2030 Internal PKI fully post-quantum capable End of 2031 No more purely classical key agreement End of 2035 No more purely classical signatures (as far as hardware boot chains allow) The inventory, roadmap, hybrid schemes and annual review also form the basis for a PQC strategy as expected by current cloud audit catalogs (see Compliance requirements ).

s: Method and principles of the product risk analysis – STRIDE per trust boundary, assessment and treatment according to BSI Standard 200-3, abstract attacker models, security assumptions and maintenance of the model.
x: The threat model is the project's product risk analysis . It assesses the software and its intended architecture, not a specific deployment. Operators carry out their own risk analysis for their information domain; the model is structured so that threats, controls and residual risks can be adopted as a template into an operator's ISMS. This page summarizes the method and principles; the controls themselves are found in the individual concepts, in particular the security model and cryptography . Method # Threats are identified using STRIDE per trust boundary and assessed and treated according to BSI Standard 200-3 . The procedure: System model: assets, data flows and trust boundaries. Attacker models and assumptions. Threat overview: STRIDE per boundary; each threat is mapped to at least one elementary threat of BSI IT-Grundschutz so that operators can import it into their 200-3 or Grundschutz++ tooling. Risk rating: likelihood × impact, each gross (without) and net (with controls). Risk treatment: avoid, reduce, transfer, accept. Consolidation of new controls and remaining risks. Feedback into the individual concepts and the development process. STRIDE maps to the security objectives: Spoofing violates authenticity, Tampering integrity, Repudiation non-repudiation, Information Disclosure confidentiality, Denial of Service availability and Elevation of Privilege authorization. Cross-cutting concerns are software vulnerabilities, products from unreliable sources, operating errors, theft and malware. Rating scales # Ratings are made for a "multi-tenant operation" reference profile over a typical year of operation. Likelihood ranges in four levels from rare (requires rare capabilities or a chain of failures) to very frequent (normal operation creates the condition). Impact ranges from negligible to existential – the latter meaning cross-tenant loss of confidentiality or integrity, or the takeover of a cell, region or PKI. Together they yield one of four risk categories: low, medium, high, very high. Acceptance criteria # Category Handling low accepted medium accepted on condition that the effectiveness of the control is demonstrated (test, pentest) high release blocker unless explicitly accepted as residual risk very high never accepted – the architecture is changed A net risk only counts as reduced once the control is implemented and tested ; until then the gross risk applies. Trust boundaries # The system model distinguishes thirteen trust boundaries, including: internet and users versus portal and API, AI clients versus the MCP interface, tenant versus tenant, tenant workload versus host, nodes among each other, the control group versus the remaining nodes, witnesses, discovery and boot network, out-of-band management, supply chain versus installation, operator versus tenant content, physical site, and external identity providers. For each boundary it is defined what crosses it and what enforces it. Attacker models # Attackers are modeled abstractly by starting position and capabilities: External attacker with access to public endpoints, from automated scans to targeted attacks. Malicious tenant with a valid account and arbitrary code in their own workloads. Compromised node with root privileges and that node's key material. Foreign device in the discovery or home network on the same network segment. Physical attacker with brief or permanent access to devices and disks. Malicious operator or insider – deliberately modeled as strong. Compromised dependency or supply chain. Compromised or manipulated AI agent , for example steered via prompt injection. Third-party operator of an external witness. In addition, operating errors, hardware and power failures, and software bugs count as threat sources within the meaning of 200-3. Security assumptions and non-goals # The model rests on explicitly stated assumptions, including: the cryptographic primitives and random number generator used are secure; CPU, virtualization hardware and IOMMU work as specified; control nodes are physically protected or have TPM, measured boot and disk encryption; at most one voter of a cell is compromised at any one time (the consensus is not Byzantine fault tolerant); people control their authenticators; operators fulfill their obligations under the shared responsibility model; time is authenticated after boot. Non-goals are protection against state-level attackers with hardware implants in new devices, protection of tenant content against operators with physical access without confidential computing, and defense against volumetric DDoS attacks on the internet uplink. Principles of risk treatment # Avoid through architecture decisions that eliminate a threat – for example no shared kernel between tenants, no interactive login out of the box, no automatic break-glass, no destructive actions based on gossip messages, no security-critical roles at adoption, no automatic admission of foreign devices. Reduce through technical controls in the individual concepts. Transfer to operators (network separation, physical protection, firmware selection) or tenants (guest operating systems, their own applications) according to the shared responsibility model, documented in the operator and tenant handbooks. Accept only what is at most medium after reduction or has been explicitly taken on by the risk owner. Guiding principles from the analysis: trust must never arise from network boot , but only from an adoption process bound to a device key with human confirmation or an allowlist; new nodes start at a lower trust level. Destructive actions by AI agents are confirmed outside the client , because prompt injection cannot be fully prevented. Maintaining the model # The model is updated when new roles, components or trust boundaries are added, when a third-party component is replaced, after pentest findings and security-relevant vulnerabilities, for new versions of the MCP specification, and at the latest before every minor release. It is maintained in machine-readable form so that CI can check that every threat has a control with a test or a documented acceptance. Every control with a net risk of medium receives at least one automated test or a pentest checkpoint. Related pages: BSI IT-Grundschutz · Compliance by design · Vulnerability management

s: Architecture decision for the web portal – why a Svelte 5 SPA embedded in the agent won out over Rust/WASM, React and server-side rendering.
x: Status: accepted on 2026-11-12 after an open-ended comparative prototype. Decision: Svelte 5 + Vite as a pure single-page app (without SvelteKit), Bits UI for complex accessible building blocks, all other components built in-house following the WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices. Context # On every node , the Rust agent serves the API, web portal and MCP itself. There is no central web server; the portal is embedded as static assets in the agent binary and must be servable even from a Raspberry Pi with a small memory budget. Parity principle: every API operation is also available in the portal and via MCP. Forms should be derived from the API schema (OpenAPI 3.1 / JSON Schema) wherever possible, so that new API features appear without manual work (see API-first ). Feature scope: initial setup wizard, node and hardware overview with adoption, live updates, tenant self-service (VMs, containers, Kubernetes, volumes, buckets, networks), serial console and VNC, charts, German/English, light and dark themes, and accessibility according to BITV 2.0 / WCAG 2.1 AA for public-sector use. Security: a strict Content Security Policy without inline scripts and without eval , a traceable supply chain (SBOM). Text supplied by tenants or devices is never rendered as HTML and is visibly marked as third-party content. Confirmation page: for out-of-band confirmation of destructive actions and of adoption, the platform renders a dedicated page with an impact report and passkey confirmation. It is part of the portal but is populated exclusively by the platform – never by an AI client. The guiding principle "own components in Rust" applies to the control plane . The portal is a client of the API, not a control component – so the choice of language was open. Decision drivers # Criterion Weight Why Accessibility (WCAG 2.1 AA / BITV 2.0) high Mandatory for public authorities; expensive to retrofit Schema-driven forms / parity high Otherwise the portal backlog grows with every API version Component ecosystem (tables, charts, terminal, VNC, dialogs) high A large share of the work Security and supply chain (CSP, SBOM) high Compliance by design, browser attack surface Maturity and longevity high The platform is to be maintained for at least ten years Contributor pool, development speed medium-high An open source project lives on contributions Type safety against the API medium "Client/server drift" class of bugs Bundle size, embedding in the binary medium Binary size, load time over slow links Load on Pi nodes medium Serving only, rendering happens in the browser Internationalization, theming medium Standard requirement Testability incl. automated accessibility checks medium Regression tests in CI Options considered # Family Options A – Rust/WASM Leptos (client-side, optionally with server-side rendering), Dioxus, Yew B – TypeScript SPA (statically built, served by the agent) React, Svelte 5 (with or without SvelteKit), SolidJS, Vue 3 C – Server-side rendering in Rust HTMX with server-side HTML templates Maturity of Rust frontends (as of November 2026) # Leptos: stable 0.8 line, version 0.9 in beta with further breaking changes; a very small circle of core developers, no 1.0 in sight. Component libraries exist, but without demonstrated WCAG conformance. Dioxus: company-backed, with accessible base components ("primitives"), but likewise pre-1.0, with the next major version bringing breaking changes; increasingly focused on desktop and mobile. Yew: in maintenance mode; no longer advisable for a new project. Conclusion: all Rust frontends are pre-1.0 and break their APIs roughly once a year. For a platform aimed at the public sector with a ten-year horizon, that is a significant risk that does not arise in the same way with the major versions of the TypeScript frameworks, which have been stable for years. Assessment # Scale: ++ very good · + good · o neutral · − weak · −− critical Criterion Leptos Dioxus React Svelte Solid Vue HTMX Accessibility − o ++ + + + + / − for dynamic widgets Schema forms − − ++ + o + o Components (charts, terminal, VNC) − − ++ + o + − CSP and supply chain ++ + o o o o ++ Maturity, longevity − − ++ + o + + Contributors, speed − o ++ + o + o API type safety ++ ++ + + + + ++ Bundle, embedding o o/− + ++ ++ + ++ Load on the Pi + + + + + + − i18n, theming o o ++ + o ++ + Testability o o ++ ++ + ++ + Key trade-offs # 1. Rust's type-safety advantage is smaller than it looks. Shared Rust types are the strongest argument for Leptos or Dioxus. But since the portal works from the OpenAPI schema anyway, the schema is the actual source of the contract. A type-safe TypeScript client generated on every build, plus a CI check, catches drift just as reliably. Generic form rendering works with JSON Schema at runtime – compile-time type safety does not help there in any language. 2. The hard widgets are JavaScript – whatever the framework. Terminal emulation (serial console), VNC, time-series charts and mature accessible data tables exist only in the JS ecosystem. Rust/WASM would need bridges for each of them – and would still bring npm into the supply chain. 3. Accessibility is the toughest criterion. BITV requires accessible comboboxes, dialogs with focus traps, sortable tables, live regions for real-time updates and full keyboard operation. The JS ecosystem has proven headless libraries for this; the Rust ecosystem has only a young approach with no audit history. In our experience, building accessible widgets in-house is the most expensive and error-prone frontend work. 4. Supply chain: npm vs. cargo. npm suffered several large-scale compromises in 2025. cargo is not immune, but has a flatter dependency landscape. The risk with TypeScript is real but manageable , because npm packages run only at build time and only the reviewed, bundled output ends up in the binary. 5. Load on the Pi argues against server-side rendering. All SPA variants serve only precompressed static files – CPU load close to zero. HTMX, by contrast, renders every view in the agent and creates a second presentation interface alongside the REST API . The API would no longer be the single source of truth, which contradicts parity. Console, VNC and charts would still need JavaScript. 6. Server-side rendering with hydration brings no benefit here. SEO and fast first page load are irrelevant for an authenticated admin portal; it would only shift load onto Pi nodes. The comparative prototype # Instead of fixing the technology up front, an open-ended comparison was carried out: Svelte and Leptos were measured against the same views that are critical for accessibility; React remained the fallback option. View Tests Node overview with adoption Table accessibility, live regions, dialog focus trap, live updates, theme "Create VM" purely from OpenAPI Schema renderer, drift check, i18n, form accessibility VM detail with console, VNC and time series Lazy loading, strict CSP, keyboard operability, bundle budgets Confirmation page Passkey integration, strict CSP, no rendering of third-party content as HTML Acceptance criteria included: meeting the performance budgets, a CSP without unsafe-inline and unsafe-eval , zero serious findings from automated accessibility checks plus manual testing with screen readers (NVDA, Orca) and keyboard only, schema changes appearing in the form without portal code changes, SBOM generation for the portal build, and measured serving from the Pi. Result: the Svelte variant came in at around 28 KiB of initial JavaScript (Brotli), ran with a CSP without any exceptions and had no findings from the automated accessibility checks. The Leptos variant was considerably larger at around 191 KiB, needed a CSP exception for WebAssembly and had a much longer build time. Because SvelteKit generates an inline bootstrap script, the choice fell on plain Vite + Svelte instead of SvelteKit. Decision # The portal is a Svelte 5 single-page app built with Vite , statically bundled, precompressed and embedded in the agent binary.
