Type safety against the API comes from code generation from OpenAPI; forms are rendered at runtime from JSON Schema with the project's own schema extensions. Building block Choice Framework Svelte 5 + Vite, pure SPA API client Types generated from OpenAPI + lean fetch client Accessible base components Bits UI (headless); in-house builds only following WAI-ARIA patterns Styling, theme CSS custom properties as design tokens; light, dark, high contrast Schema forms Own renderer for JSON Schema plus extensions for widget, order, translation keys Tables Headless table library Charts Small time-series library, complex charts loaded on demand Serial console, VNC Established JS libraries, loaded on demand Live updates Server-Sent Events with announcements via live regions; WebSocket only for console and VNC i18n Translation at build time; keys from the API reused Tests Unit and component tests, end-to-end tests with automated accessibility checks Why Svelte rather than React? React has the strongest ecosystem and remains the fallback option. Svelte wins on bundle size – important because every node carries the portal – has far fewer transitive npm dependencies, a low barrier to entry for Rust developers, and built-in accessibility warnings in the compiler. Why not Leptos? Leptos is the most serious Rust candidate, and the advantage of shared types is real. Against it are its pre-1.0 status with a small maintainer circle, a lack of proven accessible components, JS bridges for all core widgets, larger bundles and a smaller contributor pool. The decision will be reviewed at the end of 2027 . A switch remains possible because the portal talks exclusively through the public API. Rejected options # Yew: maintenance mode, weakest ecosystem. Dioxus: pre-1.0, focus on multi-platform rather than a web admin interface, larger bundles. Leptos with server-side rendering: load on the Pi, no benefit for an authenticated portal. SolidJS: technically excellent, but a smaller pool and less mature form and accessibility libraries. Vue 3: solid, but larger bundles than Svelte and a smaller accessibility ecosystem than React. HTMX with templates: a second rendering path alongside the API, load on nodes; conceivable at most as an emergency page without JavaScript. Consequences # Positive: Access to mature, accessible components – BITV/WCAG evidence becomes realistic. Large contributor pool; frontend developers do not have to learn Rust. The portal is a pure API client and thus enforces parity technically: whatever the portal can do, the API can do too. Small bundles, no rendering load on nodes; the portal works identically from any node. Effort and mandatory measures: A second toolchain in the build. The portal build runs as a separate CI step; its artifact is fed into the Rust build in versioned form. Rust contributors can build without Node using a prebuilt artifact or a placeholder portal. Actively manage the npm supply chain: locked dependencies, install scripts disabled by default, a minimum age for new package versions to guard against freshly compromised releases, a limited dependency budget with review of every new dependency, SBOMs for npm and cargo (the portal SBOM is part of the agent SBOM), vulnerability scans in CI and a reproducible portal build. Content Security Policy as a must , checked automatically: only own sources for scripts and connections, no objects, no embedding in third-party frames, no unsafe-inline , no unsafe-eval , no tenant HTML. Types are not shared but generated – OpenAPI is the source, code generation runs in CI. The binary grows by about 1–3 MB. The agent serves the precompressed files directly, without runtime compression, with long-term caching for files with a hash in their name. Performance budgets (binding from MVP) # Metric Budget Initial JavaScript (Brotli) ≤ 120 KB Initial CSS (Brotli) ≤ 30 KB Lazy-loaded parts for console, VNC, charts ≤ 250 KB each Time to interactive over a 10 Mbit/s link ≤ 2 s

s: How DCP manages models, operates inference endpoints, schedules accelerators and delivers AI services through its own AI gateway in a tenant-safe and compliant way.
h: EU AI Act and BSI AIC4
x: What "AI-native" means # For DCP, "AI-native" means three things: AI services for tenants – register models, run them as OpenAI-compatible endpoints, consume them through a gateway with keys, budgets and guardrails, and build knowledge bases (RAG). This ranges from the homelab (CPU, Raspberry Pi, integrated GPU, small NPUs) to the data center with GPU servers. The platform as a tool for agents – every function can be controlled via MCP (see API-first ). Agents are actors in their own right with intersected permissions (see Identity and permissions ). Compliance by design for AI – EU AI Act, GDPR, BSI AIC4 and C5: evidence is produced by ongoing operation (see Compliance by design ). Out of scope for this concept are AI-assisted platform operations, training large models, end-user products such as copilots, facial recognition and custom GPU kernels. The model is the AI offerings of the hyperscalers (catalog, serverless and dedicated endpoints, gateway, guardrails, knowledge bases, agent runtime). DCP adopts their common pattern: control, billing and policy belong to the platform; the inference engines are interchangeable. Key decisions at a glance # Topic Decision Resource model one API group ai.cloud-project.io/v1alpha1 , fully API-first (API, portal, MCP, CLI) Engines control in-house, engines external behind a process boundary; llama.cpp first, vLLM for GPU servers Isolation tenant-dedicated endpoints in MicroVMs with a passed-through accelerator; shared models as a platform service without tenant code Drivers standard image with open stacks only; proprietary runtimes only as a signed, explicitly enabled operator extension Models OCI artifacts in the platform registry, signed, with a cache per cell; safe formats only Scaling scale-to-zero only with a local model cache; the gateway buffers during activation Distributed inference two stages: engine-native first, own protocol only after measurement AI gateway own AI gateway developed in Rust – initially as a separate process, later as a library Agents the platform itself is controllable via MCP, with token exchange and intersected permissions Compliance AI compliance as a cross-cutting concern: model card, license, provenance, risk class, labeling, evidence The decisions were made on 2026-11-14. Resource model # All AI resources follow the platform's uniform resource schema (metadata/spec/status, URN, conditions, long-running operations, see Control plane ). Project resources are regional; the operator's catalog objects live in the global platform scope. Kind Purpose Model logical model: family, tasks (chat, embedding, rerank, speech, OCR, vision), license, provenance, model card, AI Act metadata ModelVersion immutable artifact: OCI reference with digest, format, quantization, context length, memory requirement, engine compatibility, signature status, stage ( draft to deprecated ), provenance chain, evaluation results InferenceEndpoint desired service: API kinds, traffic split across revisions, scaling, placement, network InferenceDeployment immutable revision of an endpoint (model version, engine, resources, parallelism); canary and rollback via weights AiGateway instance or tenant scope of the AI gateway with ingresses, default policies and logging policy GatewayRoute public model name → targets (internal endpoints, external providers), weights, fallbacks, limits, guardrails, cache AiBudget amount, period, warning thresholds, token limits – attached to a project, service account, key or route GuardrailPolicy ordered filter chain (PII, prompt filter, judge model, topic blocks, AI labeling) with failure behavior VectorIndex , KnowledgeBase vector index and knowledge base for RAG BatchInferenceJob batch processing from object storage, uses spare capacity AcceleratorClass operator-defined accelerator class: selector over the inventory, divisibility, price, minimum trust level A simplified example of an endpoint: yaml apiVersion: ai.cloud-project.io/v1alpha1 kind: InferenceEndpoint metadata: name: chat spec: apis: [openai.chat, openai.completions] traffic: - { deployment: r7, percent: 90 } - { deployment: r8, percent: 10 } # Canary scaling: { minReplicas: 0, maxReplicas: 4, scaleToZeroAfter: 15m, coldStartTimeout: 120s } placement: { arch: any, minTrustLevel: basic, dataClass: standard, spreadBy: zone } network: { exposure: private, gateway: default } deploymentTemplate: engine: { kind: llama-cpp, version: auto } resources: { accelerator: { class: igpu-vulkan, count: 1 }, memoryGiB: 12, cpu: 4 } No separate AI key type. Callers authenticate with platform identities: workload tokens, API keys of service accounts, or user tokens. As a convenience, the portal shortcut "Create AI key" creates, in a single step, a service account with invoke permission on the selected routes plus a budget. Platform workloads use their workload identity without any stored key at all. Permissions and audit. Calling an endpoint ( invoke ) is a separate data-plane permission, distinct from management. Deleting production model versions or populated knowledge bases counts as destructive and requires confirmation outside the calling client. Model output and document content are marked as untrusted: agents receive them as data, never as instructions, and the portal never renders them as HTML. Prompts and responses are tenant content and do not belong in the platform audit log; only usage metadata (tokens, model, route, cost, guardrail hits) goes to metering. Inference engines # Inference performance comes from hand-optimized kernels for CUDA, ROCm, Vulkan, AVX or NEON, maintained by large communities. Building our own would make no sense here. Everything around them is our own: adapters, endpoint proxy, scheduler integration, cache and distribution, gateway, metering and compliance. Engine License Role llama.cpp MIT first engine : broadest hardware support (CPU, Vulkan, CUDA, ROCm), arm64 and amd64, GGUF, also for embeddings and rerankers vLLM Apache-2.0 second engine for GPU servers: tensor, pipeline, expert and data parallelism ONNX Runtime, whisper.cpp MIT for OCR/vision and speech recognition respectively, each as a separate engine process Hailo runtime partly proprietary only as an operator extension for edge services (vision, speech, small LLMs) candle and other Rust engines permissive not used at present; candidates for later re-evaluation Ollama, TGI – not used (duplicate model management or maintenance mode, respectively) A CPU benchmark showed a candle-based Rust engine at 44–65% of llama.cpp's decode and 25–47% of its prefill performance. That is why all model types – including embeddings and rerankers – run on external engines. Engine adapter contract # Engines run as signed OCI images in the platform's container service, never directly with tenant privileges: Image from the operator's engine catalog, approved per version, with SBOM and provenance. Model as a read-only mount from the local cell cache – no download inside the engine process, no egress. Interface: OpenAI-compatible HTTP on a Unix socket. A dedicated endpoint proxy terminates mTLS or workload tokens, enforces concurrency limits, counts tokens and provides scaling signals. Engines never talk directly to tenants or the gateway. Mandatory functions per adapter: launch description, readiness, metrics (queue, running sequences, tokens, KV cache utilization), capabilities and graceful shutdown. A new engine needs only an adapter and an image. Sandbox: dedicated user, seccomp/Landlock, only the required device files, no network other than the socket. Because engines are run as processes rather than linked, copyleft licenses are unproblematic too. Model weights have their own licenses, some with usage restrictions; the catalog records them as a mandatory field, flags non-OSI licenses and can block them by policy. Accelerators and placement # The node inventory detects accelerators (vendor, model, memory, driver and firmware version, IOMMU group, NUMA node, PCIe link, divisibility). Device self-reports are treated as untrusted; suitability is decided by a smoke inference at admission and by operator labels. Device Stack Assessment CPU (AVX2/AVX-512/NEON) open baseline, always available; small models, embeddings, batch Integrated GPU (Vulkan) open good for the homelab AMD GPU (ROCm) open recommended for a fully open stack NVIDIA GPU (CUDA) proprietary userspace market standard, only as a signed operator extension NPUs (AMD XDNA, Intel) partly open watch, later Hailo modules proprietary compiler operator extension for edge services Isolation. Tenant-dedicated endpoints get an entire device, passed through via VFIO to exactly one MicroVM – there is no shared kernel between tenants (see Security model ). Devices without clean IOMMU separation serve only shared platform services. GPU sharing between tenants via containers is planned only for a later phase and only with hardware partitioning (MIG); time-slicing without hardware isolation remains excluded. Scheduler requirements: Accelerators as a hard resource (class, count, minimum memory), bin packing by accelerator memory. Gang scheduling: a multi-node deployment is placed in full or not at all. Topology: minimum bandwidth, same zone, maximum network hops. Cache affinity: nodes with the model in their local cache are preferred. Priorities: production before interactive before batch; batch jobs are preemptible. Quotas for accelerators and accelerator memory; shared models via token budgets. Trust level and data class as for virtual machines. Operating models # Dedicated Shared (serverless) External Runs the engine Tenant (platform-controlled) Operator Third-party provider Isolation MicroVM with passed-through device Operator process with additional rules Contract/DPA Billing Device hours Tokens Tokens, pass-through billing Models Any, including own fine-tunes Operator catalog Provider catalog Typical use Data protection, own models Small teams, embeddings Frontier models Fixed rules apply to shared models: no cross-tenant prefix or KV cache , quotas per tenant, no storage of prompts without consent, memory discarded after the request, engine process without network, sensitive data only on nodes with a high trust level. All three models run through the same gateway: one key, one budget, one policy. Scaling and scale-to-zero # A cold start consists of placement, container start, model loading and warmup – loading dominates. An 8B model (Q4, around 5 GB) loads from local NVMe in a few seconds, but takes around 45 seconds over 1 GbE from the cell cache; a 70B model takes several minutes over 1 GbE. It follows that: Scale-to-zero only when the model is stored locally (cache affinity, prewarming at creation). The gateway buffers requests during activation and, once the timeout expires, responds with 503 and Retry-After . The scaling signal is queue length and running sequences per replica, not CPU load. Default: in the homelab, sleep after 15 minutes of idle time; in production, at least one replica. Model distribution: OCI and signing # Format: a model is an OCI artifact with its own media type; the layers are weights, tokenizer, model card and license text. Large files are split into chunks – for parallel transfer and deduplication. Import: an import job downloads from an explicitly approved source, verifies hashes, generates a model bill of materials (files, hashes, license, source, revision) and signs it with the platform code-signing key (see Cryptography ). Vendor signatures are additionally verified where available. Without a valid signature there is no placement in regulated profiles; in the homelab there is a warning. Safe formats only: safetensors and GGUF. Pickle-based formats are rejected at import in all profiles. Cache per cell: every inference node holds a content-addressed, encrypted cache. Nodes transfer models among themselves via mTLS with range requests – first from neighbors, then from the registry. Gossip only spreads who h

s: Which service categories from AWS, Azure and Google Cloud DCP covers, how they are implemented (in-house development or external component) and in which phase.
h: Part B – Data, AI and integration
Part C – Identity, security, operations, developers
Selected decisions for existing building blocks
x: Purpose # The analysis compares the service offerings of AWS, Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud with DCP's plan. It answers three questions: Which features should the platform eventually offer? How will they be implemented? And when? In total, around 230 features were examined across three areas: infrastructure; data, AI and integration; and identity, security, operations and developer tools. The analysis was accepted on 2026-11-12. The following tables are an abridged selection of the most important categories. The platform builds control, policy and workflow logic itself – this fits the Raft-based state, authorization with Cedar, the parity of API, portal and MCP, and tenant isolation (see Rust stack and API-first ). Components with a very large maintenance or maturity effort remain external , always integrated across a process boundary: Database and protocol engines (PostgreSQL, MariaDB, Valkey, Kafka, OpenSearch, ClickHouse) – compatibility is the point here; a reimplementation would bring no benefit. Guardrail: "no database of our own" (see Vision ). Hypervisor, Kubernetes, container runtime – security- and kernel-critical, a large investment in maturity. Inference engines – they depend on GPU kernel ecosystems (see AI platform ). Knowledge bases that need constant upkeep – the scanners' vulnerability databases, DLP detectors. Python ecosystems such as Airflow, Spark, Jupyter or fine-tuning frameworks. Even with external engines: control, API, tenant isolation, backup and metering are developed in-house. An exception to "no database of our own" is block and object storage, which, following a separate decision, are developed in-house (see Storage ). All components must have OSI-approved licenses. This excludes, among others, HashiCorp Vault, Packer and Nomad (BUSL), newer versions of CockroachDB, ScyllaDB and EMQX, MongoDB (SSPL), Redpanda and Restate (see License and governance ). s: Why the DCP core is licensed under AGPL-3.0-or-later, which licenses apply to SDKs and documentation, how contributions work via DCO, and where the project stands under the Cyber Resilience Act.
h: Position under the Cyber Resilience Act
x: Note: This page summarizes the project's current technical and licensing understanding and is not legal advice. The choice of license, the trademark and the CRA role will be reviewed by legal counsel before the first public release. Starting point # DCP is written mostly in Rust and integrates numerous third-party components under different licenses. The goals: Everything open source – no mandatory "open core" components either (see Vision ). Operators – from homelabs through hosting providers and public authorities to corporate IT – should be able to run the platform freely . No proprietary cloud fork should emerge that keeps improvements to itself and sells them as a service. High acceptance among public authorities in the EU and among companies; as many external contributions as possible. The EU Cyber Resilience Act (CRA) is taken into account from the start. Licenses of dependencies # The most important third-party components – Cloud Hypervisor, Firecracker, Kata Containers, k3s, zot, Open vSwitch, Cilium – are licensed under Apache-2.0 or BSD licenses. The Linux kernel (GPL-2.0) and iPXE (GPL-2.0-or-later) are shipped in the OS image and by the boot role, respectively. The object storage building block Garage is licensed under AGPL-3.0. The policy engine Cedar (Apache-2.0) is linked directly. Key observation: As long as third-party components run as separate programs – across process, network or syscall boundaries – the project is largely free in its own choice of license. There remain, however, redistribution obligations (source code, license texts, NOTICE) for the shipped OS image. Only linking copyleft code would restrict the project's own license – and the project's process-boundary rule rules that out (see Rust stack ). Decision drivers # Driver Weight Protection against proprietary forks, especially the SaaS loophole (operation as a service without redistribution) high Acceptance among public authorities and companies, procurability high Patent protection (explicit patent license, patent retaliation clause) medium Compatibility with dependencies high Willingness of individuals and companies to contribute medium to high Operator freedom: operation without fees or permission, including commercially must Legal certainty (clarity, track record, EU law) medium Options evaluated # License Type SaaS loophole closed? Assessment Apache-2.0 permissive no standard in cloud native, maximum adoption – but offers no protection against exactly the scenario to be prevented MPL-2.0 weak copyleft (file level) no copyleft only on redistribution and only for modified files GPL-3.0 strong copyleft no pure network operation is not redistribution AGPL-3.0 strong copyleft with network clause yes the only widely proven license that closes the SaaS loophole; common in infrastructure EUPL-1.2 strong copyleft, EU license largely attractive to public authorities, but little case law, no patent retaliation, compatibility clause can weaken protection The experience of other projects (Elasticsearch, Redis, HashiCorp) shows that permissive or weak licenses later led to license changes and rifts with the community there. The price of the AGPL: some companies with internal AGPL bans will contribute less, and admission to the CNCF is practically ruled out. What the AGPL means for operators # Unmodified operation – including commercially, as a hosting provider or as a public authority: no obligations beyond passing on the license texts. Your own modifications used by tenants over the network (API, portal, MCP, S3): users must be offered the source code of the modified version. Internal modifications without external users: no obligation. To make this effortless, the platform includes a built-in source code endpoint – in the API, portal and MCP. It automatically points to the repository and the exact commit or build of the running version. Operators with their own patches only enter the address of their fork. Compliance thus becomes a side effect. Decision: the license matrix # Adopted on 2026-11-12: Component License Rationale Core: agent, control plane, services (VM, container, Kubernetes, storage, network), portal, MCP server, image build AGPL-3.0-or-later closes the SaaS loophole, patent clause, suitable for public authorities SDKs, client libraries, CLI, OpenTofu provider, API specifications, MCP schemas Apache-2.0 OR MIT clients should be embeddable in any software – including proprietary software Documentation, concepts, diagrams CC BY 4.0 free reuse with attribution, e.g. for training courses or public-authority handbooks Code examples, templates, boot scripts, configuration examples MIT-0 can be copied without conditions, including into GPL-2.0 contexts Build tools Apache-2.0 OR MIT same as SDKs Own kernel modules or eBPF programs (if needed) GPL-2.0-only OR BSD-2-Clause required by the kernel; dual license Patches to third-party projects upstream license upstream as a rule, no long-lived forks Logos, product name no free license – trademark policy protection against confusion caused by forks EUPL-1.2 remains an option under review until the first release. The AGPL is the more robust starting point: AGPL code can incorporate EUPL code, but not the other way around. "or-later" allows an upgrade to a future AGPL version without assignment of rights. Technical implementation # REUSE specification: SPDX header in every file, central license directory, automated checks in CI. License allowlist for dependencies (MIT, Apache-2.0, BSD, ISC, Zlib, Unicode-3.0 and others), checked with cargo-deny . SDK crates must not pull in copyleft. LGPL libraries are not linked. MPL-2.0 is allowed only for pure build tools that do not end up in the shipped artifact – it remains excluded at runtime. SBOM (CycloneDX and SPDX) for every release and every OS image – also a CRA requirement (see Release bundle ). Source code offer for the OS image: for every image, a complete source archive or permanent references to identical sources. The license boundary between core and SDK is visible in the crate layout. Special cases # Garage is accessed exclusively as a separate service via the S3 or admin API. Own patches are upstreamed. iPXE is shipped as a binary, so the license text and source code are included. Scripts are loaded at runtime where possible instead of being compiled in. Linux: the agent uses only syscalls, Netlink and ioctl – no derivative work. Identity: a dedicated authorization server is part of the core; external identity providers are connected only via OIDC federation, so their license is irrelevant (see Identity and access ). Contributions, trademark, governance # DCO instead of CLA # DCO CLA Effort for contributors sign-off in the commit, no contract contract, often involving the employer Relicensing by the project not possible (only "or-later" upgrade) possible – including toward proprietary Community trust high lower, especially with copyleft plus CLA Decision: Developer Certificate of Origin (DCO 1.1) , enforced by a CI check of the sign-off. No CLA. This way the project credibly commits to never relicensing as proprietary – the strongest argument for contributors and a counterweight to skepticism about the AGPL. Trademark # Licenses govern copyright, not trademarks. The product name is the most important means against confusing forks with proprietary add-ons. A trademark policy is planned: unmodified builds and distributions may use the name, modified forks only as "based on …", and compatibility claims require passing conformance tests (comparable to Kubernetes Conformance). The alpha name is Das Cloud Projekt (short DCP ); components carry the prefix cp (e.g. cpctl , cpOS , cp-agent ). Technical identifiers such as API groups keep the spelling cloud-project for now. Governance model # The organizational setup (legal entity, bodies) has deliberately not been decided yet. A staged model serves as orientation: Phase Trigger Model Founding until the first releases core maintainers; transparent decisions via ADR, public roadmap Opening several active maintainers from independent organizations or first major production deployment steering committee with a limited number of seats per organization, working groups (compute, storage, network, security) Neutral entity trademark, infrastructure and donations require a neutral legal entity foundation or registered association; the steering committee remains the technical body A possible neutral entity would be, for example, a European open source foundation that already has experience with copyleft and with the steward role under the CRA. A Code of Conduct based on the Contributor Covenant applies to all channels, with a confidential reporting channel. Security policy # The security policy also serves as the basis for the CRA (see Vulnerability management ): Confidential reporting channel, acknowledgment of receipt within 72 hours, standard embargo of 90 days, shorter in case of active exploitation. A security response team with a deputy arrangement. CVE assignment, machine-readable advisories (CSAF 2.0, OSV) and VEX statements on vulnerabilities in dependencies. Advance notification of registered operators and distributors under confidentiality rules. Supply chain: signed releases and images, SLSA provenance, reproducible builds as a goal, OpenSSF Scorecard (see Release signing ). Published supported versions and support periods per release line. Position under the Cyber Resilience Act # Timeline # Date What applies December 2024 CRA entered into force 2026-09-11 reporting obligations for manufacturers: actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents (early warning 24 h, notification 72 h) 2027-12-11 full application: essential requirements, conformity assessment, CE marking, obligations of open source stewards Views differ on when the reporting obligation takes effect for open source stewards; most sources name 2027-12-11. The project sets up its processes as if the obligation already applied – the effort is equivalent to good security practice. Roles # Constellation CRA role Consequence Community develops without profit motive, without a legal entity outside the scope no obligations Legal entity supports development systematically and sustainably, without monetization open source steward "light" regime, no fines Provider sells a product, distribution, appliance or support beyond cost recovery manufacturer full regime Hosting provider runs the platform as a service CRA does not apply to pure service operation; NIS2 instead operator compliance Public authority runs it internally neither manufacturer nor steward BSI IT-Grundschutz or NIS2 Obligations as open source steward # A documented cybersecurity policy that promotes secure development and the handling of vulnerabilities – implemented via the security policy and the security handbook. Cooperation with market surveillance authorities on request. Reporting obligations , insofar as the project is involved – for example in incidents affecting the project infrastructure (repositories, build, release signing). Voluntary: a security attestation that makes due diligence easier for manufacturers. Later commercial offerings # Monetization makes you a manufacturer. Donations without a profit motive are harmless. Product classes: the platform contains components of Class I (operating systems, boot managers, identity and access management, network management, PKI) and Class II (hypervisors, container runtimes). Class II generally requires a third-party conformity assessment. For free and open source products, however, internal control suffices if the technical documentation is public . That is why the technical documentation is kept public from the start. Manufacturer obligations include security by design, secure defaults, updates, SBOM, vulnerability management, support period, declaration of conformity, CE marking, reporting obligations and due diligence for integrated third-party components. In additio

s: Which regulatory frameworks apply to DCP, how the requirements catalog is structured, how obligations are split between platform, operator and tenant, and which precedence rules apply in case of conflicts.
x: Note: This page presents a technical requirements analysis and is not legal advice. Research status: November 2026. Binding use requires checking against the original documents. Key points # It is the operator that gets certified or attested, not the software. The platform must enable operators to implement controls effectively and provide evidence for them. To that end it delivers technical functions, secure defaults, a shared responsibility matrix and exportable evidence. The software itself is subject to the EU Cyber Resilience Act (CRA) – for anyone who places it on the market in the course of a commercial activity. Reporting obligations have applied since 2026-09-11, all other obligations from 2027-12-11. Parts of the platform (OS image, identity management, hypervisor and container runtime) are expected to fall under "important products". BSI C5:2026 has been published – with 168 basic criteria in 17 areas and new focus topics such as container management, supply chain/SBOM, post-quantum cryptography and confidential computing. It becomes mandatory for audits from mid-2027. Grundschutz++ has been published as BSI Standard 300-1 since 2026-10-26. The user catalog with around 1,000 requirements is available in machine-readable OSCAL format. Classic BSI IT-Grundschutz remains usable for a transition period of several years. NIS2 has applied in Germany since 2025-12-06. Cloud providers and data center operators are among the NIS2 sectors; for them, an EU implementing regulation specifies the technical measures. Lead catalog: ISO/IEC 27001 Annex A provides the structure, BSI C5:2026 is the benchmark for content, Grundschutz++ the machine-readable source of detail. In case of conflict the stricter requirement applies – as long as it remains configurable for all deployment sizes from homelab to data center. Overview of regulatory frameworks # Relevance is assessed separately: for the software (the project as manufacturer) and for the operator . s: How DCP models the "platform" sub-domain of the information domain from the manufacturer's perspective according to Grundschutz++, maps requirements to components and evidence, and provides operators with a protection requirements template.
h: Protection requirements assumptions as a template
x: Note: Technical modeling, not legal or audit advice. The modeling is a template; responsibility for the operator's own information domain (Informationsverbund) remains with the operator. Key decisions # No. Decision 1 The target is Grundschutz++ (BSI Standard 300-1, user catalog in OSCAL format). The IT-Grundschutz Compendium 2023 (IT-Grundschutz-Kompendium) is supplied only as a derived view for operators who still work with it – generated, not maintained by hand. 2 What is modeled is the "platform" sub-domain of the information domain (Teil-Informationsverbund) from the manufacturer's perspective : 13 technical target objects, the node hardware and seven information types. The operator adopts it as a building block of its own information domain and adds location, personnel and organization. 3 There is a single, versioned source for the mapping requirement ↔ Grundschutz++ requirement ↔ target object ↔ responsibility ↔ evidence. All operator artifacts are generated from it. 4 References to Grundschutz++ requirements carry both keys : the human-readable ID and the stable UUID. 5 The continuously updated catalog is pinned and shipped with the platform; a regular update run produces a diff report for review. No build loads the catalog live from the network. 6 For assets without a matching target object category (containers, Kubernetes, KMS, distributed state) the project provides a small supplementary catalog . 7 A protection requirements template with assumptions per information type and target object, in three deployment profiles, compatible with both classic BSI IT-Grundschutz and Grundschutz++. 8 External checking tools (OSCAL validation) run only in CI as a separate process; the OSCAL files are produced by the project's own generator. Who models what? # BSI IT-Grundschutz modeling is the task of the organization that runs an ISMS – that is, the operator . The technical part, however, is the same for all installations, so the project, as manufacturer, does it in advance: Level Who Result Manufacturer template project target objects of the platform, mapping to target object categories and requirements, implementation description per component (OSCAL Component Definition), protection requirements assumptions, suggested parameters Operator's information domain operator adoption of the template, additions for sites, rooms, personnel, service providers and business processes; protection requirements, requirements package, parameters, implementation status Use by tenants tenant for the tenant, the entire platform is one cloud service ; it models its workloads itself For the operator, the components are applications, host systems and networks within its information domain; for the tenant, the platform is a cloud service. The shared responsibility matrix connects both views (see Compliance requirements ). Grundschutz++ in brief # The user catalog comprises around 1,000 requirements in 20 practices – for example asset management, permissions, detection, configuration, architecture, development and business continuity management. Each requirement carries a security level ( normal-SdT , i.e. normal/state of the art, or erhöht , i.e. elevated), its effect on the protection goals, associated threats, target object categories and in some cases parameters that the operator defines. Around 140 requirements carry the tag "product description" (Produktbeschreibung) – exactly the requirements that a manufacturer can provide as an OSCAL component definition. They form the mandatory scope of DCP's component definition. About a third of the requirements have no target object category; these are mostly ISMS and organizational requirements that apply to the operator's entire information domain. Here the platform only provides data sources : implementation status from the configuration, recorded exceptions to the secure default, evidence exports for audits, prepared reporting data for incidents, and protection requirements labels on resources. Because the catalog is updated continuously – roughly weekly – version pinning and referential integrity checks are indispensable. Third-party mapping tables are never adopted without review. The "platform" information domain # Scope # Inside the domain (platform provides, operator runs) Outside (operator or tenant models it themselves) all technical target objects, the node hardware and the platform's information types buildings and rooms, personnel, service providers, upstream network and firewall, tenants' guest systems and applications, operators' workstations The domain's external interfaces are: obtaining releases from the project, federation with identity providers, the operator's SIEM, the upstream network with DHCP, DNS and NTP, offsite backup, optionally an HSM or external KMS, tenant access via portal, API and MCP, and out-of-band management. Build, CI and release infrastructure belong to the project's information domain (manufacturer under the CRA). They are modeled as well because their evidence – SBOM, provenance, test reports – flows as input into the operator's information domain (see Release bundle ). Responsibility takes one of four values: Code Meaning P platform or project implements P→B platform provides the capability and a secure default, operator (Betreiber) applies or configures it B operator (Betreiber) M tenant (Mandant) An example for the node hardware: Requirement Responsibility Implementation Inventory of systems, detect unauthorized systems P→B The agent reports the hardware automatically; nodes that have not been adopted appear visibly as "waiting". Supplementary catalog # For assets without a matching target object category there is a small dedicated OSCAL catalog. The requirements are worded following the sentence template of Grundschutz++ and reference their origin in the Compendium or in C5. Examples: The control plane SHOULD admit only nodes with the minimum trust level of the deployment profile as voting members. The control plane SHOULD execute destructive actions only after quorum confirmation. The control plane SHOULD replicate tenant objects only to authorized nodes. Compute SHOULD start only signed or approved images. Managed Kubernetes SHOULD run a separate control plane per tenant. Storage SHOULD make released blocks unreadable before reuse. The overlay SHOULD prevent traffic between VPCs of different tenants without explicit peering. Adoption SHOULD be bound to a key generated on the device; network boot alone does not establish trust. The KMS SHOULD support tenant-owned keys and crypto-shredding. MCP access SHOULD treat AI agents as actors in their own right and execute destructive actions only after confirmation outside the AI client. Mapping principle: requirement → component → evidence # Every requirement in the catalog is mapped to at least one Grundschutz++ requirement, one target object, one responsibility and one evidence type . The background is the rule from the requirements catalog: A requirement counts as implemented only when the platform delivers automatically generated evidence. The principles: Single source: target objects, mappings, implementation texts, suggested parameters and the protection requirements template live in versioned, machine-readable files. Tables in documents are generated from them, not the other way around. Pinned catalog: the Grundschutz++ catalog is recorded with version and checksum and shipped unchanged. A regular update run produces a diff (new or removed IDs, changed texts, security levels, categories) and flags affected mappings for review. Only after review is the new state adopted. s: DCP's 36 verifiable architecture guidelines, the CI checks and review checklist that go with them, and the "Security & Compliance" template that every architecture decision must contain.
x: Why guidelines? # The requirements catalog defines what the platform must fulfill, the BSI IT-Grundschutz modeling how this maps to Grundschutz++, the threat model what it must protect against, the cryptography concept with which mechanisms , and the security model describes the overall picture. What is still missing are rules that every single architecture decision must comply with – so that compliance follows from the design instead of being "tested in" after the fact. This corresponds to the guiding principle "compliance by design" from the Vision and to the Cyber Resilience Act's requirements for secure design. Key points # There are 36 verifiable architecture guidelines (CBD-01 to CBD-36) in nine groups. Each is a MUST rule with a source and at least one check type. There is no such thing as a guideline without a check. The checks are bundled into 20 named CI checks and a review checklist . Every future ADR or technical concept contains a "Security & Compliance" section following a fixed template. Without it, a document cannot be accepted. Order of precedence # Law – CRA, NIS2/BSIG, GDPR; not open to trade-offs. Conflict rules and requirements catalog (see Compliance requirements ). Guidelines CBD-01 to CBD-36 (this page). ADR or technical concept with the "Security & Compliance" section. Implementation and tests (CI checks). Evidence , release report, OSCAL export. The threat model feeds into guidelines and ADRs alike. An ADR may fall short of a guideline – but only with an entry in the deviation register stating rationale, compensating measures, approval and deadline. If an ADR contradicts a guideline without such an entry, it cannot be accepted. Guidelines change only through a new version; IDs are never reused. Check types # Code Meaning When PR automated check, blocks the merge every pull request N automated nightly check; a failure blocks the next release nightly R release gate per release REV review with checklist; security-critical paths with two reviewers per PR or ADR LAB check in the QEMU or hardware lab nightly or before completing a phase PT penetration test or external audit before the MVP, per major version DOC automated check of the concept documents every PR The guidelines # Principles and defaults # ID Guideline Check CBD-01 Secure by default. The shipped state is the most secure setting that can be run in a homelab without additional hardware: no default credentials, no interactive login, no active auto-adoption, strict crypto profile, all security functions on. Every relaxation is an audited API action. check of a fresh installation, REV CBD-02 Homelab fallback. No security function may be secure only with data center infrastructure; every such dependency has a documented secure fallback – for example key splitting instead of an HSM. REV, DOC CBD-03 Evidence is part of the function. A relevant function counts as implemented only when it delivers automatically generated evidence – retrievable via API, portal and MCP. PR CBD-04 Privacy by default. No telemetry or other outbound connection without opt-in; every outbound connection is configured and documented. N, LAB Identity, authorization, tenant isolation # ID Guideline Check CBD-05 No anonymous management function. Every API operation declares the permission it requires; exceptions are kept in a versioned list and return no sensitive data. PR, R CBD-06 Tenant ID in every authorization decision, at the target. Other tenants' objects yield "not found"; no other tenants' data in errors, lists, metrics or logs. Isolation is additionally enforced by technical means, not just by checking code. generated two-tenant tests per operation CBD-07 Trust never derives from network position or forwarding. The target verifies the original token itself; portal sessions are exchanged at the entry point for short-lived, audience-bound tokens. simulation CBD-08 Tokens carry identity, not permissions; short-lived, sender- and audience-bound, no pass-through. Long-lived secrets only hashed and with mandatory expiry. token tests CBD-09 Nodes are not principals for tenant operations; roles and placement follow the trust level. Eligibility is never based on self-reporting; the level drops immediately and rises only with fresh evidence. simulation, REV CBD-10 Privileged actions require step-up, a justification and – depending on the profile – the four-eyes principle; platform administration and the security role are separate. PR CBD-11 Operators do not see tenant content except via an approved access request. Every field has a data class; tenant metadata appears pseudonymized in operator views. The boundary is described openly to tenants. PR, isolation tests CBD-12 Isolation by technical means: no shared kernel between tenants, separate Kubernetes control planes, one VPC per project in its own VRF, inbound default deny, data keys per volume or bucket, no storage deduplication across tenants. isolation tests, LAB, PT AI agents and MCP # ID Guideline Check CBD-13 An agent is an actor in its own right with intersected permissions. Effective permissions = principal ∩ token scopes ∩ agent guardrails; default token is read-only; principal and actor are recorded separately in the audit log. PR, N CBD-14 Destructive MCP actions only with confirmation outside the client – on a platform page that displays the impact report itself and requires passkey presence. The confirmation token is bound to all parameters and single-use. confirmation tests CBD-15 Externally controlled data is data, not instructions. Free-form fields filled by tenants or devices are marked as untrusted, normalized and never rendered as HTML in the portal; tool descriptions are static and signed. PR How these rules apply concretely to AI services is described in AI platform . Logging, data protection, evidence # ID Guideline Check CBD-16 Every API action is audited – identically across all channels; auditing is part of the enforcement chain and cannot be switched off. generated test per mutating operation CBD-17 Audit log tamper-proof and anchored outside the cell: hash chain, signature, separate chains per tenant, external anchor; revocation lists must never fall back to an older state. tampering tests CBD-18 No secrets in logs, traces, error messages, images or repositories. Secrets only in types without output and with secure zeroization; images contain no secrets. secret scanner, canary test CBD-19 Data minimization, personal data marked: personal data fields are labeled; retention and pseudonymization configurable per data type. PR CBD-20 Evidence machine-readable, signed, identical across channels , with an OSCAL reference. PR, R Cryptography # ID Guideline Check CBD-21 Cryptography only via profiles. No algorithm hard-coded; every ciphertext and every signature carries algorithm, key ID and version; regions may tighten, never relax. lint CBD-22 No homegrown cryptography: established libraries with a single provider, kernel crypto, TPM; randomness only from the kernel. dependency check, test vectors CBD-23 BSI TR-02102 is authoritative; deviations only when registered and time-limited. handshake matrix per profile CBD-24 Quantum-safe confidentiality from the MVP: hybrid post-quantum key agreement on all of the project's own TLS endpoints; data at rest with AES-256. PR, N CBD-25 Encryption everywhere: control traffic only mTLS within the encrypted underlay, portal and API only HTTPS with HSTS, data at rest encrypted by default. lab check CBD-26 Keys are created where they are used and never leave that place; issuance via CSR, third-party processes with their own service identity, never with the node key. lint, simulation Architecture boundaries and supply chain # ID Guideline Check CBD-27 Third-party components only across process boundaries – never linked, but run as a separate process with its own user, minimal privileges and a sandbox (see Rust stack ). dependency check, REV CBD-28 Minimal, pinned, reviewed dependencies; SBOM and provenance per artifact; signed, reproducible builds (see Release bundle ). PR, R CBD-29 Least privilege: privileged operations in exactly one helper service; parsers at trust boundaries in processes without access to node keys, with size limits and fuzzing. fuzzing register CBD-30 A single enforcement point: authentication → authorization → validation → quota → audit → execution is one chain for API, portal, MCP and CLI (see API-first ). parity check Nodes, boot, control plane # ID Guideline Check CBD-31 Trust arises only through adoption, never through boot or network position. Adoption is bound to a key generated on the device; auto-adoption is off by default; critical roles are never assigned at adoption (see Boot and adoption ). simulation, LAB CBD-32 One-sided signals never trigger destructive actions. Fencing, revocation or deletion require a quorum; security decisions fail closed, running workloads remain stable (see Control plane ). simulation CBD-33 Deviations are objects, not comments – at manufacturer level in the register, at installation level as an API object, each with rationale, compensating measures, approval and deadline; both included in the compliance export. PR Deletion and recovery # ID Guideline Check CBD-34 Deletable by design. Every new data store – including caches, snapshots, backups, logs – is attached to the key hierarchy so that crypto-shredding takes effect; proofs of deletion and decommissioning in a signed format. integration test, REV CBD-35 Recoverability is practiced: encrypted platform backup, restore without a live platform, automated test restore with a log, emergency rotation per key class. nightly recovery drill Process # ID Guideline Check CBD-36 Threat model and standards references evolve along with the design. Every ADR that changes components, roles, trust boundaries or third-party components updates the threat model in the same change set; standards references carry their version. documentation check CI checks # The guidelines are backed by 20 named, automated checks. The most important groups: Area What is checked Parity and API schema same permissions and functions across all channels; mandatory declarations per operation (permission, effect, data class, markers for untrusted and personal data fields, step-up) Tenant isolation two-tenant tests per operation generated from the API description, analysis of the authorization policies Audit completeness of the audit entry per mutating operation Secrets scanner, deny rules, canary run, image scan Dependencies licenses, deny lists, sources, advisories, lockfiles Cryptography lint, handshake matrix per profile, share of hybrid key agreement, HSTS Release SBOM, signature, provenance, update metadata, rebuild Compliance mapping coverage, catalog pin, deviation register, OSCAL validation Defaults policy-as-code check of a fresh installation Simulation control plane invariants: node authorization, no destructive gossip signals, minimum levels, quarantine, no private key in the state Robustness fuzzing register with nightly run, rules for unsafe Documentation mandatory "Security & Compliance" section, existence of cited IDs Agents confirmation and step-up tests Data protection egress capture of an unconfigured installation Portal Content Security Policy without inline scripts Deletion, recovery crypto-shredding with no key remnants; test restore of a test cell The guidelines themselves are also maintained as structured data; a check ensures that every automatically checked guideline references an existing CI check. Review checklist # For every pull request with a security-relevant change: New or changed operation: are permission, effect, data class, step-up and confirmation requirement declared? Tenant scope: check at the target, no other tenants' data in errors, lists or metrics? New input across a trust boundary: sandbox process, limits, fuzzing target, marked as untrusted?
