s: Format, verification, import and distribution of the release bundle that brings a platform release into a cluster.
x: Purpose # A platform release – agent, OS base, extensions and boot artifacts under one common version – reaches a cluster by import only . There is no online fetch from inside the cluster; the operator uploads a bundle via the API, command line, MCP or portal. This way updates work in isolated (air-gapped) environments exactly as they do in connected ones, and the operator makes a deliberate decision about which release enters their region. The transport format is called cp.release-bundle/v1 . It is a single uncompressed tar archive with a fixed order . This order is the core of the design: The receiver checks signatures and release rules before the large artifacts arrive. An invalid bundle is rejected after a few kilobytes. Every artifact is hashed on receipt – streamed, without buffering the whole bundle. Compression is deliberately not used: the images are already compressed or are verity images, and compression would prevent the random access that resuming interrupted uploads requires. The signature chain itself is described in Release signing ; how an imported release is rolled out to the nodes is described in Rollout controller . Container format # The archive is POSIX ustar (512-byte blocks, two zero blocks at the end). The strict rules are meant to keep the parser small and its attack surface low: regular files only; directory entries are skipped, each name at most once, no links, no PAX or GNU long names, no paths containing .. or a leading / , sizes of 8 GiB and above in the base-256 field. # Entry Required Content 1 bundle.json yes format identifier and version (informational only; the manifest is authoritative) 2 metadata/<n>.root.json no root rotation chain, in ascending order of root version 3 metadata/timestamp.json yes signed role timestamp 4 metadata/snapshot.json yes signed role snapshot 5 metadata/targets.json yes signed role targets : all artifacts and the manifest with length, SHA-256 and SHA-512 6 targets/release/manifest.json yes release manifest cp.release/v1 , itself a signed target 7 targets/<target> yes¹ every further target from targets.json , in any order ¹ A target may be missing if the receiver already holds it content-addressed (see Resuming). Target names consist of segments of letters, digits and ._+- , separated by / , for example os/x86-64/uki.efi . The prefix boot/ marks boot artifacts for the network boot service (see Boot and adoption ). Because the format is deliberately simple, a bundle can also be created with standard tools ( tar --format=ustar ) in the order of the table; the project's release tool writes it as a stream. Release manifest cp.release/v1 # The manifest describes the release in functional terms. It is itself a target of the signed chain and is therefore protected against substitution, rollback and freezing. Example with placeholder values: json { "apiVersion": "cp.release/v1", "version": "1.4.2", "channel": "stable", "securityEpoch": 7, "minVersion": "1.3.0", "minAgentProtocol": 12, "artifacts": [ { "name": "usr", "arch": "x86-64", "target": "os/x86-64/usr.raw", "sha256": "…", "size": 287309824, "verityRootHash": "…" }, { "name": "uki", "arch": "x86-64", "target": "os/x86-64/uki.efi", "sha256": "…", "size": 61440000 } ], "sbom": { "cyclonedx": "sha256:…" }, "sources": { "bundle": "sha256:…" }, "provenance": { "slsa": "sha256:…" }, "notBefore": "2026-11-10T00:00:00Z", "expires": "2027-05-10T00:00:00Z" } Field Meaning version MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH for the entire platform release; PATCH contains only security and bug fixes channel stable , candidate (pre-release testing) or edge (development only) securityEpoch increases with security-relevant fixes; going back below the running epoch is forbidden minVersion minimum version for a direct update path minAgentProtocol minimum agent protocol level for version negotiation artifacts name, architecture, target name in the bundle, SHA-256, size, and the root hash for verity images sbom , sources , provenance references (by hash) to the SBOM, source code archive and SLSA provenance – also targets of the bundle notBefore , expires validity window; prevents nodes from being held on an old manifest indefinitely Unknown fields are rejected. The target field binds each artifact to exactly one signed target. Verification # Verification is identical for all delivery paths – import via the API, the agent during an update, and the installer. So there is no "more convenient" path with weaker rules. Signature chain against the trusted root anchor in the OS image: root rotation step by step if needed, then timestamp → snapshot → targets with signature, version reference, hash and expiry. The most recently trusted root version is recorded per region (protection against root rollback). Manifest is a signed target (length, SHA-256 and SHA-512 match). Release rules: format and version, known channel, notBefore ≤ now < expires , securityEpoch at least as high as the highest epoch currently running on nodes, and minVersion at most the lowest running version. Artifact list = signed targets: every artifact corresponds to exactly one target with the same length and the same hashes, and every target (except the manifest) to exactly one artifact. Every received artifact is checked against length, SHA-256 and SHA-512. Only then does it become visible in storage (temporary file, fsync , atomic rename). Errors are mapped to the usual API error classes (see API-first ): signature, format and hash errors as an invalid argument; epoch, minimum version or validity window as a failed precondition; the same version with different content as a conflict. A configurable size limit protects against oversized uploads. Import, resuming and deduplication # Import is an action on the region ( region:importArtifacts ). The bundle is transferred as a tar stream; for small bundles – for example via MCP – a JSON form with Base64 content is also available. Import is not a privileged action, because the signature chain decides what is accepted. With validateOnly , the server only verifies and additionally reports missingTargets , i.e. the targets it does not yet hold. The result of an import is created , unchanged , validated or incomplete . Resuming after an interruption relies on content addressing: fully received artifacts are kept. The command line and the portal therefore first send only the metadata and manifest as a dry run, and then a partial bundle containing only the missing targets. Importing the same release again is harmless ( unchanged ); identical artifacts in different releases are stored only once. Storage and distribution # Every holding node stores releases content-addressed: artifacts and metadata files as read-only blobs keyed by SHA-256, and per version a directory with the metadata, hard links to the artifacts and a local entry listing all targets and hashes. This structure matches what the network boot service expects – a release's boot artifacts are thus available for PXE and HTTP boot without copying. In addition, the boot service serves all targets of verified releases content-addressed. Holders are nodes with the role boot or control ; the target is two copies (or as many as there are candidates). Replication between holders runs over an internal, mutually authenticated TLS endpoint using node certificates. The receiver verifies the chain again – it does not trust the sender. Failure of a holder is detected by the cluster through the missing heartbeat; the next candidate fetches the release. The status of the Release resource lists the reachable complete copies. The rollout controller releases a target version only once the release is available and has enough holders. Nodes later fetch their update from these holders. Peer-to-peer distribution between arbitrary nodes is planned for a later stage. Build and signing (process) # Build and signing are separate, so that private release keys never come into contact with the build environment: Build: binaries and OS images are built per architecture; SBOM, source code archive and provenance are generated. The result is an unsigned plan containing the manifest (exact bytes) as well as the length, SHA-256 and SHA-512 of all targets. Sign offline: a separate signing environment receives only the plan, checks that the manifest and target list match, and signs the update metadata. The large artifacts do not leave the build environment; only public data (plan, signed metadata, root files) is exchanged. Assemble the bundle: metadata, manifest and artifacts are written as a stream in the fixed order. Verify: the finished bundle goes through the same verification as on import; in addition, it is checked that the trust anchor embedded in the image matches the root used. On validity: by default, a bundle's metadata is valid for as long as the manifest ( expires ), so that bundles transported offline remain importable. Protection against being frozen on an old state is provided by expires and securityEpoch . Separate roots are used for test and production; root rotation is described in Release signing .

s: Two signing paths for releases, the format of the update metadata following the TUF approach, the processes and the reproducibility of builds.
h: Update metadata following the TUF approach
x: Overview: two signing paths # DCP signs releases along two independent paths. They answer different questions for different verifiers. Path Purpose Keys Verifier Sigstore/cosign keyless public releases; evidence of "built by exactly this CI workflow" short-lived certificate from the workflow's OIDC identity, entry in the public transparency log; plus SLSA provenance people, packagers, operators before installation Offline keys ECDSA P-384 (TUF pattern) update chain of the nodes root and targets offline, snapshot and timestamp short-lived agent and installer on every node – offline , without network and without Sigstore The nodes trust only the update-chain root embedded in the OS image. Sigstore is an additional, public transparency layer, but not a runtime dependency: a cluster without internet access verifies updates just as strictly as a connected one. In a later phase, ML-DSA-87 will be added as a second, post-quantum signature per envelope (see Cryptography ). Update metadata following the TUF approach # The update chain follows the pattern of The Update Framework (TUF) with four roles. Each role has its own keys, its own thresholds and its own expiry times – a single compromised role is not enough to slip a manipulated update onto nodes. File Role Content Default expiry Keys root.json root all public keys, key IDs and threshold per role 365 days offline, k of n in production targets.json targets target name → length, SHA-256, SHA-512 90 days offline (release key) snapshot.json snapshot reference to targets.json (version, length, hashes) 30 days release infrastructure timestamp.json timestamp reference to snapshot.json 7 days release infrastructure, re-signed frequently <n>.root.json root previous/new root versions for the rotation chain – old and new root For release bundles transported offline, the metadata can be valid for as long as the release manifest (see Release bundle ). Envelope (DSSE) # Every metadata file is a DSSE envelope ( Dead Simple Signing Envelope ): a type, a Base64-encoded payload and a list of signatures with key ID. What is signed is the Pre-Authentication Encoding of type and payload. This removes the need for canonical JSON: exactly the signed bytes are verified, and only then are they parsed – rejecting unknown fields in the process. The key ID is the SHA-256 of the public point. json { "payloadType": "application/vnd.cloud-project.update-metadata+json", "payload": "<Base64 of the JSON payload>", "signatures": [ { "keyid": "<hex>", "sig": "<Base64>" } ] } Timestamps are strictly UTC in the format YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SSZ . By default, the version number of targets, snapshot and timestamp is derived from the commit time and is therefore monotonic. Verification on the node # Load the root (embedded or most recently trusted): it must sign itself with its threshold; its version must not be lower than the stored one. Process the root chain: each new root version must be exactly one higher and signed with the threshold of both the old and the new root. If the timestamp or snapshot keys change, their stored versions are reset (recovery after a fast-forward attack). Check root expiry only after the chain – so that even an expired anchor can still be rotated. timestamp: signature, version monotonicity, not expired. snapshot: length and hashes as stated in timestamp, signature, matching version, not expired. targets: length and hashes as stated in snapshot, signature, matching version, not expired. Artifact: length, SHA-256 and SHA-512 as stated in targets. Persist the versions , so that rollback protection also holds across restarts. Attack Defense Rollback to old metadata version monotonicity, persisted Freezing on an old state (freeze) expiry times, short-lived timestamp Mix-and-match of different states hash binding timestamp → snapshot → targets Endless data fixed size limit for metadata files Key compromise role separation, thresholds, root rotation Duplicate signatures only distinct keys count toward the threshold Deliberate simplifications compared to TUF 1.0: no delegated targets, no consistent snapshot , DSSE instead of canonical JSON, key ID over the point bytes. Interoperability with third-party TUF clients is not a goal; the format is versioned via spec_version . Processes # Development and CI # In development and in CI, signing uses an ephemeral one-time key that is deleted after the run. The tool refuses key directories inside the repository, so that no keys are accidentally checked in. Verification uses the same library as on the nodes. Public release # A version tag starts the release workflow: build per target platform without cache, checksum list, independent rebuild, cosign signatures and SLSA provenance. The result is a release draft . Offline ceremony on a machine without network, with keys on an encrypted storage medium or later on a hardware token or HSM: verify artifacts and Sigstore evidence (the certificate identity must be the project's release workflow), compare hashes with the rebuild, then sign the update metadata. The update metadata is attached to the release; the draft is approved under the four-eyes principle . The timestamp is re-signed regularly (at least every 7 days); automating this with an online key is an open item. Root rotation # A new root generation is signed with the new and the old root keys (each with its threshold). Bundles carry the rotation chain; nodes with an older anchor upgrade through it step by step, and the region updates the trusted root version. Bundles signed with old keys are rejected afterwards. Reproducibility # A dedicated rebuild step copies the working tree into two different temporary directories with different path lengths, builds independently in each (separate build directory, different clock time, same source time SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH ) and compares the SHA-256 of all artifacts – binaries and SBOMs. Only bit-identical results count as reproducible. During the offline ceremony, the results are additionally compared against the rebuild. SBOM # Every build generates an SBOM per component in CycloneDX 1.5 format and derives SPDX 2.3 from it – with a converter of the project's own, to avoid introducing an additional tool supply chain. The SBOM is reproducible as well: timestamps from the source time, a serial number derived deterministically from the normalized document, sorted components and dependencies. In addition, the binaries carry their dependency list embedded, so that installed nodes can also be checked against new advisories after the fact (see Vulnerability management ). Security and compliance # Integrity and rollback protection of updates, signed, reproducible builds with provenance and SBOM in two formats are fixed requirements of the project (see Security model ). The only cryptography provider is a vetted library (see Cryptography ). Fallback: without an HSM, offline keys are kept on encrypted storage media, with root keys k of n distributed among separate responsible persons. Without access to Sigstore, nodes keep verifying unchanged, since they use only the offline chain. Open: automation of the timestamp, key ceremony and choice of HSM, second signature with ML-DSA-87.

s: How DCP receives, assesses, fixes and publishes security reports – including deadlines, CRA reporting obligations, VEX and SBOM.
x: Principle # DCP handles security reports according to the principle of coordinated disclosure (Coordinated Vulnerability Disclosure, CVD): a vulnerability is reported confidentially, fixed under embargo and then published together with the fix. The basis is the European Cyber Resilience Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/2847, CRA), in particular Art. 13, 14 and 24 as well as Annex I Part II. The project regards itself as an open-source steward within the meaning of Art. 24, but runs its reporting process as if the manufacturer obligations under Art. 14 already applied . The final legal classification is still open. Roles # Role Responsibility PSIRT lead responsible for triage, embargo, advisory and CRA reporting; decides on deadlines Deputy same authority; round-the-clock availability on rotation (because of the 24-hour deadline) Component maintainers analysis and fix in the affected component Release managers security release, offline signing, update metadata (see Release signing ) Reporters external researchers, operators, upstream projects The four-eyes principle applies to: downgrading a severity, the VEX statement "not affected", extending a deadline, and publication. Reporting channels # Please do not use public issues, pull requests or discussions for security problems. Preferred: GitHub Private Vulnerability Reporting – in the project's repository, the "Security" tab → "Report a vulnerability". This creates a confidential draft GitHub Security Advisory with a private fork for the fix. E-mail: a security contact address with an OpenPGP key will be defined before the first release and will then also be published via /.well-known/security.txt . Helpful in a report are: the affected version or commit, the component (for example cp-agent , portal, OS image), the configuration, reproduction steps or a proof of concept, the expected impact, whether the vulnerability is already being exploited or is publicly known, and whether and how the reporter would like to be credited. Besides external reports, further sources feed into the same process: automated dependency checks (advisory databases for Rust and npm dependencies, daily and in CI), checking already published release binaries against new advisories using the embedded dependency list, our own findings from review, fuzzing and penetration tests (handled like external reports, just without communication with a reporter), notices from authorities and CSIRTs as well as catalogs of actively exploited vulnerabilities. Commitments and deadlines # Step Deadline Acknowledgment of receipt ≤ 3 business days Initial assessment (validity, severity) ≤ 7 calendar days Status updates to reporters at least every 14 days Fix (target) critical ≤ 14 days, high ≤ 30 days, medium ≤ 90 days, low with a regular release Publication (advisory, CVE) with the fix, at the latest after a 90-day embargo; extension only by mutual agreement Actively exploited vulnerability notification under CRA Art. 14 within 24 hours / 72 hours / 14 days In case of public exploitation or a leak during the embargo, publication is immediate, with a workaround if applicable. Triage # Acknowledge receipt , create a confidential draft advisory, start the embargo, record the reporter's preferences (credit). Validity and scope: reproduce, check for duplicates and known issues, determine the affected component. Determine affected versions using the SBOM of the respective release; for OS images using the image SBOM. Assessment: CVSS v4.0 including the threat metric Exploit Maturity , plus CVSS v3.1 for compatibility with common scanners. EPSS for third-party CVEs; from an exploitation probability of 0.1, or if listed in a catalog of actively exploited vulnerabilities, at least priority "high". Platform context: Is the vulnerability reachable from a tenant workload? Via network boot or discovery without authentication? Does it affect tenant isolation or key material? If so, it is rated higher (see Security model ). Set priority and deadline: Priority Criterion (guideline) Target for the fix P0 critical CVSS ≥ 9.0, actively exploited or tenant isolation broken ≤ 14 days, immediate mitigation if needed P1 high CVSS 7.0–8.9 or high exploitation probability ≤ 30 days P2 medium CVSS 4.0–6.9 ≤ 90 days P3 low CVSS < 4.0, build time only, not exploitable next regular release or VEX Decision "actively exploited?" : document it with evidence, source and time of awareness – if "yes", the CRA reporting process starts immediately. Fix and publication # The fix is developed in the advisory's private fork – no public pull request during the embargo – with a regression test and review by a second person. The CVE ID is requested via GitHub as the CNA; the advisory text names affected and fixed versions, the CVSS vector, workarounds and credits. A security release can be published separately from feature changes (PATCH version): build, rebuild, signatures and offline signing of the update metadata, followed by a staged rollout in the cluster (see Rollout controller ). Simultaneous publication: GitHub Security Advisory, machine-readable advisory in CSAF 2.0 format, updated VEX statements, release notes and notification of operators. Later, the portal will also show affected nodes. Vulnerabilities in third-party components are reported to the upstream maintainers (CRA Art. 13(6)); the project shares fixes and issues its own VEX statement for its products. CRA reporting obligations # The reporting obligations under Art. 14 apply to actively exploited vulnerabilities in the product and to severe incidents affecting the security of the product. Reports are submitted via ENISA's Single Reporting Platform to the CSIRT designated as coordinator – for Germany, the BSI – and simultaneously to ENISA. Deadline from awareness Actively exploited vulnerability Severe incident 24 hours early warning: product, affected member states if applicable early warning, including suspicion of a malicious cause 72 hours notification: nature of the exploitation, measures taken and recommended, sensitivity of the information notification: nature of the incident, initial assessment, mitigation measures 14 days after a fix is available final report: description, severity, information on the actor (as far as known), update or mitigation – 1 month after the 72-hour notification – final report on request interim reports interim reports In addition, affected users are informed (Art. 14(8)) – where possible in a structured, machine-readable form via CSAF and VEX. The process in brief: record the time of awareness in UTC → alert the PSIRT lead or deputy → send the early warning within 24 hours from a template and file the acknowledgment of receipt → notification after 72 hours with the current state of analysis → fix or mitigation → final report → follow-up including an update of the threat model. The deadlines also run on weekends and public holidays; that is why the deputy rule exists. A test report is planned before the first public release. Delineation: operators of an installation report operational incidents under NIS2 or data protection law themselves (shared responsibility). The project supports them with advisories, VEX and SBOM. VEX # VEX ( Vulnerability Exploitability eXchange ) describes in machine-readable form whether a product is actually affected by a known vulnerability. The project maintains VEX statements in OpenVEX format in the repository, with every change made via pull request and four-eyes review. Status: not_affected , affected , fixed , under_investigation . Mandatory information: not_affected only with a valid justification or impact statement, affected only with an action recommendation. A CI step checks this and produces normalized output that ships with the release. Effect in CI: findings from the dependency check are accepted only if a VEX statement "not affected" or "fixed" exists for exactly this vulnerability and exactly this package. Exceptions in the Rust dependency check require a justification and an expiry date and are additionally documented as VEX. Next steps: generate CSAF VEX from OpenVEX, take product identifiers from the SBOM, sign VEX in the release and reconcile it in the portal. SBOM # For every release and component there is an SBOM in CycloneDX 1.5 and SPDX 2.3 , generated reproducibly (see Release signing ). The binaries carry their dependency list embedded; advisory checks therefore also work directly on installed nodes. The portal's npm dependencies are covered by lockfile integrity, advisory checks and a license list. The OS image receives its own SBOM from the image pipeline (see OS image ); the release manifest references it by hash. Supported versions # The project is before its first release (version 0.x, API v1alpha1 ). Until then, security fixes are made on the development branch; 0.x pre-release versions are not maintained. From the first stable release on, a support period will be published – the goal under the CRA is at least five years of security updates, deliverable separately from feature updates. Scope and safe harbor # In scope is everything in the repository: agent and libraries, portal, MCP server, OS image and boot pipeline, as well as build and release tooling including signing and update metadata. Out of scope are vulnerabilities in third-party components unrelated to their use in the project, social engineering, physical attacks, denial of service through sheer volume against third-party infrastructure, and pure scanner findings without demonstrable impact. Anyone who conducts research in good faith and within the bounds of this policy – using only their own installations or test environments, not viewing, modifying or deleting third-party data, not impairing any service, and reporting confidentially – will not face legal action initiated or supported by the project. Open items # Security contact address with OpenPGP key and security.txt , staffing of the PSIRT, registration with the Single Reporting Platform and a test report, provision of the CSAF advisories, and the legal review of the CRA role.

s: Runbook for changing the portal address – what happens to the OIDC issuer, the WebAuthn RP ID and registered passkeys, and how access is preserved.
x: Background # A region's portal address is more than just a URL. It is at the same time: the OIDC issuer ( iss ) of all tokens the platform issues, and the basis of the WebAuthn RP ID – which is the hostname of the address. Under the WebAuthn standard, passkeys are bound firmly to the RP ID. Changing the hostname therefore has consequences for everyone who signs in with a passkey. This runbook describes how to carry out such a change in a planned way and what to do after an unplanned change. Background on identities, passkeys and emergency access can be found in Identity . What happens # Change Effect only the port ( https://cloud.example.org:8443 → https://cloud.example.org ) The RP ID stays the same; passkeys remain valid. The issuer changes: access tokens from the previous issuer remain valid until they expire (10 minutes), and a refresh yields tokens with the new issuer. Command-line and MCP clients must enter the new endpoint. the hostname ( cloud.example.org → portal.example.org ) New RP ID – all registered passkeys become unusable. The browser does not offer them for the new domain, and the server rejects assertions with a foreign RP ID hash. Without countermeasures, nobody can sign in with a passkey anymore. Losing the passkeys is unavoidable by design – it is precisely the phishing protection that WebAuthn provides. The runbook ensures that the change nevertheless succeeds in a controlled way and without locking anyone out. Planned hostname change # Prepare (still under the old address): prepare an admin invitation for every person with a passkey – do not create them yet, just record the list of affected people. Existing invitations and sessions can be listed via the command line or the portal. Ensure emergency access: on a control node, locally and as administrator, enable the time-limited emergency access, for example for one hour. It can only be activated locally and is fully audited. This keeps the command line operational with an emergency token in case the switchover runs into problems. Switch DNS and address: create the DNS record for the new name (when using the platform DNS role, via a dedicated zone, see DNS ) and then set the portal address to https://portal.example.org . The portal certificate is reissued; the shared issuer is picked up on all identity nodes within a few seconds via the replicated control plane (see Control plane ). Create new invitations: use the emergency access to create new admin invitations. The invitation links already contain the new address. The recipients redeem them in the browser on the new domain and register a new passkey in the process. End emergency access: after the first successful passkey sign-in, the emergency token is deactivated automatically; in addition, explicitly switch off the emergency access. Clean up: revoke old sessions (command line or portal, "Sessions" section). Old passkey entries remain in place without effect until they are cleaned up. Update clients: command-line users enter the new endpoint in their configuration and sign in again; the same applies to MCP clients. Unplanned change # If the hostname has already been changed and the passkeys are therefore invalid, the preparation step is dropped. Step 2 (emergency access locally on the node) followed by steps 4 to 7 is sufficient. Without administrative access to a control node, the only remaining option is the break-glass procedure from the identity concept (see Identity ). Checks after the change # The OIDC discovery under the new address ( https://portal.example.org/.well-known/openid-configuration ) lists the new address as issuer . For each node, the agent log shows an event about the changed issuer and the newly loaded portal certificate. The audit log contains the reactivation of emergency access, the invitations created and the first sign-in under the new address. Notes # A port-only change is uncritical and only requires updating the clients. Choose the hostname deliberately during setup: the portal address is mandatory when initializing a region and must be a DNS name (see OS image ). Emergency access is a deliberately narrow tool: local, time-limited, audited and switched off automatically after the first regular sign-in (see Security model ).

s: Overview of all concepts and processes
How DCP is built – an agent on every node, a control plane with Raft and gossip, cells and regions, networking, the OS image and the update chain.
x: Layered overview # DCP has no central controller. Every node runs the same agent, cp-agent , which serves the API, the portal and MCP, forwards requests to the responsible place and enforces the desired state of its node. The desired state is held in a Raft group per cell ; membership and reachability spread via gossip . Underneath sits the immutable operating system cpOS . Layer model. Restarting the agent does not stop any workloads, because external components run as separate systemd units. Key principles: Two levels of truth. Raft holds the desired state, assignments and leases. Gossip carries membership, reachability and short-lived metadata – and never on its own triggers a destructive action. Static stability. If the control plane fails, all workloads keep running; nodes continue with the last known desired state. Reconcilers are level-triggered, idempotent and safeguarded. Cell controllers run as shards with leases; every write carries an epoch token, and stale writers are rejected. Parsers at trust boundaries (network boot, DNS, input from devices) run in their own sandboxed processes without access to the node key. Details: Control plane architecture · Rust stack . Cells and regions # A cell is the unit of consensus and fault isolation (guideline value: up to about 1,000 nodes). Several cells form a region ; a small region Raft group holds region-wide data. With only one cell, the two groups coincide. Requests are routed to the right cell using the resource's URN and a versioned shard map. Region with two cells. "L" marks the Raft leader. The failure of a cell affects only that cell. Nodes Control group Cells Notes 2 2 + witness 1 Witness (e.g. a small Raspberry Pi) mandatory for quorum 3–20 3 1 Standard homelab 20 – approx. 1,000 5 1 Gossip for membership, Raft only for state > approx. 1,000 5 per cell n Region level coordinates cells multiple sites per region n Federation with global identity (later phase) The control group is formed automatically and grows along with the cluster: one node → two data nodes plus a witness → three → five voters. New members start as learners and are only promoted once they have caught up; there is only ever one membership change at a time. Two nodes with a witness # Two nodes on their own cannot decide which one may keep working during a network partition. A witness – a lightweight voter without user data that never becomes leader itself – provides the third vote. If one data node fails, the other continues working with the witness. If only one node is left, the remaining operation is read-only ; writing without quorum is possible only through a logged break-glass procedure, never automatically. Two nodes plus a witness form a quorum of three votes. Network # The platform always separates networks cryptographically and, where the infrastructure allows it, additionally physically via VLANs or routed segments. Overlay packets leave a node only encrypted inside the WireGuard underlay. Details: Network architecture · Platform DNS . Boot and trust chain # Every boot starts from signed specifications. The chain is implemented differently on UEFI systems and on the Raspberry Pi, but follows the same principle. Boot and trust chain (UEFI). The Raspberry Pi uses its native bootloader with its own A/B mechanism. / is an ephemeral tmpfs, and /etc is generated from the signed specifications on every boot. Persistence exists only in the encrypted state partition. Role-specific runtimes (hypervisor, storage, Kubernetes) are added as signed system extensions. Details: OS image · Boot and adoption · Security model . Release and update chain # Release and update chain. The agent, the installer and the import verify a bundle by the same rules. Details: Rollout controller · Release bundle · Release signing . Technology decisions # Area Decision Language Rust (Edition 2024), unsafe forbidden in principle, exceptions only when registered Runtime tokio, axum (REST, SSE, MCP), tonic/gRPC internally with mTLS Consensus / membership openraft per cell, SWIM gossip (foca) Local storage redb (embedded) Authorization dedicated relationship store + Cedar policies Virtualization Cloud Hypervisor/KVM, MicroVMs for containers Object storage Garage behind a dedicated S3 front end OS image mkosi from Debian 13 packages, systemd building blocks (UKI, repart, sysupdate, sysext) Portal Single-page app with Svelte 5 and Vite, types and forms generated from the API schema Architectures amd64 and arm64 (incl. Raspberry Pi 4/5), cross-compilation Rationale: ADR Rust stack · ADR portal technology .

s: How to contribute to DCP, which licenses cover code and documentation, and how to report vulnerabilities.
x: Contributing # "Das Cloud Projekt" (DCP) is set up as a community project. The source code repository will be opened as soon as the license files, security policy and REUSE compliance are complete. Until then, we welcome feedback on concepts and architecture. Especially welcome are: Feedback on the concepts in the documentation – assumptions, gaps, better alternatives. Operational experience from homelabs, edge sites and data centers: hardware, network topologies, requirements from compliance audits. Tests on unusual hardware (ARM boards, older notebooks, servers with and without BMC), as soon as pre-release versions are available. Code in Rust for the agent, roles and tools, TypeScript for the portal, documentation and translations. Rules for contributions # DCO instead of CLA: contributions are made under the Developer Certificate of Origin 1.1 . Every commit carries a Signed-off-by: line ( git commit -s ). There is no transfer of rights to a company. Quality before speed: formatting, lints without warnings, tests, license and dependency checks, a security audit of the dependencies, SBOM and MSRV check run in CI and must be green. No unsafe without a justified entry in a dedicated register; new dependencies only centrally in the workspace and after checking license, maintenance status and process boundaries. Every file carries SPDX license information (REUSE-compliant). Security-critical paths – PKI, consensus, authorization, boot and discovery, update – require two reviews. New features in all three access paths: whatever works via the API must also work in the portal and via MCP; the parity check in CI enforces this. Architecture decisions as ADRs with the mandatory section "Security & Compliance" (see Compliance by design ). sh # typical workflow for contributors (once the repository is opened) cargo xtask setup # install tools in pinned versions cargo xtask ci # run all checks locally git commit -s -m "Short description" License # The license decision is justified in the ADR License and governance (accepted 2026-11-12). Component License Core: agent, control plane, services, portal, MCP server, image build tools GNU AGPL-3.0-or-later SDKs, client libraries, CLI, API specifications, MCP schemas Apache-2.0 OR MIT Documentation, concepts, diagrams (including this website) CC BY 4.0 Code examples and configuration templates MIT-0 Logos and product name not freely licensed, trademark policy The AGPL ensures that improvements to the platform benefit the community even when modified versions are offered as a service over the network. Clients and SDKs are under permissive licenses so that they can be embedded in any software. The license is decided, but is subject to a final legal review before the first publication. Reporting a vulnerability # Please do not use public issues, pull requests or discussions for security problems. Preferred: GitHub Private Vulnerability Reporting in the project repository ("Security" tab → "Report a vulnerability"). Alternatively by e-mail: the address, together with an OpenPGP key, will be defined before the first public release and also published at /.well-known/security.txt . Step Deadline Acknowledgment of receipt ≤ 3 business days Initial assessment (CVSS v4.0) ≤ 7 calendar days Status updates to reporters at least every 14 days Fix (target) critical ≤ 14 days, high ≤ 30 days, medium ≤ 90 days Publication with the fix, at the latest after a 90-day embargo Actively exploited vulnerabilities are reported under Art. 14 of the Cyber Resilience Act. The full process is described under Vulnerability management . About this website # This site is statically generated – without cookies, tracking, external fonts or third-party scripts. Search runs entirely in the browser. The content consists of edited versions of the project documents and is licensed under CC BY 4.0. The site is available in German and English; where the two differ, the German version prevails.

s: Which services, roles and platform capabilities DCP provides – from the node lifecycle through networking, storage and identity to AI inference.
x: Services like a hyperscaler # The platform offers core services modeled on the well-known public clouds. All services are resources of the same API and can therefore be used equally through the portal, the API and MCP. Category Service Roughly equivalent to Compute Virtual machines (Cloud Hypervisor/KVM) AWS EC2 · Azure VMs · Compute Engine Compute Container Instances (MicroVM-isolated) Fargate · Azure Container Instances · Cloud Run Compute Managed Kubernetes EKS · AKS · GKE Storage Block volumes EBS · Managed Disks · Persistent Disk Storage Object storage (S3-compatible) S3 · Blob Storage · Cloud Storage Storage File storage (NFS) EFS · Azure Files · Filestore Network VPCs, subnets, security groups, load balancers, floating IPs VPC · VNet · VPC Network Platform DNS with DNSSEC Route 53 · Azure DNS · Cloud DNS Identity Tenants, projects, users, roles, service accounts, API keys IAM · Entra ID · Cloud IAM Platform Registry, key management (KMS), monitoring, audit log ECR · Key Vault · CloudWatch · CloudTrail AI Model catalog, inference endpoints, AI gateway, vector search Bedrock · Azure AI Foundry · Vertex AI Further services – databases, secrets, queues, serverless functions, GPU/NPU pools – will follow in later phases. A detailed comparison with AWS, Azure and Google Cloud is available in the hyperscaler feature analysis . Three equivalent access paths # Every feature is available through the REST API (OpenAPI) , the web portal and MCP (Model Context Protocol, for AI assistants and agents) – at every level: platform, tenant, project, resource. The portal and the MCP tools are derived from the same API schema; a CI check prevents any access path from gaining features the others lack. In addition there is the command-line tool cpctl . Details: API-first principle . yaml # Example resource (simplified) apiVersion: compute.cloud-project.io/v1 kind: VirtualMachine metadata: name: web-01 parent: cp:global:tenant/acme/project/shop labels: { env: prod } spec: # desired state machineType: small-2c-4g arch: any # arm64 | x86_64 | any image: cp:global:image/debian-13 network: { vpc: default, subnet: web } status: # actual state, written only by the system phase: Running Roles # Every node runs the agent cp-agent . It takes on additional tasks through roles , which are assigned manually, by rule (for example "all nodes with at least two disks → storage-block ") or on the scheduler's recommendation. Role Task agent implicit on every node: lifecycle, local API, portal and MCP, forwarding control control group (Raft) of a cell witness quorum vote only, e.g. on a small Raspberry Pi boot network boot service: proxyDHCP, TFTP/HTTP boot, image cache dns platform DNS: authoritative zones, DNSSEC, virtual IPs identity OIDC/OAuth authorization server, users, tenants, federation kms key management, tenant keys network-gateway north-south traffic, NAT, load balancers, floating IPs compute-vm virtual machines compute-container Container Instances in MicroVMs kubernetes Managed Kubernetes for tenants storage-block block volumes storage-object S3-compatible object storage observability metrics, logs, traces Node lifecycle # A node goes through a clearly defined lifecycle. Unknown hardware never automatically gets access to tenant data – only adoption assigns it an identity. Node lifecycle (simplified). Quarantine can be reached from any adopted state; returning requires fresh attestation and human approval. Discover: A new node boots over the network (PXE/HTTP boot, Raspberry Pi network boot) or from a USB stick into an in-memory discovery system. It writes nothing to disks and reports a hardware profile. Adopt: Approval via portal, API or MCP – protected by a confirmation code and, at higher expansion stages, additionally by TPM attestation. The node's private key never leaves the node. Provision: Installation of the signed OS image (or diskless operation), issuance of the node certificate, admission to the underlay network and gossip. Operate: Assign roles, maintenance with drain, self-healing on faults. Retire: Verifiable erasure, revocation of the certificate, rotation of the gossip keys – with proof of erasure for compliance. More: Boot and adoption . Updates and releases # Immutable OS image (cpOS): /usr is read-only and protected by dm-verity, / is ephemeral, state lives in an encrypted partition. A/B updates with automatic rollback: The update is written to the inactive slot. The new version only takes effect once a health gate reports green after the reboot; otherwise the node falls back to the old slot on its own after a few attempts. Signed release bundles: Images, extensions and the agent are delivered as a bundle with a manifest, checksums, SBOM and signatures; update metadata follows the principles of TUF (The Update Framework) with offline root keys. Rollout controller: Updates roll out in waves with a canary stage, maintenance windows and maxUnavailable . At most one voter per cell is updated at a time, the leader last. If a gate fails, the rollout stops. More: OS image · Rollout · Release bundle · Release signing . Platform DNS # The dns role (service cp-dnsd ) answers authoritatively for the names of the platform and the tenants, signs zones with DNSSEC , assigns virtual IP addresses (VIPs) for platform services such as the portal and the API, and protects itself against abuse with rate limiting. Within tenant networks, every host answers DNS, DHCP and metadata locally – with no central service in the data path. More: Platform DNS . Identity and tenants # Hierarchy platform → tenant → project → resource , optionally with folders inside a tenant. A dedicated, lean OIDC/OAuth 2.1 authorization server with passkeys first and federation with existing identity providers (OIDC/SAML). Short-lived, sender-constrained tokens that are verified locally on every node. Authorization via a Zanzibar-style relationship store plus Cedar policies for conditions and guardrails. Strict separation between operator and tenant content: operators see metadata; content only through a justified, time-limited and logged access request. AI agents are a separate actor type; they act with the intersection of user permissions, token scope and agent guardrails. Tenant deletion with crypto-shredding and a signed proof of deletion. More: Tenants, identity and permissions . Storage # Block volumes over a dedicated Rust data path: local (dm-thin + dm-crypt) and replicated (two to three copies) – the same path from 2 to thousands of nodes. Metadata in the cell's existing Raft group; user data never goes through consensus. Tenant encryption on the compute node: storage nodes only see ciphertext. Object storage , S3-compatible, behind a dedicated S3 front end with permission checks and quotas. File storage via NFS on replicated volumes, in the network of the respective VPC. Placement across failure domains; a maturity gate before replicated volumes are used for tenant data. More: Storage concept . Network # Underlay: one WireGuard interface per node, IPv6-only inside; peers come exclusively from the replicated state. Additionally, a pre-shared key from a post-quantum scheme. Tenant overlay cp-vnet : its own control logic in the agent, Linux kernel data path (VRF per VPC, VXLAN inside the WireGuard tunnel, nftables) – no second consensus database. Security groups are stateful, with inbound traffic blocked by default. North-south traffic via the network-gateway role: NAT, floating IPs, L4 load balancers; advertised via Layer 2 in a homelab and via BGP in a data center. Three expansion stages: flat (a single LAN), vlan , routed (L3 to the host). More: Network architecture . Security and compliance # Chain of trust from Secure Boot with the installation's own keys through Measured Boot and TPM-bound disk encryption to mTLS between all services. Node identity with short-lived certificates from an internal PKI, trust levels T0–T4, remote attestation. Cryptography according to BSI TR-02102 , crypto agility and a roadmap for post-quantum schemes. Complete audit trail of every change, break-glass procedure with logging. Compliance by design: 36 architecture guidelines, a requirements catalog drawn from ISO 27001, BSI IT-Grundschutz, BSI C5, GDPR, NIS2 and the Cyber Resilience Act; evidence becomes exportable. Supply chain: reproducible builds, an SBOM per artifact, signed releases, VEX for vulnerability assessments. More: Security model · Cryptography · Compliance by design . AI-native platform # A dedicated API group for models, model versions, inference endpoints, AI gateways, budgets, guardrails, vector indexes and knowledge bases. Inference engines (llama.cpp first, then vLLM) run as signed containers behind a unified adapter; dedicated endpoints run in MicroVMs with a passed-through accelerator. Two operating models: dedicated per tenant or shared/serverless with per-token billing – without a cross-tenant cache. Accelerators (GPU, NPU) as a scheduler resource, scale-to-zero with a local model cache, models as signed OCI artifacts with a cache per cell. The platform itself can be controlled via MCP ; tenants' agents use platform tools with restricted permissions. AI compliance as a cross-cutting concern: model cards, provenance, labeling, logging under the EU AI Act, mapping to BSI AIC4. More: AI-native platform .

s: Das Cloud Projekt (DCP) – an open-source, decentralized, multi-tenant cloud platform written in Rust. From a two-node homelab to a data center with thousands of nodes.
x: Open Source · Rust · AGPL-3.0 · Alpha Your cloud. On your hardware. Das Cloud Projekt (DCP) turns Raspberry Pis, laptops, mini PCs and rack servers into a cloud with the core services of a hyperscaler – VMs, containers, Kubernetes, storage, networks, identity and AI. From a two-node homelab to a data center with thousands of nodes, with no central controller. See what DCP does Read the docs Plug in node appears approve assign a role done 2 – 10,000+ nodes per installation, in cells and regions 3 interfaces API, web portal and MCP – same feature set ARM64 + x86_64 mixed from day one 0 controllers no central control node – Raft per cell, gossip Principles Hyperscaler comfort, without the hyperscaler. Public clouds hand out machines, storage and networks at the click of a button. If you want to keep control of your data, costs and dependencies, today you have to assemble that comfort from many separate products. DCP bundles it into one platform that runs on the very hardware it manages. Decentralized No central controller. State via Raft per cell, membership via gossip. If the control plane fails, workloads keep running. API-first, three interfaces Every function at every level via API, portal and MCP – including initial setup and adoption. CI checks that they stay equivalent. Zero-touch after the cable No screen, no keyboard, no SSH. The only deliberate step is approving (adopting) a new node. Scales both ways Two nodes are a fully supported mode of operation. Grow to thousands of nodes through cells and regions – without reinstalling. Immutable nodes Purpose-built image OS cpOS with dm-verity, A/B updates, Secure Boot and TPM-bound encryption. Secure & Compliant by Design mTLS everywhere, tenant isolation at every layer, a complete audit trail, evidence for ISO 27001 and BSI IT-Grundschutz. Open source throughout Open-source dependencies only, own components in Rust, signed releases with an SBOM. Integrate what works No homegrown hypervisor, no file system from scratch: DCP builds the control, the automation and the unified interface. How it works From cable to cloud service in four steps. New hardware never gets access to data automatically. Only approval grants it an identity – after that, everything runs on its own. Plug it in The node boots over the network (PXE/HTTP, Raspberry Pi network boot) or from a USB stick into an in-memory discovery system. The node is discovered It reports its hardware profile, writes nothing to disk and waits in quarantine – with a confirmation code. Approve & assign roles Approve via portal, API or MCP. Then assign roles manually, by rule or as suggested by the scheduler – control plane, VMs or storage, for example. Use the services VMs, containers, managed Kubernetes, block and object storage, virtual networks, DNS and AI inference – for multiple tenants. Comparison Like AWS, Azure or Google Cloud – but yours. The services are modeled on the well-known public clouds. The difference is where they run and who owns them. Public cloud hyperscaler runs in the provider's data center, under the provider's jurisdiction the provider sets prices and the billing model proprietary interfaces make switching costly a large service catalog via click and API DCP yours runs on your own hardware – from Raspberry Pi to rack, ARM and x86 mixed data, keys and audit log stay with the operator open source (AGPL), open interfaces: OpenAPI, MCP, S3-compatible core services via portal, API and MCP – more follow phase by phase DCP services and their hyperscaler counterparts DCP service Roughly equivalent to Virtual machines AWS EC2 · Azure VMs · Compute Engine Container Instances Fargate · Azure Container Instances · Cloud Run Managed Kubernetes EKS · AKS · GKE Block and object storage EBS · S3 / Managed Disks · Blob Storage / Persistent Disk · Cloud Storage VPCs, Load Balancer, DNS VPC · Route 53 / VNet · Azure DNS / VPC · Cloud DNS Tenants, roles, keys IAM · KMS / Entra ID · Key Vault / Cloud IAM AI inference, AI gateway Bedrock · Azure AI Foundry · Vertex AI Details and phases: Features · Hyperscaler feature analysis . Security & sovereignty Trust that starts in the hardware. Every node boots only signed software, binds its keys to the TPM and talks to other nodes exclusively over mutually authenticated TLS. Every change lands in the audit log. Secure Boot with the installation's own keys, measured boot TPM 2.0 -bound disk encryption, remote attestation Signed updates : release bundles with an SBOM, A/B updates with automatic fallback mTLS everywhere , short-lived certificates, cryptography per BSI TR-02102 Compliance by design : requirements from ISO/IEC 27001 and BSI IT-Grundschutz, exportable evidence ISO/IEC 27001 BSI IT-Grundschutz BSI C5 NIS2 CRA GDPR DCP provides building blocks and evidence for the operator's certification – the platform itself is not certified. s: Where DCP stands, in which order features are being built and how the MVP is measured.
x: Current status # Before the first release. Version 0.x, all API groups in v1alpha1 . Not yet suitable for production use. "Das Cloud Projekt" (DCP) is an alpha name. Completed: architecture and concepts – milestone "Architecture in place" on 2026-11-12. License decision (AGPL-3.0-or-later for the core) on 2026-11-12, decisions on the storage concept on 2026-11-14. In progress – Phase 1 "Foundation": agent and control plane (Raft per cell, gossip, witness), resource API with REST, MCP and command line, portal, internal PKI, identity service, network boot and adoption, installer, OS image cpOS for amd64 and arm64 with A/B updates, signed release bundles, rollout controller and platform DNS. Planned: the further phases below – in this order, without fixed dates. Phases # The numbering follows the role catalog of the vision concept; listed are the phases to which roles and services are assigned there. Phase Focus Roles and services 1 Foundation agent, control group ( control ), witness ( witness ), API/portal/MCP, security foundations 3 Boot and adoption network boot service ( boot ), discovery quarantine, installation, updates 4 Identity and tenants role identity , passkeys, federation, permission model, quotas 5 Network tenant overlay, security groups, network-gateway with NAT, floating IPs, load balancers 6 Compute virtual machines, container instances, managed Kubernetes 7 Storage block volumes, S3-compatible object storage 8 Observability metrics, logs, traces, role observability 9 Advanced services databases, secrets, DNS service for tenants, queues, serverless, file storage, GPU/NPU, OpenTofu provider, AI inference 10 Federation multiple regions and sites, global identity and API After the MVP come further stages such as hardware attestation as a prerequisite for permanent auto-adopt rules, replicated block volumes once they pass a maturity gate, a topology model for racks, and erasure coding for object and archive classes. After the MVP, the API groups move from v1alpha1 via v1beta1 to v1 . Quality gates # Phase 1 gate: fault tolerance (two nodes plus witness, no single point of failure from three nodes up) is demonstrated both in a deterministic simulation with 10,000 random seeds without invariant violations and on real hardware . Before every phase gate: tests on real hardware (Raspberry Pi, notebooks, servers). Before every minor release: Jepsen-style consistency checks. Before tenant data on replicated volumes: maturity gate with simulation, fault injection, long-running tests, recovery test and external review. Success criteria for the MVP # # Criterion E1 First node via USB stick; setup via portal, API or MCP – at most 15 minutes to the portal E2 New node via cable to the "waiting" state in at most 5 minutes (Raspberry Pi 4/5, x86 notebook, server) E3 Two nodes plus witness survive the failure of one node E4 Mixed cluster of ARM64 and x86_64 with matching placement E5 Two tenants fully isolated (network, compute, storage, keys); penetration test without critical findings E6 A tenant creates a VM, container instance, Kubernetes cluster, volume and bucket on their own – via all three access paths E7 Parity check 100% fulfilled – goal: no exceptions for mutating operations E8 No single point of failure from three nodes up: boot, API, portal and MCP survive a node failure E9 Evidence exportable (control matrix for BSI C5, ISO 27001, BSI IT-Grundschutz) Non-goals # DCP builds no hypervisor of its own , no distributed file system from scratch , and does not use Kubernetes as the foundation of the platform. Proven open-source components are integrated behind clear process boundaries. More on this in Vision, terminology and scope .
